“Reentry” Is Vital Every Day of Your Relationship

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love.
  • Every time you and your partner say “goodbye”—whether for the day or until your next hangout—you’re not exactly “exiting” the relationship.
  • In a recent CNBC Make It article, psychologist Mark Travers notes, “‘Reentry moments’ are the first minute or two when a couple comes back together after time apart.” And what you do with these moments can make all the difference when it comes to how you and your partner connect in your relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Every time you and your partner say “goodbye”—whether for the day or until your next hangout—you’re not exactly “exiting” the relationship. But, according to sex and relationship experts, you might still have to actively make a “reentry” when you come back together. In fact, it may be something you have to do every single day.

In a recent CNBC Make It article, psychologist Mark Travers notes, “‘Reentry moments’ are the first minute or two when a couple comes back together after time apart.” And what you do with these moments can make all the difference when it comes to how you and your partner connect in your relationship.

When we’re deep in a relationship—whether because you’re a few years in or live together—we sometimes go into autopilot when we see each other again. We might get home after a long day of work and just continue with our evening routine while maneuvering around our partners, rather than with them. And while it’s totally okay to decompress after the day by yourself or even spend some evenings just doing our own thing, it’s still notable to make a conscious effort to connect with our partners.

It has been revealed that “Oftentimes, we are wearing so much protective armor to navigate the outside world and we don't even realize it,” Anastacia Sams, LMFT tells Cosmopolitan. “There is a certain way that we need to show up with our jobs, our friends, or in our other responsibilities, that we forget to lay our armor down and connect with our partner, human to human.”.

In a recent development, laTrease Nwosu, LPC explains that everyday reentry can look like giving each other a meaningful hug (one that lasts longer than 30 seconds), sharing a kiss, or—most effectively—asking them how their day was. It can look like just being curious about each other.

Reentry looks different for every couple depending on their core values and relationship goals. Sams explains that for couples that value good conversation, a 30-minute debrief about your day or something you learned is a great way to connect. For others, something as simple as an acknowledgement—“I miss you,” or “I’m looking forward to reconnecting later”—can make a partner feel secure and attended to.

“Small moments that show your consideration of one another add up, and reentry is the best time to do this,” Sams says.

In a recent development, if you and your partner already initiative date nights and have uninterrupted quality time together, you might think that “reentry” isn’t going to make much of a difference. But a relationship is a continuous conversation. And sure, you might have a romantic date night once a month, but they shouldn’t feel like the only time you really feel close to your partner. “Reentry” can help maintain the connection every day of the relationship.

“When couples consistently skip these moments, it creates feelings of disconnection that lead to resentment,” Sams warns. “This is when couples start to feel they are just passing by each other throughout the day, or starting to feel like they are more roommates than romantic partners.”.

Industry observers note that she explains that over time, skipping these moments wear at the emotional safety of the relationship. Your partner may feel less inclined to share details about their life or take part in other forms of intimacy if this baseline of connection isn’t achieved.

In a recent development, but the good thing is that “reentry” isn’t the responsibility of one person in the relationship—both partners can work to initiate these moments so that it doesn’t always feel like only one person is trying to reconnect. Sams explains that “reentry” needs to be reciprocal in the sense that their needs to be mutual care, mutual respect, and mutual consideration between partners—but you don’t have to literally take turns checking in on each other.

“Either partner can initiate these moments of reconnection, and it is important for both partners to prioritize the intentionality of these moments without turning it into something that's transactional,” Sams says.

It has been revealed that there are going to be days when you want to be alone, are having an argument with your partner, or are simply too overwhelmed to think about anything but your to-do list. Even in these times, I’d challenge you to keep “reentry” consistent. It doesn’t always have to be something that doesn’t honor your feelings, but being an attentive partner even when you’re tempted not to goes a very long way in relationships. It creates mutual respect and will encourage your partner to lead with consideration as well. No matter what’s going on in your life or as hectic as simply existing gets, remember that you chose to partner with this person for a reason. And by making an effort to “reenter” the relationship after time apart will do wonders for your connection.

Latest Update: Robert Pattinson Might Be the Most Fashion-Forward Bond Yet

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (444 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, from Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr.
  • Daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops.
  • Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a newly introduced Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear.

According to recent reports, from Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr. No to Daniel Craig’s thigh-bearing trunks in Casino Royale, each man who has played James Bond has brought a fresh aesthetic sensibility to the role. For Connery, this meant soft-shouldered Savile Row tailoring, polo shirts, and knit ties to suit the era of Ivy Style, while Roger Moore’s wardrobe of safari jackets and nylon ski suits embodied the sporty hedonism of the 1970s. In the 21st century, Daniel Craig’s Bond was built around a timely blend of Brioni, Tom Ford, and stalwart British brands that complemented the contemporary #menswear scene. Today’s news that Robert Pattinson—a longtime Dior ambassador and one of the most consistently thrilling dressers in Hollywood—has been cast as 007 suggests Bond’s most fashionable era may be yet to come.

Daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops. Pattinson, meanwhile, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for a decade, during which he’s established his impeccable taste and a willingness to take massive swings with his outfits—not to mention a reputation for wearing the absolute heck out of a gray suit. Now, with fellow Brit Jonathan Anderson (who cast Craig in Loewe’s quirked-up fall 2024 campaign and posted this heartwarming pic today) running the show at Dior, the stage is set for a Bond with a taste for capital-F fashion.

Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a newly introduced Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear. Pierce Brosnan’s era had structured Brioni suits and made the Omega Seamaster a star, while Daniel Craig helped cement Tom Ford’s tailoring as a red-carpet staple and juiced sales of N.Peal ribbed Army sweaters and Drake’s suede chukkas. As GQ’s Cam Wolf noted in a 2018 article about Skyfall, Daniel Craig’s Barbour jacket, sweater, jeans, and brogue boots from that film—a classic but fairly unremarkable outfit—became the aspirational template for untold numbers of men on r/malefashionadvice. A few years later, when Craig wore a Rag & Bone slim-fit henley in No Time to Die, the brand sold out of the unassuming undershirt in a matter of days.

It’s been five years since No Time to Die’s release, and it will likely be at least a couple more before Pattinson’s first outing as 007 hits screens. That’s a long wait to see how the next Bond era aesthetic comes together, but given Pattinson’s distinctive approach to fashion, it should be well worth it for the clothes alone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Holland and Zendaya were among the stars attending this past weekend’s Governors Awards in Los Angeles, where both made interesting choices when it came to their watches.

Holland, dressed in a black double-breasted Louis Vuitton dinner suit, white shirt, and black bow tie—with tan leather Christian Louboutin boots—was photographed pulling back his cuff to reveal a rose-gold Tank Louis Cartier on a leather strap.

Introduced in 1922, it's one of watchmaking's great enduring designs, with a list of famous admirers that includes Andy Warhol, Yves Saint Laurent, and Princess Diana.

Zendaya, meanwhile, went vintage. Her choice was a small, chic, solid-gold Rolex dating from the 1960s, believed to be the very watch she bought at a vintage market in her hometown of Oakland just over a week ago.

Industry observers note that according to the San Francisco Chronicle, the actress spotted the watch at a stall run by independent dealer Wrist Glow Co., tried it on, went off to browse and returned an hour later to buy it. The price? A little over $6,000.

Watch-spotters have identified the Rolex as a ladies' cocktail watch, reference 8196, although that identification has yet to be independently confirmed.

In a recent development, so, what have we learned? Perhaps that for two stars who do old-school Hollywood glamour so well, there are few better choices for an awards-night watch than a classic in gold. Which one you go for, though, remains a matter of personal taste.

According to recent reports, harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson were eliminated from Dancing With the Stars during the semifinals despite two flawless performances—including an emotional tribute to Harry’s late Glee costar Naya Rivera.

Industry observers note that but, despite not making it to the finals, Harry says he feels at peace with the decision. “I oddly feel at ease. I don't feel sad—it's really weird,” he told E! News after getting eliminated. “I kind of felt like we accomplished everything we wanted to.”.

Harry also spoke about dancing to Naya’s cover of “Valerie” by Amy Winehouse, saying the song “meant so much to so many people” and “It was a moment where you kind of saw the underdog be able to have the spotlight, and I always remember that feeling.” He also teased another routine from him and Jenna on their own terms, saying, “It would have been nice to do a finale, but I think we'll have our own finale in some sort of way, shape, or form in the future.”.

I'm now a trained dancer because of her.”.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Jenna mentioned that they had an “epic” dance planned for the finale, saying, “That’s the part that I'm most heartbroken about. We had concocted this incredible journey that the ballroom won't see this time. But maybe we'll put it out there somewhere.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as you might imagine, my coworkers and I, well, we see a crap ton of clothes on a daily basis. We’re fashion editors, after all. Our working hours are spent poring over the latest collections, visiting showrooms to experience the pieces for ourselves, and analyzing every trend. All that noted, we can be a tough bunch to impress. I mean that earnestly. But when my colleague and I saw a sneak preview of the collaboration between Shopbop’s in-house label, Le Bop, and Julia Berolzheimer, we nearly squealed with delight.

It has been revealed that the collection hits all the right notes. It’s colorful. It’s fun yet sophisticated. And for Berolzheimer, the collaboration felt like a full-circle moment. “I have been a customer of Shopbop since the very beginning of my blog (15 years ago!),” Berolzheimer exclusively told ELLE in an email. “Even back then, Shopbop was a destination for style inspiration and discovery...All of that still holds true for the retailer today. When their design team reached out to me last year to co-design a collection for their private label, Le Bop, it was a no-brainer.”.

The collection features taffeta and satiny fabrics adorned with fringe, tonal animal prints, brocade jackets, and jacquard knits. The rich color palette includes dusty rose, chartreuse, espresso, and ocean blue. It is, I must admit, perfect for party dressing that feels a bit unexpected.

“The inspiration came naturally,” Berolzheimer indicates. “It stemmed from my personal style and what I love and want to wear around the holidays. I call my style ‘polished maximalist,’ and the collection is just that. There are some bold statement pieces and coordinating sets, which I love to style together, but you can also wear them separately for a more pared-down look. What I love most about this collection is how you can mix and match the pieces for any festive occasion and continue to style them beyond the holiday season.”.

The Le Bop x Julia Berolzheimer collection is available now on Shopbop.com.

Looks like there’s yet more drama behind the scenes on Dancing With the Stars—and this time Derek Hough is at the center of it. Take this with a grain of salt, but turns out the pros are (allegedly!) upset with Derek over his judging this season.

“There’s a lot of frustration from the pros towards the judges this season but surprisingly, it seems most of the animosity is aimed at Derek specifically,” a source tells The Sun. “He keeps praising the contestants while giving lower scores. He offers little to no constructive feedback and the pros feel it’s impossible to please him since he isn’t offering any critique.”.

According to recent reports, on top of that, “he just seems like he’s in more of a bad mood on set this season. It’s rubbing the cast the wrong way and they feel he just doesn’t want to be on set this year. It’s a strange shift from past seasons where he’s usually the most energetic on set. At least with Carrie Ann and Bruno, they justify their lower scores with feedback. Derek is just phoning it in.”.

It has been revealed that this comes amid Derek getting called out by fans for comments he made during Ezra Sosa’s livestream on TikTok last week, where he joked “Listen, I’ve had three hours of sleep. I came from Seattle this morning on tour. I’m going to Florida right after this Disney special, and then back on tour…That’s why I think I’m giving nines to everybody today.”.

Nines aside, can’t wait to see Derek and the rest of the judges during the Dancing With the Stars finale next Tuesday!

Recent findings suggest that one of the greatest things about the best kinds of jewelry is that it has no limits. Unlike clothing, it can pretty much be made out of anything, so long as it’s durable. Glass, in jewelry, dates as far back as around 3500 BCE in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, via beads and carvings. Yet all these years later, designers are revisiting the humble material, along with wood, porcelain, and beyond. It makes sense: We’re definitely in an era of experimental jewelry, and materials that push beyond the typical precious metals and gemstones allow for bolder shapes and silhouettes, with major impact. Enter: wooden pendants, glass rings, and porcelain chains.

On the runways recently, we’ve seen Chanel and Dries Van Noten toy with glass necklaces, Margiela play with porcelain (in the form of an ASMR-worthy dress that was an undercover nod to the house’s famous ’90s vest made of the material) as well as multilayered tidbits in standout pieces like Celine’s charm necklaces.

Likewise, fine jewelers are integrating various materials into their work. Marla Aaron, for instance, reimagined her Lock connector pendant in an official collaboration with Nymphenburg porcelain. Marie Lichtenberg makes beautiful dice pendants rendered in black ebony and diamonds. Anna Maccieri Rossi recently released an entire collection dedicated to wood, including chunky necklaces and carved bangles set with gemstones. “I love wood because it is a living material, warm and natural,” she remarked of the collection. “This material offers me the chance to dream and work on a large scale, with a bolder approach.”.

The cost of gold rapidly ascended in 2025, reaching an all-time nominal record high of $5,589.38 per troy ounce in January 2026. Driven by historic market shifts and a broader surge in precious metal prices, this sharp economic rise has dramatically reshaped how fashion insiders, collectors, and everyday jewelry lovers approach their collections. As traditional solid gold pieces become increasingly rare financial splurges, buyers are actively diversifying their wardrobes with creative, tactile alternatives. In addition to gravitating toward vintage sterling silver and archival heirlooms, jewelry aficionados are now getting their fix with these alternative materials—ranging from hand-carved wood and delicate hand-blown glass to sculptural porcelain and unconventional metals.

Some designers, too, are looking to build and reinvent the legacy of those who came before them. “I think when most people hear ‘glass jewelry,’ a pretty specific image comes to mind,” Colin Keane Lynch of Keane New York tells ELLE. “I’m interested in building on that history while exploring some of the less familiar possibilities.” Lynch, who has devoted his life to working with glass, designs sculptural glass petal rings and sinuous cuffs, all made to order. “Another thing I love about glass is its ability to take on the appearance of so many different materials through explorations of form, texture, and color. It also allows me to create things that might be difficult or even impossible to achieve in other materials.”.

Sources indicate that much like the language and energy of crystals and gemstones, others are interested in these materials because of what they represent. Take Thatch, for instance. Founded by Amy Goin and Laura Laing, the brand sells huge wooden heart pendants as well as fish-shaped wooden bangles and charms. “We feel that wood holds energy the same way gemstones do,” indicates Goin. “A different kind of energy. Something quieter and more grounded. It’s soulful and raw. We love the bohemian beauty of wood, paired with a touch of gold and sparkle.”.

For today’s designers, the most precious thing about jewelry is the possibility.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dancing With the Stars is making a major change heading into the finale next Tuesday! The show will air its three-hour finale live on both the East Coast and the West Coast, instead of only going live on the East Coast and having West Coast viewers watch the show late and risk being spoiled.

In a recent development, according to Deadline, the Dancing With the Stars finale will air Tuesday, November 24, at 8 p.m. ET and 5 p.m. PT. It will then re-air at 8 p.m. PT for everyone on the West Coast unable to catch the live viewing.

Of course, this means that an enormous amount of viewers on the West Coast will be able to vote live in the finale for the first time ever, which could definitely influence the outcome of the show!

So, why doesn’t Dancing With the Stars air live on both the West and East Coasts every week? Showrunner Conrad Green told The Hollywood Reporter that it conflicts with local news on the West Coast. As he put it, “local news and the coveted primetime programming slots” get in the way of a live show—but there’s also an issue with rights.

Sources indicate that “It’s a significant issue for [affiliates] is if everyone starts watching the show at 5 p.m. when it airs,” he said. “If you’re in L.A. and you watch at 5 p.m. when it airs [at 8 p.m.] on the East Coast, then it’s going to massively affect the people who will watch the show when it comes over to these different territories and those markets. The affiliates are hugely crucial in the bigger picture for the overall economic structure of the show and for the history of ABC and all of those things.”.

Clearly ABC made an exception for the finale!

And after years of watching him play Carmy in The Bear, we know he can do angry and exhausted and permanently one minor inconvenience away from losing it. That’s basically three quarters of the Wolverine job description.

According to recent reports, jackman has owned the role since the first X-Men film landed in 2000. He’s played Wolverine across 10 movies, most recently returning for 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine. His version became so definitive that it’s difficult to picture anyone else with the claws (other than the time Troye Sivan briefly had them in 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine), even though the 6’2" actor looked very different from the shorter character drawn in the OG comics.

Maybe White just fancied some giant sideburns. Maybe the flowers are covering three adamantium claws. Either way, Marvel should probably give him a call—assuming it hasn’t already.

#31195. 40 More Million-Dollar Watches Just Sold at Auction

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1170 w)

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

40 More Million-Dollar Watches Just Sold at Auction

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in June, I reported on the bonanza of watches crossing the million-dollar-plus mark at auction.
  • Sources indicate that in just the first half of 2026, the number of million-dollar watches sold nearly eclipsed the total from all of 2025.
  • If you’re keeping score at home, we’ve seen 133 watches sell at or above seven figures this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in June, I reported on the bonanza of watches crossing the million-dollar-plus mark at auction. What once felt like a unicorn price for watchmakers, auction houses, and the industry as a whole no longer feels so magical. “I joke with people that $1 million is like the newly introduced $250,000 of five years ago,” Paul Boutros of Phillips auction house remarked over the summer.

Sources indicate that in just the first half of 2026, the number of million-dollar watches sold nearly eclipsed the total from all of 2025. Now, after a raft of high-profile auctions in Geneva a couple of weeks ago, the industry has set yet another record. In just the last month alone (including Monaco Legend Group, which kicked things off in late October), 40 million-dollar watches hammered, according to numbers provided by EveryWatch. That’s more sold than in any entire year before 2020.

If you’re keeping score at home, we’ve seen 133 watches sell at or above seven figures this year. And we’ve still got plenty of year left.

Industry observers note that the question is: How much steam does the auction world have left? And what’s driving this radical spike in significant-ticket timepieces?

In a recent development, A $10 million Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph ref. 2499.

Mike Nouveau, WatchTok King and dealer, has told me that if more kids knew how much growth potential there is in the vintage market, they’d put down the creator-style tiny microphones and start studying reference numbers. The vintage market spiked in the middle of the pandemic, when prices on sport watch grails like the Patek Philippe Nautilus and Rolex Daytona went crypto-mode as a new wave of speculators flooded the high-end collecting scene.

Sources indicate that but while the steel sport watch craze has cooled—or at least leveled off—the market has continued riding a remarkably durable wave, helped in part by the arrival of a previously quiet category: the insiders-only independent brands. “For many years at auction, we always noted, ‘You have Patek Philippe and Rolex. What’s the third brand that can compete?’” Alexandre Ghotbi, a deputy chairman at Phillips auction house, told me in 2024 for a story on the beloved watchmaker Rexhep Rexhepi. “Today’s third brand is not a brand—it’s a genre: independent artisanal watchmakers.”.

Sources indicate that think F.P. Journe, Berneron, Phillipe Dufour, Rexhepi’s Atelier Akrivia—companies helmed by watchmaking auteurs turning out hyper-limited runs, most of which sell out long before a perfectly-lit product photo ever hits the web. Oftentimes, the only way to get your hands on one of their wares—if you haven’t yet achieved friend-of-the-brand status—is by raising a paddle at auction.

Sources indicate that when I asked dealer Eric Wind if he thought the indie insanity would remain strong, he was unequivocal: “At the top end, yes.” The dealer Zoe Abelson, of Graal Watches, actually believes we haven’t reached the peak yet. “I do think there's still room for the pieces that are actually rare to continue to grow in value with a continuance in newly introduced interest in collecting watches and the yearning to build the most impressive collection,” she stated.

Two weekends ago, a latest independent brand joined the list of million-dollar watchmakers. Sylvain Pinaud cut his teeth restoring antique watches and established his eponymous brand in 2018. He’s known for showing his work—the instrumental components of his watches are often highlighted on the dial. A unique version of his Origine, a model that only launched in 2022, sold for 1,011,200 Swiss francs (roughly $1,211,500).

Pinaud’s success is indicative of what happens to the elite independent brands that hit the massive time. Compared to many of the heavyweight Swiss makers working at scale, independent watchmakers are seen as artisans who hand-produce their designs in extremely limited quantities. It’s why a watchmaker like Kari Voutilainen, considered a master of his craft, has sold more million-dollar pieces this year than many of the big fellas getting rap lyric shoutouts. “There's a growing appreciation for what these watchmakers are producing,” mentioned Ben Horesh, EveryWatch’s CEO. “It’s great to see more independents challenging the old guard.".

Recent findings suggest that look at that list above. Voutilainen ranks just after Rolex and Patek Philippe but ahead of Cartier for the most million-dollar watches sold at auction in 2026. The list is heavy on independents, including Rexhepi’s Akrivia, George Daniels, Philippe Dufour, and Vianney Halter. The real headline, though, is seeing F.P. Journe—the godfather of the indie scene—at the very top. If one area of the market doesn’t feel entirely sustainable, it’s the inferno around FPJ’s pieces. For deep-pocketed newcomers to the “hobby” of catching substantial-ticket whales, the Geneva-based maker has come to represent the grailiest of grails. Nearly every Journe piece that comes to auction sells for multiples of its estimate. And I mean everything: an empty watch box made for a set of FPJs sold for $230,000 at Christie’s! “The less rare—or in Journe's case, current production—pieces that get swept up in the overall market growth will slow down soon,” Abelson said. “I don't think it's sustainable; at a certain point the values will price out enough people that there should be a correction.”.

Would you pay $230,000 for this box?

A $13 million F.P. Journe Chronomètre à Résonance "Régence”.

If six-figure watches were once rare, 10-million-plus pieces were true spectacles. Between 2020 and 2023, not a single watch crossed that threshold. In the last decade, from 2015 to 2025, there were just seven 10-million watches total. But with some time still on the clock, seven watches have already topped that threshold in 2026. A solid chunk of that is thanks to the wild one-of-one Daytonas that Rolex made for a charity auction—three out of the four sold for seven figures—but it’s still an astounding feat. The rest of the list is filled out by:.

It has been revealed that these days, it’s hard to find a category of watches that isn’t doing well at auction. Cartier hasn’t fallen off—in fact, the brand keeps setting records: a very cool clock known as Portico No. 4 hammered for approximately $5,768,400 at Phillips the weekend before last, becoming the most expensive Cartier ever sold in the process. Breguet is, rightfully and finally, on the rise. And after relaunching just last summer, Urban Jürgensen’s vintage pieces are hotter than ever. A super sexy pink-gold version of the brand’s Reference 2 went for 358,400 Swiss francs (about $430,000) at Sotheby’s.

To put a fine point on all this, just look at how overall sales are soaring. Last year, Phillips set the record with $83,018,538 worth of timepieces sold in a single auction. It only took 12 months to shatter that number. This month saw Phillips reset the record with a $112.3 million auction. I would say 2026 is an inflection point for the industry…if I didn’t anticipate that we’ll be back here talking about even more record-setting sales every year for the foreseeable future.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, few jackets have managed to cross as many style tribes—and decades—as the Harrington.
  • For one, it's incredibly practical: Water-resistant, pocket-forward, lightly insulating, and ever-adaptable to the day's conditions thanks to its full-zip and collar.
  • Industry observers note that the original Harrington—a Baracuta G9—is still available almost a century on from its release, and still excellent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, few jackets have managed to cross as many style tribes—and decades—as the Harrington. In fact, if you were to enroll in Classic Menswear 101, the Harrington jacket would be a prerequisite. The transitional season staple—a favorite of Elvis, James Dean, Steve McQueen, and every member of The Clash—is constantly found across lookbooks and style Instagram accounts, because it does so many things so well.

For one, it's incredibly practical: Water-resistant, pocket-forward, lightly insulating, and ever-adaptable to the day's conditions thanks to its full-zip and collar. But the almost-cropped length—and popped collar, if you so dare—is also a style swerve that makes every wearer feel one dose cooler than they did before. No wonder it’s been embraced over the decades by everyone from golfers to preppies to A-Listers and punks.

Industry observers note that the original Harrington—a Baracuta G9—is still available almost a century on from its release, and still excellent. But if you’re looking to broaden your horizons, today’s Harrington jackets aren’t resting on their laurels. Below, the standout versions worth adding to your rotation before we’re into parka territory.

The classic Baracuta G9 golf jacket is as British as beans on toast. This is the original tartan-lined, ribbed-cuff Harrington, the jacket you picture when you think of Steve McQueen or Paul Newman, and the brand that insider-y menswear favorites like Engineered Garments and Noah have collaborated with when they wanted to make Harringtons of their own. Baracuta got its start making raincoats for other brands—Burberry included—before branching out with its own designs, and the G9 is still made in England today. Crafted from a water-resistant cotton-poly blend, and featuring the signature Fraser tartan lining and iconic umbrella back yoke (which keeps rain off your back while letting air circulate) it really doesn't get any better than this.

Industry observers note that uniqlo delivers a whole Harrington jacket without sacrificing anything, and in fact saves you some precious dollars along the way. We’re talking a slightly cropped, slightly relaxed silhouette, a touch of stretch, classic slant pockets and even a genre-affirming plaid lining. And while it’s not water-resistant like some other options, it makes up for it with a durable cotton fabric that’ll dry off in no time, and still keep you protected from a few unforeseen raindrops. If you’re after the workaday Harrington aesthetic without spending a lot, this one gets the job done and then some.

If you're looking to purchase a Harrington jacket that'll serve you for seasons to come, but don't particularly want to spend half your rent check on it, J.Crew's faithful take on the Harrington is as true as it gets. And this is no compromise pick: It still comes with plenty of details to get excited about, from the handsome, buttoned interior chest pocket to the warming full lining, leather zip tag, and 10-ounce cotton twill that's already been washed a few times by the brand to make it feel lived-in and well-loved from the jump. It also comes in multiple colors, partly because J.Crew is confident you'll be back for more. Oh, and if you want a winterized Harrington, check out the corduroy iteration, which also has a quilted, Primaloft-stuffed lining.

A pared-down, easygoing take on the classics, Quince’s Harrington strikes a smart balance of polished and sporty, without even the faintest fuss. Offered in khaki, navy and black, this one is the modern minimalist’s Harrington—a clean, contemporary style that does what a staple should do: make you look good without causing a scene. Oh, and that twill outer will break in wonderfully over time, in case you were wondering.

Industry observers note that one of the best parts about a Harrington Jacket is that the idea is fully formed. As such, it can be a hard style to riff on, mostly because the source material is so dialed in that it’s often best to leave well enough alone. Ernest W. Baker designers Reid Baker and Inês Amorim, however, couldn’t care less about that tradition and went nuclear with this one: it’s a true-blue Harrington complete with a cropped fit, ribbing at the waist, barrel cuffs and a point collar. But then the inclusion of a leather collar and Western-inspired yoke details in lieu of the classic back vent turns it into something else entirely, without changing the fit one bit. And they nailed it. It’s transformative without being performative, utterly distinct and eminently familiar and, most improbably, contradiction free.

This has most of the trappings of your classic Harrington—stand collar, cool back vent, functional cuffs—but it also eschews the classic ribbed hem for a cinched waist, which adds a little bit of drama to the notoriously no-drama silhouette.

Todd Snyder often plays it straight—Ivy-ish classics with just the right details. Here, they’ve ditched part of the trad playbook and leaned into the modern with water-resistant tech cotton-nylon blend, but it's also a bit cropped and fits very much like you'd remember. And now, it's also on sale.

A Harrington is already pretty pared down, but Barbour trimmed every ounce of fat on this one, leaving us with a slightly longer silhouette, all the *essential* bells and whistles and a brown cotton outer that gets to take center stage.

We could get into the buttery leather collar or the insane Italian wool serge fabric that Wanze deployed on this stunner, or even lock in on that two-way RiRi zipper, but that'd be burying the lede because you're not going to get a red like this anywhere else.

We wouldn't typically include different versions of the same style in one guide, but when our Best Overall version also comes in a buttery suede, exceptions are made.

Stone Island traffics in the unexpected, so, in a way, it should come as no surprise that the Italian label's take on the classic is a Gonzo, teched-out one—one made with a garment-dyed fabric that's been treated with an "anti-drop" finish.

The Harrington is an icon of preppy style, so of course Ralph Lauren has blessed us with its lightweight cotton take, complete with the signature Polo pony on the chest. It’s preppy, American, and exactly the kind of jacket your kids will proudly say “This used to be my Dad’s” about.

It has been revealed that you might not think of a Harrington as a "winter jacket," but hear us out: it can be. This Percival joint, for instance, is made out of a hardy birdseye wool blend that will hold up to some chilly weather and layer up nicely when calling things "chilly" is understatement.

Why is it called a Harrington jacket?

The funniest thing about the Harrington? It wasn’t originally called a Harrington at all. The original—and, as you've read above, our favorite—was called the “G9.” It was cooked up by Baracuta in 1937 in rainy old Manchester, England, as a golf jacket—the “G” stands for “golf.” (The idea was to make a garment that could take a beating from British weather without cramping your backswing.) But the jacket earned its now-iconic name thanks to Rodney Harrington, a character from the 1960s TV show Peyton Place, who wore one so often that the name just stuck.

How should a Harrington jacket fit?

In a recent development, the traditional Harrington jacket fits close to the shoulders and chest, but still has enough room for a full range of arm motion—it is a golfing style, after all. The hem then typically sits either at the waist, or for a more stylized look, just above the belt line. It should be easy to spot from product shots whether the designer in question has stuck to this traditional shape, or elongated the style a touch. From that point, the only thing left to consider is whether you blueprint to wear it over thick sweaters, or lighter T-shirts and shirts. If it's the former, you may want to consider sizing up.

Sources indicate that style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

Sources indicate that to kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally newly introduced to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.).

How the Grocery Store Became Travel’s Hottest Destination

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • It has been revealed that last winter, for a friend’s birthday, a large group of us rented a chalet in Courchevel, France.
  • Industry observers note that I ended up at Sherpa Supermarché, an unfussy grocery chain with 116 locations across the mountains of France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It has been revealed that last winter, for a friend’s birthday, a large group of us rented a chalet in Courchevel, France. There were the usual Alpine excesses—elaborate supper-club dinners, après-ski that stretched well into the evening—but, as with any ski holiday, there came a point when somebody had to buy groceries. This responsibility fell to me. I approached the task with all the enthusiasm I usually have for making my bed or taking out the garbage.

Industry observers note that I ended up at Sherpa Supermarché, an unfussy grocery chain with 116 locations across the mountains of France. I expected to be in and out in five minutes. Instead, I found myself standing before a cheese section that puts the Library of Congress to shame—there were varieties of Comté I had never heard of, some aged longer than certain marriages, others washed in wine or wrapped in herbs. The chocolate section was equally impressive. I had not known there were so many ways to make chocolate, or that I would, like a kid with eyes bigger than his stomach, start shoving them by the armful into my basket.

According to recent reports, sherpa wasn’t particularly fancy or large. It was an ordinary shop serving ordinary people, only its definition of “ordinary” happened to feel particularly French, and unlike anything we have back home. I returned to the chalet with way more chocolate and cheese than anyone had requested, and the sense that I had just experienced something meaningful.

Apparently, I’m not alone. According to Hilton’s 2026 Travel Trends Report, 77 percent of travelers said they enjoy visiting grocery stores abroad. Grocery store tourism has become one of travel’s more unexpected obsessions in recent years, with visitors increasingly building supermarket stops into itineraries once reserved for museums and monuments.

Looking back on my travels, the grocery store was always there. I’ll never forget my horror when I went to an IGA in Montréal for the first time and learned that Canadian potato chip flavors are vastly superior to our own. (If you ever find yourself north of the border, All-Dressed, Ketchup, and Poulet Rôti-flavored chips are a must.) Or on a trip to Seoul, where Lotte Mart introduced me to a wide variety of truly restaurant-quality instant noodles and elaborate packaged desserts. I’ve heard similar stories about Major C, a grocery chain in Thailand, which even offers hands-on workshops where visitors can indulge in tastings of Thai curry pastes. Doesn’t that feel a step above the free samples at Costco?

Grocery stores shape the way you see a destination. One friend keeps telling me about a to-die-for babka from Panama City’s Super K, billed as the world’s largest kosher supermarket. Would I necessarily think of kosher food in a destination best known for its beaches and tropical rainforests? Probably not. But that’s precisely the point: a supermarket can reveal an entirely different side of a place.

We’re seeing grocery store tourism get increasingly luxe, too. In Los Angeles, Erewhon has become a destination in its own right, where visitors can observe the city’s wellness aristocracy paying $22 for a celebrity-endorsed smoothie. New York City’s Meadow Lane opened in Tribeca last year with beautifully packaged pantry staples and artisanal chicken fingers so good that you don’t care about the $17 price tag. And in Tokyo, Kayanoya, a Japanese brand known for its hard-to-find seasonings and traditional ingredients, just opened a new flagship in Ginza designed by Kengo Kumba. It honestly looks about as luxe and appealing as a Prada boutique. Grocery tourism is increasingly becoming something you experience, not just a utilitarian shopping stop.

But the alpha and omega of grocery store tourism remains French butter. For years, bringing home a few blocks of Maison Bordier was the ultimate edible souvenir from Paris, and La Grande Épicerie makes the process seamless, vacuum-sealing purchases for the journey home. (I’ve also learned from TikTok that you can take your butter back to your hotel, ask for it to be frozen overnight, and, by the time you land in the States, it should be just about thawed.) And this year, Paris got another dedicated butter destination in Le Butter Shop, a retailer within walking distance, specializing in du beurre and all its regional varieties.

Which brings me back to the cheese case in Courchevel. I went in expecting a quick chore and came out with a better sense of the town than I’d gotten from any of its chi-chi, Champagne-drenched supper clubs. The monuments and must-dos tell one side of a place’s story, but the supermarkets show you another. I’ll be packing an extra bag for butter next time I’m in Paris.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, between sniffing out paternal autism and perfecting his Robert F. Kennedy impression, you may have noticed that John Mulaney was wearing an extraordinary watch while hosting Saturday Night Live this weekend. It’s a beauty—a gold vintage Patek Philippe with swoopy Breguet numerals—but its backstory is even more impressive. On December 12, 1948, New York Yankees legend Joe DiMaggio purchased this timepiece and owned it until his death in 1999.

The Patek Philippe, a ref. 130 circa 1947, is already a rare bird before you add in its Joltin’ Joe provenance. The model is one of just 180 made in yellow gold with Breguet numerals, and only 55 with this same combination have ever reached the secondary market. In late October, dealer Eric Wind of Wind Vintage put this specific watch up for sale with a $1.2 million asking price. “I think it’s the greatest Patek that’s known and tied to any athlete,” Wind told Robb Report last month.

Sources indicate that for his seventh time hosting SNL, Mulaney came to Wind in search of “an vital watch,” the dealer explains now. After surveying Wind’s entire catalog, the comedian landed on this piece, whose ties to a legendary New Yorker felt right for helming one of the city’s most hallowed institutions. To be clear, Mulaney only borrowed the watch for the show, which means its legend will have only grown by the time it reaches an eventual buyer. Talk about an illustrious provenance: A DiMaggio-owned Patek that also appeared on Saturday Night Live. “It was a very special moment and another cool moment of history for this important Patek Philippe,” Wind notes.

As a known history buff and devoted baseball fan, the watch likely appealed to Mulaney on several levels. But its eggshell-hued dial also happened to go perfectly with the brown suit Mulaney sported during his opening monologue. “John has classic styling,” Wind indicates, “and the Joe DiMaggio Patek Philippe was the chef’s kiss on his wrist.”.

According to recent reports, over the past several years, Mulaney has emerged as one of Hollywood’s most prolific and tasteful watch collectors. He is an eager and omnivorous admirer, bouncing between his beloved Rolex Air-King, loud Chopard chronographs, and glamorous Grand Seikos.

Mulaney, styled by Michael Fisher, wearing Cavour.

Industry observers note that during our watch-focused interview last May, Mulaney told me that he steers away from more obvious models like your garden-variety Rolex Submariner. “I don’t ask any questions about it, I know what it is,” he explained. “And I’m just more interested in watches that [are a little more] mysterious.” As an example, Mulaney specifically referenced a Patek Philippe Calatrava his wife Olivia Munn bought him.

The DiMaggio Patek is full of intrigue. The watch obviously has key provenance, but it’s historic on its own accord, too. The ref. 130 is named for the movement inside, known as the Calibre 130. That engine was the basis for Patek’s 1518, the first serially produced watch to combine a perpetual calendar and chronograph.

According to recent reports, funnily enough, this isn’t the first Mulaney, DiMaggio, and SNL crossover. In his 2018 special Kid Gorgeous at Radio City, the comedian explained what it was like working with famous SNL hosts during his time as a staff writer. “It’d be like if you went into your childhood bedroom and Joe DiMaggio was sitting there,” Mulaney quipped. “Yeah, he’s Joe DiMaggio, he’s a legend, he had sex with Marilyn Monroe, but only you know where the bathroom is.” And only Mulaney has had DiMaggio’s watch on his wrist, for now.

Industry News: Which Ultra-Processed Foods Are the Worst for You? A Dietitian Breaks It Down

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • Research over the years has shown exactly how ultra-processed foods (UPFs) negatively affect the body.
  • Most researchers use a system called NOVA, developed by a Brazilian epidemiologist, Carlos Augusto Monteiro, who coined the term “ultra-processed foods.” Hosmer explains that NOVA sorts foods into four groups based on how much they’ve been processed and not by their nutrients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Research over the years has shown exactly how ultra-processed foods (UPFs) negatively affect the body. What’s still being studied is how many of these specific foods, and how much of them, impact the rise in certain cancers and other diseases. Although the internet is rife with stats showing an uptick in certain cancers among younger adults, a recent study conducted among a massive 460,000 Americans debunked one of the many fear-mongering rumors that ultra-processed foods are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk specifically. But before you place your next fast food delivery order, Caitlin Hosmer, MS, RD, LDN, a registered dietitian and co-founder of MenoPantry alongside Mark Gilbert, nutritionist from The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Blueprint, explains which parts of the meal are potentially the most harmful, and what you should know about the study’s findings to understand which ultra-processed foods are actually the worst for you.

Most researchers use a system called NOVA, developed by a Brazilian epidemiologist, Carlos Augusto Monteiro, who coined the term “ultra-processed foods.” Hosmer explains that NOVA sorts foods into four groups based on how much they’ve been processed and not by their nutrients.

Sources indicate that gilbert argues that the system is questionable. “Even nutrition experts were unable to categorize foods reliably or consistently into one of [these] four categories, from unprocessed to ultra-processed. Other systems, including IFIC, Nutri-Score, and the proposed CHIPS system, exist but are similarly controversial,” says Gilbert.

To better understand what these foods are exactly, Hosmer indicates the simplest way to put it is that a processed food is still recognizably food that’s been preserved or prepared. An ultra-processed food has been taken apart. “These foods are designed to be cheap, shelf-stable, convenient, and very easy to overeat. The key caveat is that NOVA describes how a food is made, not how nutritious it is. So the Ultra-processed category can hold both a hot dog and a packaged whole-grain bread,” says Hosmer.

Gilbert further explains that the processes many of these foods undergo often reduce healthy, essential nutrients, remove fiber, and make the resulting food easier to consume, absorb, and digest, leading to untoward blood sugar levels, less satiety and, in the longer term, poorer metabolic health.

Sources indicate that gilbert notes that it’s difficult to deem any one type of UPF as “worst” simply because genetic and environmental risk factors to various diseases and ill health vary so vastly. “So, just like no single diet is ‘best’ for everyone, no single food is necessarily worst. For instance, if someone has a high heart and vascular disease risk, they might benefit from less saturated fat. If someone has a high risk of diabetes, they should avoid sugar and other refined carbohydrates that raise their blood sugar levels,” Gilbert explains.

Recent findings suggest that however, Hosmer points out that when researchers break ultra-processed foods into subgroups, processed meat consistently comes out on top. The aforementioned study of more than 460,000 adults, conducted by the National Cancer Institute (NCI), found that ultra-processed food intake overall wasn’t linked to colorectal cancer—but higher consumption of meat from ultra-processed food sources was. Hosmer references a 2024 Harvard analysis in The British Medical Journal that found the same pattern for mortality.

“Across more than 30 years of follow-up, meat-, poultry-, and seafood-based ready-to-eat products revealed the strongest and most consistent associations, followed by sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened beverages, dairy-based desserts, and ultra-processed breakfast food. That category includes processed meats such as hot dogs, deli meats, bacon, sausages, and many frozen breaded meat products,” Hosmer summarizes.

In a recent development, second to processed meat are sweetened drinks—both sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened. “Sodas, sweet teas, energy drinks, and diet drinks give you sweetness and calories (or the expectation of calories) with no fiber, protein, or real food structure. They show up consistently across heart, metabolic, and mortality research,” Hosmer notes.

Industry observers note that sugar-laced and dairy-based desserts alongside sugary breakfast foods follow on the list. “Many sugary cereals and pastries are basically dessert dressed up as breakfast,” says Hosmer.

Industry observers note that these foods won’t necessarily give you cancer or lead to other diseases; Hosmer explains that the more useful message is that “worst” means low in what the body needs and high in what it doesn’t. In the NCI study, higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium from ultra-processed food sources was linked to a lower incidence of colorectal cancer. “A packaged whole-grain bread and a package of bologna are both “ultra-processed,” but they are not the same choice,” she adds.

It has been revealed that many UPFs are often made to be irresistible, meaning you’ll likely eat more than the recommended serving size. Gilbert explains that this leads to large spikes in blood sugar and doesn’t reduce satiety as much as most whole foods do. UPFs can also increase overall calorie intake. “Increased calorie intake and excess blood sugar spikes cause weight gain, high blood pressure, inflammation, diabetes, unhealthy blood lipids, generally poor metabolic health, and a variety of other effects which increase a person’s odds of the most common serious health conditions and diseases, reducing health span and lifespan,” Gilbert warns.

To illustrate, Hosmer points to what she calls a small but elegant 2019 National Institutes of Health (NIH) trial led by Kevin Hall, which she says has the strongest causal evidence. Twenty adults lived on a metabolic ward and ate either an ultra-processed or a minimally processed diet for two weeks each. The diets were matched in calories, sugar, fat, fiber, and sodium, and people could eat as much as they wanted. On the ultra-processed diet, participants ate about 500 more calories a day, ate faster, and gained weight—about two pounds; on the minimally processed diet, they lost about the same amount. “That points to something about the food’s form, not just its nutrients: it’s soft, energy-dense, quick to eat, and slow to trigger fullness,” says Hosmer.

Considering these results, she claims there are multiple mechanisms present that likely work together:.

According to recent reports, turn the package over and read the ingredient list. That tells you far more than the front of the box. Some signs:.

Context matters too. A whole-grain bread with one dough conditioner is a very different food from a toaster pastry, even though both may technically count as ultra-processed. Ask two questions: how processed is it, and what is it actually giving me? Fiber, protein, whole grains, and added nutrients count for a lot.

It has been revealed that this depends greatly on the specific foods in question. “That’s what makes this newly introduced study that differentiates between the different kinds of processed foods particularly crucial,” indicates Hosmer. “The clearest evidence is for processed meat. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen for colorectal cancer. That’s the category for strong evidence that something causes cancer, though it says nothing about how massive the risk is,” Hosmer clarifies. More practically, she further explains that the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) estimated that eating 50 grams of processed meat every day—about one hot dog or a few slices of deli meat regularly—is associated with roughly an 18 percent increase in baseline colorectal cancer risk. “That’s a relative increase: for an average person, it moves a lifetime risk from approximately four to five percent to roughly five to six percent,” says Hosmer.

The proposed mechanisms are specific:.

Industry observers note that for ultra-processed foods as a whole category, Hosmer indicates the picture is less clear. The latest NCI study is one of the largest ever done on this question. When the team looked by food group, whole grains and dairy were linked to lower risk and meat to higher risk. The researchers note possible opposing effects of some ultra-processed foods on colorectal cancer etiology—mainly that the helpful and harmful foods cancel each other out in the total. More specifically, the total consumption may matter more than the specific foods or food groups.

In a recent development, according to Hosmer, there’s also an indirect pathway. “Diets high in ultra-processed foods are linked to obesity, and excess body fat is an established risk factor for many cancers, including breast cancer after menopause, endometrial cancer, and colorectal cancer,” she notes. Hosmer warns, though, that this study’s findings shouldn’t be read as ultra-processed foods are fine. “Read it as a reminder that it’s hard to make a single recommendation about such a large and varied category of food.” When the researchers broke ultra-processed foods down by type, the results lined up with what we already know: whole grains, fiber, and dairy were linked to lower colorectal cancer risk, and processed meat to higher risk. Hosmer’s challenge is to check the new data against well-established research. “Headlines alone can be misleading, especially on topics as emotionally charged as what we eat.”.

Turn the package over and read the ingredient list. That tells you far more than the front of the box. Here’s what to look for:.

Context matters too. A whole-grain bread with one dough conditioner is a very different food from a toaster pastry, even though both may technically count as ultra-processed. Hosmer says to ask yourself two questions: “How processed is it, and what is it actually giving me?” Fiber, protein, whole grains, and added nutrients count for a lot.

Hosmer explains that the risks associated with ultra-processed foods include two things: how much of someone’s diet comes from these foods, and how much room their body has to absorb the negative effects.

It has been revealed that one caveat from the new study that Hosmer points out is that participants were mostly older white Americans, so results may not generalize to younger or more diverse populations. “That matters because colorectal cancer is rising in adults under 50, the group that has grown up recently, and with the most ultra-processed food available,” she cautions.

In a recent development, gilbert adds that knowing your family’s health history and getting various tests can offer some indications of individual risks, but predicting these risks is by no means foolproof. “Ultimately, those who have prediabetes, diabetes, high blood pressure, cardiovascular disease or cancer, or are living with overweight or obesity are the most at risk because these conditions can often be avoided or improved with better nutrition,” says Gilbert.

Myth: All processed food is bad.

Both Gilbert and Hosmer agree here. “Some foods can be intentionally processed to increase and improve their nutritional profile rather than reduce it,” Gilbert explains. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, plain yogurt, canned salmon, and bagged salad are strong examples. They are processed and still very good for you. Processing often makes healthy food more affordable and accessible. Gilbert’s 1:1 Diet is designed to align with this. “The products we produce are processed, but instead of reducing the essential nutrient content of the products, we actually increase it, adding vitamins, minerals, essential fats, and quality protein,” Gilbert notes, adding that extensive research has shown his diet improves blood sugar, blood pressure, inflammation, metabolic health, cardiovascular health, and reverses diabetes in about half of dieters.

Myth: This fresh study proves ultra-processed food is safe.

Hosmer notes explicitly that it doesn’t. “It looked at only one disease, colorectal cancer, in a mostly older population, and participants reported their diets just once, back in the mid-1990s. The authors themselves point out that ultra-processed foods became far more common and varied over the following two decades, so the study likely underestimated how much people were actually eating,” she clarifies. “The fairer reading is that which ultra-processed foods you eat matters more than the category itself: a whole-grain bread and a hot dog may both be “ultra-processed,” but they don’t affect the body the same way.”.

Myth: It’s only about nutrients, and processing doesn’t matter.

Recent findings suggest that kevin Hall’s controlled feeding trial suggests otherwise. People ate significantly more on the ultra-processed diet even when nutrients were matched, so a food’s structure and how fast you eat it matter too.

Myth: Organic, plant-based, or “clean label” means it isn’t ultra-processed.

Myth: You have to completely eliminate ultra-processed foods.

Perfection isn’t the goal. Hosmer points out that in the NCI study, replacing 10 percent of the total weight of ultra-processed foods with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2 percent lower incidence of colorectal cancer. “We don’t yet know exactly what that looks like on an individual’s plate. The study measured diets statistically, not swap by swap. But the direction is clear, and it fits decades of nutrition research: incremental shifts away from ultra-processed foods appear to matter, even when they’re modest. Start with categories that matter most: processed meats and sweetened drinks,” she concludes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

In a recent development, toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story contains spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.
  • After sleeping alone, it takes some getting used to sharing a bed with someone.
  • It has been revealed that it is mid-September 2025 at the legendary Shepperton Studios just outside London, and there has been another request for more real moss to elevate Bower’s head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story contains spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.

After sleeping alone, it takes some getting used to sharing a bed with someone. This is a challenging proposition in the third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power for the recently reunited Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband, Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), when they use a tree nest as a makeshift bedchamber, as the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers) hunts them down. But Elves are not mere mortals, and after centuries apart, they slip back into slumbering beside each other as if not a day has passed. On set, however, things were much more awkward: Galadriel’s sword gets in Clark’s way, she struggles to roll over in chainmail, and the couple’s moss pillow is too small.

It has been revealed that it is mid-September 2025 at the legendary Shepperton Studios just outside London, and there has been another request for more real moss to elevate Bower’s head. (He likens this grassy pillow to the mattresses in The Princess and the Pea when we talk a year later.) The mood up in the tree nest, as Clark and Bower rehearse a scene from the fifth episode, is much lighter than what plays out on screen. Under the watchful eyes of director Sanaa Hamri, the actors figure out the logistics of spooning in this confined space, mimicking sleep so the camera can see their faces, and allowing Clark to shift to her side, then quickly back away when Galadriel imagines Sauron lying beside her. Later in the day, Vickers will switch in. The shock sends Galadriel falling backward out of the tree and straight into danger. This is not your run-of-the-mill love triangle or burgeoning throuple.

Recent findings suggest that to put it mildly, Galadriel has been going through it in the adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien’s history of Middle-earth. After she rejected Sauron’s offer to be his queen (again) at the end of season 2, he has since taken much of Middle-earth, and his quest to create the One Ring—and thereby rule over all—continues. In the previous episode, he attempted to locate an elf being held prisoner in Gundabad who knew the secrets of forging the One Ring. It turns out the last Elven-smith was already dead, but Galadriel’s long-lost husband, Celeborn, was locked up in a neighboring cell. Celeborn likely knows those same secrets that Sauron needs, making him invaluable. During their escape, Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) is slain, and Sauron comes face-to-face with Galadriel for the first time this season. Well, other than popping into her subconscious.

When Sauron appears in Galadriel’s dreams again in the fifth episode, “The Lady of Lórien,” the safety of the tree canopy is immediately shattered as Galadriel’s sleeping mind pictures Sauron lying inches away where she expects to see Celeborn. When I catch up with Clark on Zoom a year later in September 2026, her face lights up when I mention this scene. “I loved being up there [in the tree nest],” she says. “It was so cozy.” While the episode ends with Celeborn being captured by Sauron—separating the couple once again—there is a brief respite from the horrors of this war-torn land. “There’s a real unabashed lean into the gorgeousness of fantasy,” Clark says of this season, including the foray into swoon-worthy romance in the cocooned foliage.

While the Elves have only just reunited, Clark and Bower had already established the foundation of Galadriel and Celeborn’s relationship during a dance sequence in the season 3 premiere episode, revealing a far lighter Galadriel than we have seen for some time. This also gave the actors an opportunity to get to know each other. “There is a magic about him,” Clark claims of Bower. “We did get to rehearse that together, which also took away a certain type of magic in that learning a dance with someone is pretty vulnerable. We got to know each other doing that, which was really nice. He was so lovely, and he is elf-like.”.

As we learned in season 1, Celeborn left to fight in the war during the First Age and never came home—Middle-earth is now in its Second Age. Galadriel and Celeborn share battle stories, but it is Sauron informing Celeborn that they have previously met (Celeborn claims he has no memory of this) that throws more fire onto this already sizzling dynamic. But before Sauron storms in like a jealous ex, Celeborn and Galadriel manage some K-I-S-S-I-N-G in the tree. “It was a tight space,” Bower laughs over the phone earlier this month. “Towards the end of that scene, there’s that beautiful moment of physical reconnection, and our intimacy coordinator [Sophie Cooch] was so helpful in finding a beauty and almost like a dance and a grace within that physical reconnection into the falling down [together], and being able to lie side by side,” Bower says.

Recent findings suggest that having just played Stranger Things’ big bad Vecna, Bower (who is a huge fan of Tolkien’s work) remarked he was looking for a character who represented love, and Celeborn radiates light even in the darkest circumstances. In the episode, Celeborn senses Galadriel is holding back, but doesn’t press too hard about what. “She definitely feels like she’s lost a sparkle, and he’s a mirror to her,” says Clark. “She can’t ignore the parts of it that have changed.” Clark recalls discussing with Bower that there should be zero “feeling of ownership between them.” When I mention this to Bower, he references the line from Breakfast at Tiffany’s to sum up this dynamic: “We belong to nobody, and nobody belongs to us. We don’t even belong to each other.”.

Tolkien’s marriage and experience in World War I provided inspiration for this union, but it was The Magnetic Fields song “Abigail, Belle of Kilronan” that Clark claims she became obsessed with while filming. “It’s about someone going off to war, and it’s like, ‘And when I come home, if I come home, you’ll be a grown woman. And when I come home, if I come home, don’t be alone, Abigail, Belle of Kilronan,’” Clark says. “That’s almost been her biggest betrayal of him that she allowed herself to be lonely for so long, which I found really beautiful.”.

One person Galadriel was close to before knowing his real identity was Sauron. Although she vocalizes that she doesn’t want Sauron present in this moment—not even uttering his name—the image of him lying next to her is a jolt back to reality, even if he is a figment of her imagination. “Even though in many ways her dreams are coming true with being reunited with Celeborn,” Clark claims, “they can’t live in a simple vacuum of happiness. The world is still out there, and she’s part of the world.” Unfortunately for Galadriel, as she promptly backs away, she falls from the tree, alerting the nearby orcs to their presence.

Industry observers note that the vision seems to be Galadriel’s own doing; Sauron is living rent-free in her mind instead of intentionally popping into her dreams. Vickers discussed this approach with Clark. “The way I play it was determined by what she [Clark] had in her mind—because it’s Galadriel’s experience, it’s not Sauron’s experience—and that was to be the scariest I could be in Galadriel’s mind,” Vickers notes.

Industry observers note that when I met Vickers on set, he was in costume, grabbing a juice from craft services before joining Clark up in the tree nest. Having spent a lot of time on a nearby soundstage, where Sauron’s bleak Barad-dûr lair is located, the Australian actor was happy to experience this change of scenery. “Barad-dûr this season is incredibly intense. It was 35 degrees [95°F] on the days we were filming there,” Vickers says over Zoom. “There was a lot of sweat. It was wonderful to go into the forest on a soundstage.” Still, there were some logistical issues for Vickers up in the nest, first finding the same eyeline to match Bower’s sleeping position and then trying not to stab Clark with Sauron’s pointy gloves. “Lying down in all that stuff is incredibly challenging,” Vickers says.

Recent findings suggest that of course, you don’t see this human behavior in the final cut. “It’s a very particular thing to film something fantasy in this way because the look is so important,” Clark says. “It does matter that their hair looks absolutely lovely in that light, and they move like they’re artists with their bodies.” This includes scenes that might require a stunt double, like the one I observed. “Your stunt double is always a huge part of creating the character, but I think more so than ever with an elf, because she’s got to be excellent,” Clark says. “We do as much as we can with me being as excellent as I can be.” For everything else, Clark’s stunt double Hannah Grant (who has a ballet and martial arts background) steps in.

Industry observers note that while the version of Sauron in this scene is a figment of Galadriel’s imagination, the real Dark Lord is traveling to the Eryn Galen woodland. Celeborn sacrifices himself to stop his wife (who is lying unconscious nearby) from being discovered. What comes next will likely be incredibly unpleasant, but Bower enjoyed going head-to-head with Vickers as the twisted trio enters its next phase.

Industry observers note that “It’s where sparks can fly,” Bower says. “You need to build a rapport, have a friendship, a comfortability, and a trust in one another. Charlie made that so easy from day one.” However, Sauron won’t be as accommodating. “Celeborn has something that Sauron really needs,” Vickers says. “It’s the key to his whole existence up to this point, so you have all the emotional interplay, but then beneath that you have this real psychological drive, which is, ‘I will do anything. I will not stop. I will do all I can to get this secret out of you.’” It seems unlikely that Celeborn, Galadriel, or Sauron will get any sleep anytime soon.
