📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that between a stacked roster of Hollywood icons in their prime (Newman, Poitier, Redford) and a cadre of auteur directors on the come-up (Kubrick, Peckinpah, Coppola), the late 1960s produced some of the 20th century’s most stylish movies. Right up there with the best of them is The Thomas Crown Affair, a 1968 caper film directed by Norman Jewison and starring Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway. Fast-forward a few days and the same could be noted about the 1999 remake starring Bond-era Pierce Brosnan, which is worth watching for the suits alone.

It has been revealed that now, in other news of a formerly Brosnan-led, menswear-centric franchise being rebooted: Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan is the producer, director, and star of a third riff on The Thomas Crown Affair, as he announced at CinemaCon back in April. Judging by the first trailer that dropped last week, the film aims to uphold the sartorial reputation of its forebears.

Hitting theaters in March 2027, Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair remake follows the same premise as the 1968 and 1999 versions: a wealthy playboy businessman plots art heists for fun while being pursued by a sexy insurance investigator, played in this iteration by potential future Wonder Woman Adria Arjona. There’s crime, there’s glamour, there’s sexual tension—but most of all, in the spirit of the Thomas Crowns before him, there appears to be plenty of high-octane menswear. The movie’s style credit is bolstered by Ruth E. Carter, the two-time Oscar-winning costume designer of the Black Panther movies, who also dressed Jordan for his Oscar-winning turn in Sinners.

But how will MBJ’s high-fashion Thomas Crown land? In the trailer, he can be seen wearing a stiff gray shirt with a matching tie and trousers by Bottega Veneta. The shirt, marked by the luxury brand’s signature triangle pocket detail, had an odd fit: taut around the torso yet puffy around the biceps. Here’s hoping we’ll see some sharper tailoring in the next preview.

Still, to understand Thomas Crown’s legacy as one of the best-dressed guys in film, and why the forthcoming reboot will likely be a smorgasbord of major-time menswear, it’s worth looking back at what made the original such a gem of classic American style. Beyond Jewison’s use of Mondrian-esque split-screen and a very cool soundtrack by French composer Michel Legrand, McQueen’s wardrobe is a perfect embodiment of late 1960s cool, and a how-to for anyone looking to capture it.

Equal parts finely tailored and adventurous, Crown is the ultimate man’s man: He closes million-dollar deals by day, but also flies planes, plays polo, and does donuts on the beach in a juiced-up dune buggy. Likewise, his wardrobe is split between incredible tailoring and a supremely dialed-in lineup of casual pieces. Crown’s suits are a primer on old-school Savile Row: structured, traditional, and precisely tailored, and his shirts, ties, and pocket squares are equally on point. Crown’s double-Albert style watch chain (attached to a Patek Philippe pocket watch, naturally) is a decidedly advanced swerve, but his Cartier Tank Cintrée looks as good in 2026 as it did in 1968 (or 1928, for that matter).

Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway in The Thomas Crown Affair (1968).

According to recent reports, off-duty Crown’s casual looks include a parade of hall-of-fame menswear pieces like the Baracuta G9 Harrington jacket (classic navy blue with a red tartan lining), brown suede desert boots, and Persol aviators he wears while piloting his glider (gliders—also extremely cool). Club rules be damned, he plays golf in a non-regulation long-sleeved tee, whacks polo balls in an outfit straight out of a Ralph Lauren campaign, and later dons an Aran sweater for a romantic evening clambake at his beach house. It’s often noted that Steve McQueen could look good in anything, and that might be true, but the clothes in this movie hit hard enough to make anyone look several orders of magnitude cooler.

According to recent reports, set to the funky bars of Fela Kuti’s “Gentleman,” the trailer for Jordan’s forthcoming Thomas Crown Affair offers several tantalizing tidbits of what’s in store, including a Ferrari F40, several razor-sharp tuxes, and a glimpse at a watch that’s almost certainly a vintage Piaget. That monochrome Bottega look aside, between Jordan’s leading man chops and Carter’s knack for high-concept menswear, we’re assuredly in good hands.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m never one to out myself on main, but I’m here to declare: I am a proud (but once-closeted) gaymer.

As someone who rarely watches the latest movies or TV shows, people always retort: “Well, how do you spend your free time?” The answer is, and always has been: By booting up my Xbox. I’ve long found joy in immersing myself in a virtual world. When I was younger, it was through Super Mario on the Nintendo 64. (Aging myself much. . . I need a new night cream.) In my teen years, things evolved to the Resident Evil and Grand Theft Auto franchises. Even now, well into my early thirties, I still find myself slipping on a headset after a stressful day and blocking out the real world—by recently playing video games like Dead by Daylight, where one teams up with three fellow survivors to escape a blood-thirsty killer. That’s my idea of fun.

It has been revealed that this week, however, my attention is shifting back to Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto series—mainly, because Grand Theft Auto VI is finally releasing on Thursday. Over a decade in the works, the buzzy new game is one of the most anticipated (and pre-ordered) games in history—so much so that it’s already surpassed the $1 billion mark before it’s even out.

There’s certainly a lot to be excited for: The latest installment introduces two new characters, Jason and Lucia, and promises its biggest map to date (twice the size of GTA V’s world), interactive features (how strong Jason and Lucia’s relationship is depends on you), and even a star-studded soundtrack (featuring tracks by Cardi B, Travis Scott, Yung Lean, and Tove Lo, not to mention in-game radio commentary from notable names like Alex Consani and Lana Del Rey).

It has been revealed that sure, all of these innovative elements may have been what coaxed me to shell out $99.99 for the game’s ultimate edition ahead of Friday—but most of all, I’m excited to play around with all of the customizable fashions. (Yes, really.).

Characters in Grand Theft Auto VI.

Some may choose to play Grand Theft Auto for the high-stakes speed racing or dangerous crime missions, but I personally play it to flex cute outfits while doing it. Customizing your character’s look, after all, has long been an integral part of the GTA fun: Over the years, having the ability to choose your character’s ensembles, hairstyles, tattoos, and more has been one of the best parts of the game.

I’ve spent countless hours perfecting my saucy in-game ’fits—running around and causing chaos in my sleek biker jackets or stiletto booties. I don’t spend hours completing missions or bank heists to save money for my (virtual) savings account: I rack up the cash to spend it on the lavish fashions, duh! And the good news for me is: GTA VI is rumored to have several clothing, shoe, and jewelry shops to explore across Leonida. Meaning, if I’m going to become the most ruthless crime lord in town, I’m going to be able to look good doing it. (And yes, I will be maining Lucia, who is bound to have the cuter options.).

Lucia in a “Vice City Style” outfit from Grand Theft Auto VI.

In a recent development, it hasn’t taken high-fashion brands long to catch onto this idea that gaming can be glamorous. In Grand Theft Auto V, for one, your character could sport pieces from real-life streetwear labels such as Civilist, MISBHV and Born x Raised. And it’s not just GTA that’s been getting more and more into the fashion space. Over the years, video games have slowly becoming a high-fashion playground in general—releasing purchasable skins that can make your character feel completely tailored to you. Balenciaga has collaborated with games like Fortnite, Louis Vuitton with League of Legends, and Burberry with Roblox. Makes sense: Why shouldn’t your avatar reflect your personal tastes and likes?

Grand Theft Auto VI’s Lucia and Jason.

Sources indicate that so yes, come Thursday, I will be crashing cars, shooting absurdly-violent weapons, and being overall mischievous—but those are all side quests, because come launch day, the very first thing I will be doing is securing cash (perhaps a quick corner store robbery?) to buy me some latest chic shoes. Priorities, people.

The real question is. . . Who do we think will be the first luxury designer to get on board and collaborate with Grand Theft Auto VI? Demna, for one, has proven he is a gaming fan: Can we expect a Gucci x GTA wardrobe sometime soon? I, for one, wouldn’t mind running the streets in this fab faux-fur coat from spring 2027.

Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare.
  • More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.
  • In a recent development, place 1–1¼ lb.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

In a recent development, place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it was Friday the 13th, and Turin, Italy, the site of the Nitto ATP Finals, glowed with cobalt light as a fingernail moon hung in the air.
  • At the Piazza San Carlo, a blue carpet had been laid out lengthwise for the world’s eight best (and currently active) men’s tennis players as fans called out for autographs and selfies.
  • In a recent development, speaking of the dreamlike: the evening included an ATP-commissioned portrait session with the photographer Szilveszter Makó, a man who has skyrocketed to industry prominence for having shot multiple covers this year—including for the American, British and Italian editions of Vogue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it was Friday the 13th, and Turin, Italy, the site of the Nitto ATP Finals, glowed with cobalt light as a fingernail moon hung in the air. It looked almost like a Tintoretto painting.

At the Piazza San Carlo, a blue carpet had been laid out lengthwise for the world’s eight best (and currently active) men’s tennis players as fans called out for autographs and selfies. Carlos Alcaraz in Louis Vuitton and Ben Shelton in Ralph Lauren walked among them; missing was the home favorite, Jannik Sinner, who qualified for the field but is sidelined with a knee injury. The scene delivered a surreal, Hollywood-esque half-hour of public stagecraft—paparazzi flashbulbs, police escorts—with all of it designed to celebrate the end of a very notable, and sometimes odd, year in men’s pro tennis.

In a recent development, speaking of the dreamlike: the evening included an ATP-commissioned portrait session with the photographer Szilveszter Makó, a man who has skyrocketed to industry prominence for having shot multiple covers this year—including for the American, British and Italian editions of Vogue. Makó’s aesthetic itself is rather painterly; photographs as aged frescoes, both cerebral and unusual. Within Turin’s Inalpi Arena, he forged two vignettes with his signature box sets. We stepped in to take a look as Arthur Fils, wearing Balenciaga, was instructed to stand tall and lift his right foot, balancing it on the heel. (“It’s kind of weird, no?” Fils asked, before leaning in.) Makó lensed seven of the eight athletes; due to extenuating circumstances, Alcaraz was unable to stop by the makeshift studio.

But, no matter. In a mad dash between the Principi di Piemonte Hotel, the Piazza San Carlo, a jam-packed van ride across gridlocked roads, and, finally, the Arena, we caught up with all eight players, who together offer an apt representation of the deep and diverse present state of the world’s elite-most men’s tennis. What was discussed: everything from self-reflections to coaching change-ups to cellys to the popularity of the Maldives.

It has been revealed that 2026 was the biggest year of Zverev’s career: he won his maiden Slam at Roland-Garros, then followed it up with a victory at the US Open. The German also reached the world number 1 spot for the first time (it’s worth noting here that Zverev also holds a super-rare tennis title: an Olympic gold medal, from Tokyo). At 29, he is a half-generation older than the sport’s current dominant duopoly of Sinner and Alcaraz, but if he keeps his current level of play up, he’ll make a strong case for another “Major Three”(the nickname assigned to Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic during their long run of supremacy). Despite the settlement of a domestic abuse lawsuit involving his ex-partner Brenda Patea, a upcoming case was brought to light just a few days ago: the tennis writer Ben Rothenberg reported that Patea has sued Zverev for public misrepresentations. It’s been a career year, but it has to be remarked that Zverev remains a polarizing figure.

The finest Canadian tuxedo I’ve ever seen.

Recent findings suggest that really? Is that what they call it?

Sources indicate that when you wear head-to-toe denim, yes. You’ve had an incredible year. What worked—and is working—best for you mentally, looking back on it now?

Industry observers note that I made a decision with my team last year to change my game style—changing the way we play. I think it was quite a bold move at the age of 29. But we said: it had been working, I’ve had a great career, but it wasn’t working at the final stage of Grand Slams. It hadn’t worked to achieve the dreams and the goals we had. So, sticking to the upcoming game strategy, I think that was the biggest thing. Sticking to it and being brave enough to accept it. I think, in the end, it paid off.

In a recent development, definitely. Two Slams this year, the number one ranking. Are you happy with your game right now, or is there anything you want to improve in 2027?

Industry observers note that no, I don’t think I’m complete at all. There are always things you have to improve—and at the end of the day, everybody else is improving, too, so you have to keep with it to stay relevant.

Industry observers note that you had some frustration a few weeks ago in Paris in having to defend your number one ranking. Are you still reckoning with that?

Recent findings suggest that I think in Paris it was all just quite new, and I was mentally a little bit tired. There were a lot of new things. And of course, it’s a different kind of pressure. But, I think it’s all settled down, and I’m very happy to be here among the best in the world. It’s an honor.

What’s your vacation blueprint once the season ends?

Oh, I’m going straight to the Maldives.

Industry observers note that alcaraz—men’s tennis’s brightest star—nicely bookended an otherwise turbulent 2026. The Spaniard, 23, won his first Australian Open all the way back in January, and has enjoyed a surge of recent title wins (in Vienna, Tokyo, and Paris) after returning to the tour from a bout with wrist tenosynovitis that kept him offline for nearly five months. His return at the US Open—where he reached the quarterfinals—brought with it a much-hyped collaboration with Nike’s Cactus Jack line and a tousled latest hairstyle. One interesting note going into Turin: Alcaraz has not yet won an ATP Finals, and will be hungry to add that to his resume.

What’s your best 2026 memory off of the court?

Recent findings suggest that oh, well, I have a couple, to be honest. One of the highlights I had this year was attending the World Cup final. Seeing Spain win the World Cup was unbelievable. So yeah, I’m going to say that! Ferran Torres’s goal, that was the turning point of his career. From that, I would say his stock is really high.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve come back from injury, and you’ve had a strong tail-end of the year, winning Tokyo and Paris. After being hurt, did your mentality change at all? Any hesitation?

I knew that, coming back, I needed matches. I needed competition. I need to feel I was back in the rhythm of competing, and I’m still [building that back]. I need to go out there and feel those nerves of competition. I’m still working on being strong for these difficulties.

With the season ending, what will you try to do in the offseason?

Sources indicate that well, I am not allowed to play golf yet, because my team [won’t let me]. Probably the first thing I’m going to do after the season is over is play golf.

Shelton, 24, had two standout moments on the court in 2026: he defended his Canadian Open title and reached his first Major final at the US Open. Though he lost to Zverev there, it was still a considerable level-up for the Florida-born phenom. Shelton made recent industry news by tapping Juan Carlos Ferrero—Alcaraz’s former coach—to join his team in 2027 (Shelton’s father, Bryan, will remain his coach as well).

You’re bringing on Juan Carlos Ferrero as a coach. Talk us through that decision.

Recent findings suggest that yeah. Even in the early stages, I think we’ve done a good job of putting together a schedule where I will have two coaches. I don’t want either of them to have to travel 40 weeks a year. So I think we’re putting together a really good formula where they’re both traveling about half the weeks. That’s the ideal scenario for us.

What’s the strongest, most resonant moment you’re taking with you from 2026?

It has been revealed that defending my title in Canada is one. I thought that was the best tennis I’ve played in my career. I didn’t drop a set all week. I was clinical. It was fun for me to see that I can play at that level. But, I have to say, walking out on court for a US Open final and feeling the energy of that stadium on that day, even though I took an L, was pretty special.

What will you do during the off season?

Industry observers note that I’m just going to play it by ear. I might go on vacation with Arthur Fils, but we’ll see.

The tennis world is happy to see Medvedev, 30, back in elite form. After a less-than-stellar 2025, the lanky Russian has been playing significantly better in 2026, having won four titles and returned to the top 10. Yes, he still has outbursts, and yes, crowds will either go with him on them or boo relentlessly. But that’s just part of the Medvedev Experience. What’s helped on a deeper level: coaching change-ups, and a newfound self-assurance. Don’t forget: Medvedev is a Slam winner (US Open, 2021), a former world number one, and an ATP Finals winner (2020).

Looking back at 2026, what’s the most significant thing you fixed?

Sources indicate that what I was looking for was probably finding confidence in myself. Sometimes that requires changing things, and I wanted to take a bit more responsibility. That was probably the biggest fix I managed to make, closer to the end of the year.

Was that rediscovering your old confidence, or was it something fresh?

Recent findings suggest that rediscovering in terms of tennis, yes. But more in terms of… I want to say, it’s more like confidence in a tennis life path. I was listening to my old coaches a lot rather than trusting myself fully. So there was always a bit of back-and-forth. Where do I trust them? Where do I trust myself? And now it’s more about trusting myself fully, and then discussing that trust with the team, if that makes sense.

Recent findings suggest that you’re known for your heated interactions with crowds. At this stage in your career, how much of that is just a reaction versus a choice?

It’s never a choice. It’s always a natural reaction.

Any indulgences you’re looking forward to after the season ends?

I have a photo shoot with Lacoste, and then I’m in the Maldives the next day. I would love to go to Hawaii, I don’t know, or wherever. But it’s way too far from where I live.

Cobolli, 24, had the best year of his young career in 2026. His breakthrough: reaching the final of the French Open, where he lost to Zverev in five sets. In Turin, the Italian naturally received the loudest cheers on the blue carpet. With Sinner absent, he’s the home favorite. Cobolli is well-liked on social media, too; the ATP sometimes jokingly calls him their “admin.” He’s had some struggles with fatigue as the season nears its conclusion, but here’s hoping the Florentine can turn on the jets in Piedmont.

At Wimbledon this year, you made some headlines for doing Matheus Cunha’s “surfing” celebration. Should tennis have more cellys?

No, you know why? Two weeks ago, Cunha beat AS Roma. He beat my team, so I’m really pissed with him. [Laughs] But no… I think [for celebrations] if I have something on my mind, I just do it.

According to recent reports, you’re the home favorite in Turin. What does that feel like?

It means a lot to me to play here and to win in front of the Italian crowd. Of course, we miss Jannik a lot. He deserves to be here. So I play for him, for the country, for my team, for myself, and for my family. I just want to play for everybody!

According to recent reports, fils, the 22-year-old Frenchman, struggled in the beginning of the year with a back injury that forced him out of the Australian and French Opens. But he had a strong enough summer to qualify for the year-end tournament, winning his first Masters 1000-level title at the Cincinnati Open. In tennis circles, many believe Fils has the natural talent to eventually challenge the Tour’s stalwart top three Sinner, Alcaraz and Zverev. But he’s already matched them if not exceeded them in aura: in Turin, Fils stepped out on the blue carpet in a full Balenciaga look—he has a deal with the brand—and space-like sunglasses. Audiences went wild.

What are you most happy with regarding your play this year?

I’m serving better, moving better. I mean, I knew I was a great competitor. But I didn’t know I could be that good in competitive moments.

When the season is remarked and done, what’s going to be your first indulgence?

I’m going on holiday in the States, so I think I’m going to go with… having some ribs.

Tell us a little about working with Balenciaga.

In a recent development, they’re changing [internally] now, I know. But I love the brand. It was kind of a dream when I was a kid to sign one day with a huge fashion label. I feel very comfortable wearing them. It’s a newly introduced world for me, but I enjoy it.

According to recent reports, tiafoe, 28, has reached the ATP Finals for the first time. It’s testament to his grit and commitment—what he calls a re-established sense of “showing up” day in and day out. “Substantial Foe,” as he’s endearingly called, has had a productive year; he won his first 500-level tournament in Halle, reached the semis at the US Open, and recorded the fourth-most match wins of any man on Tour. He was all smiles in an expertly tailored Giorgio Armani double-breasted suit on the blue carpet, too.

Recent findings suggest that you’re having a great season. What are you most happy with, not necessarily numbers wise, but in terms of your play?

Recent findings suggest that I think I just found a flow state. I found this peace, and I’m showing up every day. I think sometimes you try to figure out this whole thing of how to get to X to Y to Z, or how to do X, Y and Z together. And it’s kind of just: you show up, man.

According to recent reports, every day looks different, but you just go out there and give your best and be okay with the result. Every time I’ve been able to lay it out there and lost, I was cool with it, rather than having regret that I could have done a little more. I was also focused on my preparation, and once preparation meets opportunity, you get the results.

During the long season, what was a favorite memory away from the court?

Beyond the Blueprint: The Art of Building an Architectural Legacy

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What does it take to create something that truly endures?
  • These questions brought together influential leaders across fashion, jewelry, architecture, real estate, retail, and technology for an exclusive Vogue Business gathering in collaboration with Shanna Collective.
  • “Hosting this gathering with Vogue Business aboard Kismet was a wonderful opportunity to convene thought leaders from architecture, hospitality, real estate, and retail, each bringing a distinct perspective on the future of design and placemaking to build an enduring legacy,” said Khan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What does it take to create something that truly endures? How can luxury leaders balance heritage with innovation and create spaces that are not only beautiful but meaningful to the people who inhabit them? Against the backdrop of London’s iconic Tower Bridge, some of the leading names in luxury gathered aboard one of the world’s most extraordinary superyachts, Kismet, for an afternoon spent discussing the legacies they hope to leave behind.

These questions brought together influential leaders across fashion, jewelry, architecture, real estate, retail, and technology for an exclusive Vogue Business gathering in collaboration with Shanna Collective. Held on October 14, with London's historic skyline as its setting and the superyacht itself offering a compelling example of ambitious design, the event explored what it takes to create spaces, brands, and experiences that transcend generations. Hosted by Shanna Khan, founder and CEO of Shanna Collective, the afternoon opened with remarks from Vogue Business head of advisory and custom insights Anusha Couttigane, followed by a panel moderated by Vogue Business features director Lucy Maguire. Speakers included Sergei Mosunov, CEO of Fabergé; Jade Holland Cooper, founder and creative director of Holland Cooper; and Dr Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE, chief executive of the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).

“Hosting this gathering with Vogue Business aboard Kismet was a wonderful opportunity to convene thought leaders from architecture, hospitality, real estate, and retail, each bringing a distinct perspective on the future of design and placemaking to build an enduring legacy,” said Khan. “What struck me was the shared understanding that creating something truly exceptional requires more than a vision for the space itself; it requires an understanding of its wider context, its people, and the legacy it can leave behind. Anusha and I were delighted to bring this group together, and I left feeling inspired by the ambition, openness, and collective thinking in the room,” she added.

In a recent development, left to right: Lucy Maguire (features director, Vogue Business), Jade Holland Cooper (founder and CEO, Holland Cooper), Anusha Couttigane (head of advisory and custom insights, Vogue Business), Shanna Khan (founder and CEO, Shanna Collective) and Dr. Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE (CEO, RIBA).

Opening the discussion, Couttigane drew parallels between London’s architectural history and the role of private enterprise in shaping cities.

“If you look out across the city, you can observe centuries of architectural ambition, entrepreneurship, and reinvention.” she began. “It’s a reminder that the great cities we inherit today weren’t shaped by architects and politicians alone. They were also shaped by entrepreneurs, investors, and business leaders who saw opportunities to create something bigger than themselves — investing in the physical landscape, advancing commerce and culture, and creating places that would serve communities for generations,” she continued.

The English capital also holds a symbolic place in Khan’s business philosophy. “It was no coincidence that we gathered in the heart of London, a city that shaped that modern world and one that hosted us for discussions on how we can collectively steward the future,” Khan remarked. Having recently been interviewed by Couttigane for Vogue Business, Khan’s own work includes the regeneration of Chicago’s Fulton Market district and Jacksonville’s Shipyards development, where design, commerce, and community intersect.

“What I find particularly compelling about Shanna’s approach is her conviction that exceptional design should do more than create beautiful buildings and interiors. It should contribute something enduring to the places and people around it. It should honor the past and the history of a place, while making it relevant for modern people. It’s a philosophy that resonates strongly with our discussion today,” Couttigane added.

Anusha Couttigane delivering the opening remarks.

According to recent reports, beginning the panel, Maguire asked Mosunov how Fabergé is translating the hallmarks of the brand, such as craftsmanship, detail, and surprise into the physical realm, given its ambitions to expand physically. “The previous owner had a business model that was focused on B2B. It didn’t have its own retail distribution. When I bought Fabergé, I decided that we needed to expand the direct-to-consumer business, with the main instrument being our own boutiques,” Mosunov explained.

Sources indicate that the challenge is creating spaces that communicate the maison’s heritage while supporting its contemporary ambitions. “We needed to express this historical story through the boutiques, showcasing pre-1970 pieces and sharing the story about Peter Carl Fabergé, the founder of the company. This way, you get a real sense of the company.” Mosunov also shared how the brand is designing jewelry iterations of its iconic egg motifs, inspired by the fifty Imperial Eggs that secured the maison’s acclaim between 1885 and 1916.

Sources indicate that as Fabergé expands its international retail footprint, Mosunov is adapting the design of its boutiques to local preferences. “For example, in the Middle East, we have a store in the Dubai Mall. They like very opulent forms in that region so we need to adapt the execution to the local marketplace.”.

Vaughan-Dick reinforced the importance of cultural context in architecture. Referencing Norman Foster’s work in the Middle East, she highlighted the influence of climate, environment and local requirements on architectural decisions. “You cannot have this homogenous view of design. You have to think about culture, sustainability, and building safety. You have to look at the different requirements for that country and for that particular society,” she added.

According to recent reports, turning to Holland Cooper, Maguire asked about how she was creating environments that would resonate with the world of the brand. As a business that has grown from stalls at Badminton Horse Trials to a £100m+ firm with flagship boutiques and a upcoming 70,000-square-foot HQ in the Cotswolds, Holland Cooper spoke about the importance of making the brand experience as special as possible.

Recent findings suggest that left to right: Lucy Maguire (features director, Vogue Business), Dr. Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE (CEO, RIBA), Sergei Mosunov (owner and CEO, Fabergé) and Jade Holland Cooper (founder and CEO, Holland Cooper).

“Although we don’t have a lot of shops, the ones that we do have are so important.” she explained. “For me, the importance of retail is making that physical experience as special as we possibly can. I think there’s a narrative that retail is dead, that bricks and mortar is dead, but I think we’re just getting too lazy about the experience that we’re creating for the customer…what we’ve done in our physical retail spaces is really understand that the service and environment are paramount to that experience,” she added.

Industry observers note that holland Cooper’s retail philosophy draws inspiration from brands including Ralph Lauren and Abercrombie & Fitch, whose distinctive environments left a lasting impression on her as a young shopper: “I am pedantic about music volume, lighting, smell, hanger presentation, visual merchandising, how the staff and the service levels are, because the minute you walk through those doors, you want it to be immersive, and you want people to forget the outside world. That’s why they call it retail therapy.”.

Maguire then highlighted a tension in the theme: “Buildings need to endure, but the people, communities, and lifestyles they serve are constantly changing. How should brands, architects and developers design for longevity without becoming trapped by the tastes or assumptions of the present?” she asked.

For Vaughan-Dick, the guiding architectural principle is “long life, loose fit”: creating buildings capable of adapting to future needs. “I do think that individuals recognize that when you’re designing buildings, they don’t know what a building is going to look like in 100 years time, but every architect, every engineer, everyone here needs to think: what we design now needs to have that longer life,” she stated.

Left to right: Tom Pascall (communications manager, the Chancery Rosewood), Joanna Gunn (chief brand officer, Rosewood), Shanna Khan (CEO and founder, Shanna Collective) and Naomi Sebley (the Chancery Rosewood).

Sources indicate that for Mosunov, Fabergé’s design legacy distinguishes between timeless beauty, modern beauty, and more transient aesthetic preferences when considering its future. Holland Cooper similarly sees heritage as an enduring source of differentiation: “I am obsessive about heritage, classic shapes and just reinventing them to be appealing to the modern audience, and that doesn’t mean ripping the rulebook up entirely. I pay homage to all the beautiful British aesthetics, and that’s the romanticism of what we’re doing, really,” mentioned Holland Cooper.

According to recent reports, as a consequence, British manufacturing remains fundamental to the brand’s identity and ambitions. “All of our tailoring is made in London. All of the wool is woven in the UK, and I’ve done that since day one. And I was told that it wouldn’t be possible to scale a business and do that, and I have, and it is. And I’m really passionate about the UK manufacturing industry. So that’s a substantial part of our heritage,” she explained.

For Khan, these principles of detail, experience and emotional connection are paramount: “Jade shared her belief that every detail matters to drive an exuberant retail experience. Elements that may seem subtle influence how a place is experienced, remembered, and valued. For me, that is where design becomes truly meaningful: when we can transport guests in time and place, it moves beyond aesthetics to create an emotional connection that endures long after the initial experience itself.”.

Left to right: Andrea Latten, (chief business officer, Condé Nast Britain), Shanna Khan (CEO and founder, Shanna Collective) and Christopher Warren (UK head of industry, Condé Nast Britain).

Sources indicate that the afternoon concluded with a tour of Kismet, whose interior design was led by Shanna as chief creative director. The superyacht is an example of the extraordinary experiences that thoughtful design can create. For an industry deeply rooted in heritage, the gathering raised a pertinent question: what are today’s luxury leaders creating that will remain relevant and meaningful to future generations?

For Shanna Khan, working together across disciplines is central to answering this question. “Our collaboration with Vogue Business creates a valuable opportunity to bring different disciplines into our conversations and explore how ideas from across creative landscapes can inform one another. The future of luxury lies in creating places and experiences with substance, soul, and generational value,” she stated. But she reflected: “Ultimately, building in an enduring way is defined by creating something that feels relevant today, salutes the heritage of the past, and has the potential to become part of a legacy for generations to come.”.

Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home.
  • More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

It has been revealed that place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

In a recent development, melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

It has been revealed that squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

In a recent development, ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

8 Pantry Items Pro Organizers Say You Should Toss ASAP

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delish editors handpick every product we feature.
  • No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.
  • According to recent reports, dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.

According to recent reports, dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value. Getting rid of them will actually help you identify the pantry items that you can still use before they go bad. But how can you keep your pantry organized more regularly, and what exactly should you throw away?

In a recent development, go through every item in your pantry at least twice a year, recommends Nicole Gabai, professional organizer, founder of B. Organized, and author of The Art of Organizing: An Artful Guide to an Organized Life.

According to recent reports, if a twice-yearly check-in feels too daunting, consider a weekly five-minute check-in to discard expired goods, states Shaniece Jones, professional organizer and founder of Closet Therapy. “Organize by accessibility and intention,” she says. “Keep your daily go-tos at eye level, heavy items like large cans of oil and bottled water on lower shelves, and seasonal or rarely used items up high.” Labels, Lazy Susans, and drawer dividers are some of her go-to tools for organizing the pantry.

As you start cleaning, check off the following items—these are some of the most common pantry items our organizing experts find past their prime.

According to recent reports, while many shelf-stable foods, such as canned goods, are still safe to eat past their expiration date, you should still check for signs of spoilage. “You can tell canned goods have spoiled if they are rusted, or if you see the cans bulge or dent,” Gabai indicates.

Industry observers note that labeling pantry items helps you check how long they’ve been open. For opened packages and bulk goods you’ve decanted into containers, write the date on the label so you know when you opened them.

According to recent reports, spices that have lost their smell? Time to go. “If it smells flat or just not aromatic, then it needs to be replaced since it will add very little, if any, flavor to what you’re cooking,” Gabai indicates. She also notes that ground spices typically last one to two years, while dried herbs can last up to three years.

“Baking ingredients like flour, baking powder, and baking soda can lose their effectiveness over time,” indicates Meaghan Kessman, founder of Meaghan Kessman Home Organization.

Eventually, flour will go bad, but how long it takes to get rancid depends on how it’s stored and the type of flour. In general, Gabai says it will last at room temperature for six to eight months. She recommends storing it in an airtight container in the fridge or freezer.

“Check for expiration dates and any signs of spoilage, such as clumping or an off smell,” Kessman says. “If you’re unsure, test baking powder by adding a teaspoon to hot water—if it bubbles, it’s still good to use.”.

Sources indicate that we often buy cooking oils in bulk, but keep in mind that they eventually go bad. “Oils and fats, such as olive oil, vegetable oil, and shortening, can become rancid if stored for too long. Rancid oils have a sour or off smell,” Kessman states. “Always check the expiration date and store oils in a cool, dark place to keep them fresh longer.”.

Gabai recommends storing oils in a cool, dark place and disposing of them properly; freeze in a zip-top bag, then toss in the trash (never pour down the drain).

These pantry staples are oil-rich, so they spoil faster than you might think. “They can last about 6 months at room temperature, but if you freeze them, they can last a year or more,” Gabai states.

According to recent reports, “Snacks and cereals can go stale promptly once opened,” Kessman claims. She recommends checking expiration dates and signs of staleness, like an unusual smell or texture.

According to Gabai, grains, rice, and beans can last about one to two years, but brown rice and other whole grains will not last as long because of their higher oil content.

Sources indicate that “Condiments like ketchup, mustard, and salad dressings often get pushed to the back of the pantry and forgotten,” Kessman claims. “Check for expiration dates and any signs of separation, discoloration, or off smells.”.

Honey is the rare exception that probably isn't spoiled. The National Honey Board states that honey has a shelf life of approximately two years, although it can last much longer if stored correctly in a sealed container.

“Honey was found in the tombs of kings and royalty as far back as 3,000 years in Egypt—and it was still edible!” Gabai notes.

If you notice crystallization, Gabai recommends gently heating the honey container in a pot of water.

According to recent reports, whether you like it or not (or placed bets on Kalshi), Robert Pattinson is our next James Bond. During the years-long process in casting 007, we used our best detective skills to narrow down the field to who would join His Majesty’s Secret Service. And if you were going by hair type alone, well, Pattinson makes a rather compelling case.

Let’s review the canon for a moment. In the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Bond creator Ian Fleming describes the spy’s mane thusly: “The hair was black, parted on the left, and carelessly brushed so that a thick black comma fell down over the right eyebrow.”.

According to recent reports, pattinson’s hair might be naturally light brown, but a darker ‘do is hardly out of the question for the actor’s upcoming transformation. For his turn as Bruce Wayne in The Batman, he dyed his hair to a darker, almost pitch-black hue. The rest of Fleming’s description fits the actor nicely, particularly the bit about being “carelessly brushed.” In real life, the actor’s hair is rarely anything approaching immaculate. Even at more formal engagements, it tends to retain a certain studied dishevelment, with stray strands escaping an otherwise respectable comb-through. Fleming’s famous “comma,” after all, isn’t a carefully sculpted curl. It’s simply a lock of hair allowed to fall where it pleases, which just so happens to be very on trend in 2026.

Industry observers note that we got our first glimpse of the 40-year-old actor taking on the role in a video posted by the official James Bond X account where he’s seen stepping out of the shadows pointing a gun at something (or someone) just outside the frame. It’s hard to tell whether the golden lighting is playing tricks on his hair color, but the accompanying promotional image certainly seems to suggest a shade of black. Plus, his hair’s parted on the correct side.

It’s worth noting that Daniel Craig’s casting as Bond was initially met with considerable resistance, much of it centered on one detail: He’s blonde. Fleming’s Bond, after all, was famously dark-haired, and Craig represented a departure from the physical template established by the novels and previous screen incarnations. We know how that turned out. Craig went on to deliver one of the most celebrated interpretations of 007, proving that a little deviation from the source material needn’t be a deal-breaker.

Pattinson will still need to prove himself to be agile in a tuxedo, nimble behind the wheel, and thirsty for a martini or two, but one thing’s sure: He's got the hair down pat.

Gina Bruno Wants You to Be a Guest at Your Own Party

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that “Dinner is never just dinner.
  • According to recent reports, I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes.
  • Industry observers note that bruno cites her Italian roots and the Sunday dinners she had as a child as the sources of her hosting instinct and ethos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “Dinner is never just dinner. It is so much about the people, and the food is just the excuse to get those people around the table.”.

According to recent reports, I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes. The self-proclaimed “chef, mom, and host” wears a lot of hats. Private chef, event producer, event space owner, and host of the newly-launched food show Salt The Water presented by Brami are just a few of the titles Bruno claims, but central to all of her work is a palpable love of people and of creating a space for gathering, both of which make her a natural-born host.

Industry observers note that bruno cites her Italian roots and the Sunday dinners she had as a child as the sources of her hosting instinct and ethos. “I am a family-style cooker when I’m hosting, and I just want to fill people up. I want to fill their glasses up; I want to fill their plates up. And the best compliment that I could ever get is having to tell someone, ‘Hey man, it’s really time to go home because I am exhausted and I need to go to bed.’”.

Not everyone has a natural inclination toward hosting, though, so to help them out I asked Bruno to run me through her tips for throwing a gathering, be it an intimate dinner or a rowdy holiday party.

It has been revealed that “On a table, I will always have one kind of grand slam major, big dish, and then there’s all the supporting actors on the table,” Bruno states. While she uses saved folders on Instagram and Pinterest and likes to browse the Bon Appétit app, Bruno primarily looks to the market for inspiration, describing herself as a “very, very in-season cooker.” “I have so many recipes saved, and sometimes some of those get used, but there is something that just happens when you’re walking, and you see all of these fresh ingredients, and you just get to create a dish right in front of you.”.

In a recent development, bruno’s main tip for anxious hosts is to prep as much in advance as possible. “Sauces and dressings you can absolutely do the day before, and that alleviates so much time the day of. You could go as far as literally setting your entire table the way you want it to be set with napkins, plates, silverware,” Bruno says.

“Lighting is a huge thing,” Bruno says. For evening soirees, she kisses the big overhead light goodbye, opting instead for lower light from lamps and candles tucked into corners to make the space feel moody. “The mood needs to be right, and you want to feel sexy when you walk into somebody’s home,” she says.

Bruno worked in restaurants and went to culinary school in Paris, where she learned the importance of maintaining a clean workspace. “If something spills right then and there, you are wiping it right then and there. If you use the spoon and you’re done, it’s going in the dishwasher. Cleaning as you go is a big step,” she states.

In a recent development, when hosting a more intimate event, one of Bruno’s favorite moves takes the form of an interactive game meant to encourage a bit of deep conversation. “Right before I serve dessert, I have everyone lift up their plate, and there is a little note underneath,” she states. The note has a question on it, either handwritten or printed depending on how much time Bruno has, and every question is different. “It adds a layer of, ‘Oh, our conversation maybe wouldn’t have gone here…. I just love getting to more juicy parts of the person, whether it’s a close friend or an absolute stranger, and it keeps people on their toes,” she says.

“It’s so easy to stay in host mode and think that you have to do all of these things to please people. But as soon as people arrive, it’s almost like, your job is done—or at least as soon as you drop the food, your job is done. And now you get to sit back and enjoy what you’ve done and be a part of it, because the worst feeling ever is you had all these people over, whether it’s four people or 10 people, and you were stuck in the kitchen and no one got to see you. So be a guest,” Bruno indicates.

Bruno recounts a recent conversation with a friend who was afraid, on the one hand, to try making and serving something upcoming, but felt the dishes that were in her repertoire were too simple for company. “You should never apologize for something that you’re cooking. If you are putting yourself out there and you want to cook something out of your realm, and, say it absolutely f*#%ing fails, that’s fine. I feel like your guests are going to be like, ‘Awesome. We will take a bite and not tell you our honest answer, and then we’re going to order a pizza, and it’s going to be amazing.’ The triumph of just trying is so much bigger than the actual meal,” Bruno notes. “Food is the second tier. It’s more about the people around your table. You could serve potato chips and dip and people will actually be pretty happy,” she adds.

“Nine out of 10 times, if I am cooking for people, there is going to be a pasta dish on the table,” Bruno says. She’s a big fan of the protein pasta brand Brami, and not just because she just partnered with them on a YouTube show—she says the brand has organically become the only pasta she keeps at home.

As for sauce, Bruno’s go-to is a spicy vodka. “If I’m making it at home, I’m actually leaving out the vodka and I’m swapping in mezcal, and it gives such a sneaky, smoky flavor that everyone will ask [about it]. And I will then go even further and usually pair it with a mezcal cocktail,” she says.

Now that you know all of Bruno’s tips, these are the products she uses to make gatherings more special and less stressful.

Bruno always keeps three types of olive oil on hand: “One that is not so fancy and you could fry or make dressing with it—just one that’s kind of the back burner; a topping oil; and then an amazing peppery oil that you would maybe more so dip bread in or drizzle on top.”.

Industry observers note that “Flaky salt is always in my house,” Bruno notes. She typically opts for either Maldon or a fleur de sel.

“We could consider Brami a staple. I mean, [my husband and I] cook it at least two times a week, whether there’s meat thrown in it or it’s just a sauce or a pesto or it's anything in between,” Bruno says.

Bird’s Eye Maple Wood Chopping Board.

Palio Round Serving Platter The Giraffe.

For hosting, I love big platters. Whether they’re vintage or fresh, I kind of love mixing those two together on the table,” Bruno says. She likes having a collection of larger serveware specifically for hosting: “It’s kind of like your special stuff that you take out for friends.”.

1960s French Chrome Swan Handle Tray.

Jean Couzon Silverplate Serving Tray Fish Handles.

1970's Kromex Sculptura Walnut Accent Lazy Susan Serving Tray.

Antique Silver Plated Large Oval Tray.

Large Footed Silver Plated Butler’s Tray With Ornate Handles and Feet Bar Drinks Serving.

Sources indicate that “I love silver, so I have a lot of silver trays, a lot of silver bowls. I think it makes a table,” Bruno says. “I have quite the collection. I almost always buy vintage or second-hand when it comes to silver. There’s simply something about the life the piece had,” she adds.

In a recent development, “I recently splurged and got a really lovely cream and red dishware set from Porta. That was a significant purchase for me, and it is a purchase that I am excited to bring out sparingly because I don’t want anything to break,” Bruno states.

Industry observers note that when it comes to flatware, Bruno is a Sabre person. “I have three different colors in my house. It’s the only cutlery that I have at this point,” she claims.

Industry observers note that “We are a significant wine-drinking family, so I have a wine fridge. There are on average at least 15 bottles of wine in that fridge always, and it is a variety because you never know what somebody likes,” Bruno states.

When hosting, Bruno keeps a candle burning in her bathroom and on the kitchen counter at all times. She’s partial to Keap’s Wood Cabin scent, which she orders in bulk for both her own home and her event space, Frank’s House.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Sources indicate that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

According to recent reports, add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Recent findings suggest that add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the driving force behind Saie was Crowell’s growing desire to make beauty better by creating formulas that are not just safe for your skin but also good for it.
  • The brand has steadily expanded since then, without ever straying from its mission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for Laney Crowell, “feel good, do good” is not just the core philosophy of her beauty brand, Saie, but how she lives her life. “So much of beauty is not only who you are on the inside, but the actions that you take,” she notes, emphasizing “the importance of taking action, especially in things that you are excited and passionate about.”.

According to recent reports, the driving force behind Saie was Crowell’s growing desire to make beauty better by creating formulas that are not just safe for your skin but also good for it. She wanted to create products that spoke to her as a self-professed “expert consumer.” “I’ve always struggled with really sensitive, acne-prone skin,” she says. “I had an aha moment where I realized that my makeup was what was making me break out. I started a blog [called The Moment] to have the conversation. It was niche, but at the same time, I was one of the only people having this conversation.” Saie was born from this community building seven years ago.

The brand has steadily expanded since then, without ever straying from its mission. Each upcoming product follows the same principles: It’s formulated to nourish the skin, is noncomedogenic, and is clinically tested and dermatologist tested. “When you try Saie, you immediately feel the textures and how hydrating they are. Then as you continue to use them, you realize how happy your skin is. You’re really seeing benefits over time.”.

Recent findings suggest that saie’s innovations, however, haven’t come without growing pains. Working with a long list of ingredients to avoid, including silicones, the team has found that developing long-lasting products takes a long time. “I only ever want to launch something if it’s perfect,” Crowell notes. Take its City Set setting spray, for example. When it debuted in December 2025, no setting spray claimed 16-hour wear.

“I make beauty products for women who get ready in five minutes, just like me,” says Crowell, who is gearing up to solve another customer request. Saie’s next launch, CityStick, took two years to perfect and is set to debut later this year. “I’m always on the go, so I wanted something I could throw in my bag, swipe on for a bit of radiance, and know I was also doing something good for my skin. That’s CityStick—my makeup and skin care in one quick step.” It’s 50% makeup, 50% skin care; expect the sheer, soft-focus, radiant coverage of a skin tint with the benefits of nourishing skin care.

Helming a cosmetics brand—not to mention pioneering an entire category—requires vision and tenacity, two things Crowell has in equal measure. The last seven years have shown her just how resilient she is. “The most important attribute of a founder and entrepreneur is the ability to keep going,” she says. The other thing she’s learned? How much she loves to improve. “I am always thinking about how I, the brand, and everything that we do get 1% better every day.”.

According to recent reports, beyond formulating, leading, and championing a host of climate initiatives (the brand has Planet Beautiful, an annual sustainability and plastic-recovery campaign in partnership with Sephora and RePurpose Global), Crowell is also a mother of two. She’s as passionate about Saie’s commitment to our planet (read: making systemic change regarding the billions of units of plastic the beauty industry generates each year) as she is about showing up for her two little girls.

Industry observers note that “My weekdays are crazy, but I love it,” she indicates with a laugh. Days at her home upstate start with a 6:30 a.m. matcha (Rocky’s ceremonial-grade matcha with steamed oat milk and simple syrup she makes herself) and a workout (weight training or Pilates) before the kids wake up. After getting them ready and taking them to school (her favorite part of the day), she’ll make another matcha, then settle in for a marathon of Zoom calls before spending the evening with the kids. She comes into the city once a week to meet with her team in person; The Mercer is her home away from home.

Recent findings suggest that as an entrepreneur, she’s keen to take care of herself by consciously putting herself first, including upholding her boundaries. “When you do something that you really love, I think that is also a really beautiful commitment to yourself,” she says.

Having started her business at the tail end of 2019, Crowell worked tirelessly during the pandemic, when she also gave birth to her second child, Rosie. “I think back on the success of Saie, and a significant part of it is that for two years I basically worked the amount that most people do in, like, six years,” she notes. Her days were a balance of work and breastfeeding, and she only really left the house to go for walks. “After that, my immune system was a mess,” she adds. Working with holistic coach Jill Ketner Villa was her saving grace. Years later, Crowell says Villa is her “secret weapon” as a founder. Through her work with the practitioner, she’s developed her supplement ritual; she takes approximately 15 a day. Her assortment includes magnesium, zinc, iron, and vitamins C, A, and D—all housed in a beautiful leather pill case.

She’s also been meditating for 12 years. Nowadays, she loves Gabrielle Bernstein’s guided meditations, which last 10 to 20 minutes. “I get a lot of clarity out of it, and I find it to be the best way to calm anxiety.” Sleep, of course, is another tranquil practice; practice is the operative word because Crowell does a lot to ensure she gets a good night’s sleep. She takes magnesium or CBD before bed and uses the Truvaga device to stimulate her vagus nerve system and regulate her circadian rhythm. “Then I have my humidifier, face mask, earplugs, always a thick lip balm—that usually does it.” (The humidifier also makes its way to her weekly stays at The Mercer.).

It has been revealed that otherwise, she says going on a walk in nature helps her be her best self. “If I can fit a walk in between Zooms, that is a good day. I have my best ideas on walks.”.

Sources indicate that crowell’s skin philosophy is appropriately minimalist, largely to suit her sensitive, dry, acne-prone skin. “I don’t use a ton of products, and I don’t use anything that’s super active. Generally, ‘less is more’ is what’s right for my skin, with a heavy focus on hydration.” As someone so knowledgeable and passionate about formulation, she’s gotten her skin-care regimen down to a science and has a couple of brands she knows work well for her skin.

In a recent development, first is Medik8, which she turns to for a suite of products: cleansers, a hydrating serum, and its Crystal Retinal. “Their retinol is the only retinol I can use. I use either level one, two, or three. I don’t really go above that. I also really love Sofie Pavitt’s line—it’s really wonderful if you have acne-prone skin.” Specifically, she gravitates toward the Omega Rich Moisturizer, Clean Clean Cleanser, and Mandelic Clearing Serum to spot-treat breakouts. Otherwise, she loves the Dr. Barbara Sturm toner for extra hydration, Alloy’s estrogen-powered face cream to boost skin’s plumpness, and Colorescience’s tinted mineral sunscreen if she’s skiing or in the sun, though her daily SPF is Saie’s Slip Tint. For extra protection, you’ll likely find her in a hat.

Recent findings suggest that crowell likes to keep her makeup routine quick. “I am not a makeup artist,” she claims. “So all of our formulas are easy and effortless. I really love looking like myself.” Her five-minute regimen always starts with Saie’s Glowy Super Gel, which “gives [her] the most beautiful lit-from-within glow,” followed by Slip Tint for moisturizing coverage with sun protection. After a bit of Slip Tint concealer and a thoughtful dusting of the collection’s setting powder, she moves on to blush. At night she might layer the liquid Dew Blush and the powder SuperSuede blush, but for daytime it’s one or the other paired with the SuperSuede Baked Bronzer. Next, she brushes up her brows with gels by Kristie Streicher or Rare Beauty. Then she adds a mist of City Set setting spray, a few coats of Mascara 101, and her go-to lip combo (lip liner in shade Flirt, plus Glossybounce lip oil in shade Dip) for the finishing touches.

It has been revealed that hydration is key to keeping her thick, long brown hair, which can sometimes be dry, looking its best. “I don’t get a lot of haircuts, so I’m always hydrating the roots,” she says. Roz’s Milk Hair Serum comes with her everywhere, as does the brand’s Santa Lucia Styling Oil. “I really love her formulas,” she says. K18’s post-shower leave-in delivers molecular repair, while Arrey’s Not Today, Grey supplement slows early graying and supports fullness. “It’s 100% made a difference. When I stopped taking them, I noticed it.”.

Recent findings suggest that another product she doesn’t leave home without is Dae’s styling wand, which comes in handy for taming flyaways. For her beloved beach waves, she swears by T3’s curling iron (specifically the 1-inch and 1.5-inch barrel sizes) and a bit of Dae’s styling cream.

Crowell is as thoughtful with her style as she is with her skin care and makeup. “I definitely believe in quality over quantity, so I wouldn’t say I buy a lot,” she says. When she does shop, however, she always asks herself if the item fits her “’90s, a little sporty, and minimalist” ethos. That said, she gravitates toward pieces from The Row, Khaite, and Kallmeyer or really special vintage finds. Most days, you’ll find her in jeans, a T-shirt, and Adidas sneakers—or Manolos to dress things up.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately.
  • In a recent development, A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

In a recent development, A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

In a recent development, cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Sources indicate that reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

There’s something rather unnerving about a woman who is always perfectly turned out. The Attico’s spring collection takes the idea of composure and gives it a mischievous twist, imagining a cast of ladies whose immaculate appearances belie rather less conventional instincts. Think The Stepford Wives relocated to Milan, where good breeding, impeccable tailoring, and a well-managed domestic interior are still considered valuable social assets. At least until someone lets her hair down.

Sharp shoulders, sculpted jackets, corseted tops, and rigorously constructed dresses establish an almost 1940s-inspired formality, with a touch of Milanese perbenismo (bourgeois respectability). But the facade, as ever at The Attico, is deceptive. Crinkled fabrics undermine the precision, lingerie details escape their appointed boundaries, and florals introduce an unlikely note of romance. Beneath the buttoned-up exterior, a streak of kink is alive and well: pencil skirts that can be unbuttoned at the sides, thigh-high slits and revealing openings that turn propriety into a rather flexible concept.

In a recent development, there is a more grown-up, composed attitude extending into daywear and a cleaner approach to evening, where the emphasis shifts from decorative extravagance (feathers, sequins, fringe) to cut, silhouette, and construction. Even the most restrained looks, however, seem to harbor a secret. The Attico’s perfect woman may know how to behave. Whether she chooses to is another matter.
