📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that start your engines: the 2027 Oscars race is officially underway. Awards Season always starts in earnest with the Governors Awards, a ceremony held in a smaller ballroom in the same Dolby Theater complex where the main event will take place early next spring. It’s where they give out honorary Academy Awards (and the esteemed Irving Thalberg Award) to the legends who, woefully, have yet have won a competitive Oscar—last year’s marquee honoree was Tom Cruise, this year’s were Glenn Close and Ridley Scott. But it’s also where Best Picture and the other awards narratives we will discuss endlessly for the next four months really begin to take shape.

Dune 3, Artificial, and Misty Green all had substantial presences in the room, which, duh. (Tim and Kylie in the cut, mostly sitting and not mingling, but it was interesting that he highlighted up this year but not last for the big Marty Supreme push.) But there were a few other films represented whose presence made their campaign intentions clear. Mahershala Ali presented the first award of the night to Floyd Norman (a 90-year-old trailblazing cartoonist who worked with Walt Disney and later Pete Docter) but the Your Mother 3x squad was deep, from director Bassam Tariq to John Cho. Jesse Eisenberg, Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore put on for A24’s The Debut, Eisenberg's second directorial effort. (Watching Jesse and Andrew Garfield reconnect made for a beautiful Social Network reunion.) And Curry Barker and Inde Navarette being there would certainly imply a real push for Obsession. The duo with the most motion in the room, though, was unquestionably Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The only time they didn’t seem like the big dogs that everyone was gassed to chat with was when they were talking to King Big Dog himself, Christopher Nolan, front and center receiving will-wishers at The Odyssey table. Nolan and Fielder is a crossover that needs to be cemented on wax, a drum I will continue to beat. But it was cool to see Zendaya talking intently with Oppenheim; her collaborator curation has been pretty elite—imagine her in whatever Oppenheim chooses to follow Primetime with?

Recent findings suggest that when I asked Fielder about embarking on the campaign trail and how far the doc can actually go, he sighed and stated “one day at a time,” in that Fielder monotone where you can’t quite tell if he’s being earnest or not. But he laughed off the idea of being too invested in any nominations either way.

But most importantly: the Governors Awards is just a really fun room in which to be an interloper or fly on the wall. I spotted Shawn Levy and my brain immediately started spamming the word “sublime.” Daniel Kaluuya started cracking up at the mention of his great airport interview with Tyriq Withers. Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Ed Norton joined ranks for a brief Invite huddle. Everywhere I turned, there was either a person so famous or certified that it startled me to see them walk by (like Zendaya breezing in right as the show started, or turning around to find myself face-to-face with personal favorite Carla Gugino. (Karen Sisco mentioned!) Unlike some stuffier award ceremonies, the Governors Awards is kind of like the cocktail hour before the big sit-down dinner in March.

Industry observers note that ambling around the room with a stiff glass of Johnnie Walker in hand—“Did you just get carded”? an exec asked me incredulously; the bartender replied that he thought I was “like, 14"—I briefly caught up with David Corenswet, who, true to form, was unfazed by the forces beyond his control as ever. When I said “weird week huh?” he didn’t even realize I was referring to James Gunn’s DC exit, then laughed when it dawned on him and said “above my pay-grade” with a genuine shrug. We should all be so blissfully unbothered.

According to recent reports, later, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II told me he was excited for this week’s Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth red carpet premiere, noting that this film will be the first time he only read his scenes for a project and no other part of the story. Without wanting to give too much away, Yahya said Tarantino’s script is structured in a way where he could comfortably read his parts and get enough of the gist to stay in the dark about the rest, because the only thing better than starring in a newly introduced Tarantino joint is getting to still experience it like a fan.

Other notable sightings, interactions, and crossovers: Travis Scott doubled down on what he told me at our Men of the Year party: he wants that golden statue for his original Odyssey song, and he’s willing to play the campaign game for it, dutifully sitting through the whole night (and jetting off immediately after the ceremony ended to go catch Future’s 10 pm set at Camp Flog Gnaw up at Dodger Stadium.) Speaking of Odyssey collaborators, James Blake was also in attendance—I watched him meet H.E.R. and talk about potentially collaborating. Tom Cruise was the belle of the ball at last year’s ceremony but played it super lowkey this year, to the point where I didn’t actually realize he was there until I saw him sneak out of a secret side exit after briefly talking with Tessa Thompson. Digger’s divisive reviews and reactions have evidently not knocked Tom off of his Best Actor pivot.

It has been revealed that as for the actual awards, after Floyd, John Malkovich charmed the room with a great toast to Glenn Close, and King Storyteller Matt Damon regaled everyone with a great impression of triple-OG crank Ridley Scott from their time together on The Martian. (Matt was hesitant to do another movie about a loner astronaut right after Interstellar, to which Ridley apparently replied “No one gives a shit.”) Both tributes and subsequent speeches were expectedly emotional; Damon pointedly mentioned that "it’s about time we see Ridley Scott with an Oscar in his hand,” but Ridley’s remarks were all about how much the late great Tony Scott would’ve deserved one too, leading to misty eyes and standing ovations. Close addressed going 0 for 8 but said the work is the real reward as her daughter tearfully watched on. But there were great moments of levity, too, like Todd Haynes presenting Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with an award by revealing that he and Christine both slept with the same guy back in college.

Either way, a narrative of being long overdue seems to be emerging. An Awards Season where the Tom Cruises and Glenn Closes of the game finally get theirs, while upsets like You Can See Everything shake the table. What more could you ask for?

Fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

Recent findings suggest that the lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final.
  • The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Latest York City on Monday, and the winner was announced the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards.
  • Sources indicate that representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in Latest York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final. A panel of judges selected her roasted squab with chanterelle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat, black raspberry, and Swiss chard purées to represent the United States at the Grand Finale in Milan.

The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Latest York City on Monday, and the winner was announced the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024–25 US winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, DC, and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Sources indicate that representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in Latest York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

According to recent reports, saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he said. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

The chefs had five hours to prepare and execute their signature dishes in the Test Kitchen. With an hour remaining, guests had the opportunity to mingle over food and drinks. Chef Rachel Bindel, a 2022 US Finalist, served rye toast piled high with Maryland blue crab, horseradish crème, and pickled green tomato. Chef Akshay Kumar, a 2024 finalist, tucked Kumamoto oysters into a pani puri with cucumber gel and lemon foam. Tomato pie from Philadelphia’s Pizza Freak Co., spoonfuls of Petrossian caviar, and a selection of wines, S.Pellegrino beverages, and cocktails rounded out the reception.

Sources indicate that nilou Motamed, a culinary expert and Iron Chef judge on Netflix, hosted the competition. Accomplished chefs from several states served as judges: chef and co-owner E.J. Lagasse of Emeril’s in Upcoming Orleans; executive chef and partner Fariyal Abdullahi of Hav & Mar in New York City; Isabel Coss, executive chef at Pascual and founding pastry chef at Lutèce in Washington, DC; Jon Yao, head chef and owner at Kato in Los Angeles; and Ryan Ratino, executive chef and owner at Bresca and Jônt in Washington, DC.

Motamed explained that each competitor had spent several months developing their dish alongside a chef mentor. The mentors were in the Test Kitchen throughout the competition, but were not permitted to participate in the cooking. She also outlined the three pillars of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy: Community, Competition, and Mentorship, which support its mission to discover and nurture the next generation of culinary talent.

Each chef’s arrival was declared by a burst of music and a live video feed from the Test Kitchen, where a fleet of servers collected the finished plates before delivering them to the judges. First up was chef Adolfo Pucci of Michelin-starred Ariete in Miami. His dish, “Three Shores, One Table,” told the story of his Venezuelan heritage, his family’s roots in Southern Italy, and his current home in Miami. The ambitious plate featured a lamb ragù inspired by his grandmother’s cooking and lacto-fermented Florida blueberries.

Chef Amit Kumar of three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park in Upcoming York City presented the competition’s only fully vegan dish: “Sunchoke with Banana Blossoms, Chanterelles, and Sherry.” Drawing on memories of the banana trees he grew up with in India, Kumar combined banana blossoms, sunchoke purée, chanterelle mushrooms, and a ragù of sherry and banana flowers to create a hearty and deeply satisfying dish. Judge Fariyal Abdullahi called it “a very successful dish, not just a very successful vegan dish.”.

In a recent development, representing Auro at Four Seasons Resort and Residences Napa Valley, chef Evan Neumann presented “From the Valley to the Shoreline,” a love letter to the terroir of Northern California and Provence, where he grew up. Kombu-poached wild razor clams mingled with Napa verjuice and coastal seaweeds in a dish the judges found exceptionally creative. Neumann took home the S.Pellegrino Social Responsibility Award for his thoughtful approach to social responsibility and sustainable practices.

At just 21, chef Lucy Field of Fresh York City’s fine dining bastion Per Se was the youngest competitor. Her dish, “Pekin Duck, Cherry, Plum,” was a study in restraint with only six components.

Chef Marcus Osorio, chef de cuisine at Living Room in Los Angeles, drew inspiration from his Salvadoran and Indigenous roots for his “Tamal de Pollo.” The dish featured corn sourced from Somos Maíz, the company founded by his mentor, chef Ron Oliver, and a mole poblano the two developed together. Judge Isabel Coss noted the challenge of preparing a mole with such limited time, but the judges were impressed by Osorio’s ability to marry European cooking techniques with soulful Indigenous ingredients and flavors.

In a recent development, chef Nickolas Abbott hails from the small Appalachian town of Waynesville, North Carolina, and leads Chop Shop Butchery in Asheville. At the competition, he told the story of his community on a plate. His “Smoked Pork Loin, Fennel & Cheese Slaw, Sweet Potato, Asparagus, Fried Sausage, Pork Sauce Robert” reflected the people who shaped him, particularly his grandmother, his greatest inspiration as a chef.

Los Angeles–based chef Natasha Daniels of Providence showcased her vegetable-forward, zero-waste approach with “The Whole Bird, The Whole Garden.” The dish incorporated every part of a chicken across four preparations, alongside an array of vegetables and herbs inspired by her time working at The Chef’s Garden.

Daniels received two honors: the Acqua Panna Connection in Gastronomy Award and the Fine Dining Lovers Award. Voted on by regional mentors, the Acqua Panna award recognized the dish that best demonstrated a connection between culinary traditions. Daniels’s approach also resonated with Fine Dining Lovers insiders, who selected her for their award that honors “a chef’s expression of personal belief.”.

With only minutes to spare, chef Nicolas Lopez of 888 in Nashville arrived with “Pozole or Chawanmushi…?” Combining pozole, corn, and langoustine, Lopez connected his upbringing in Mexico with a culinary journey that has been shaped by Scandinavian ingredients and Japanese techniques. Although the judges could have used more time to explore the dish, they were intrigued by his influences and impressed by his technique.

Sources indicate that the final competitor, Juwon Lee, is the chef of Octavia in San Francisco. Lee was born in South Korea and grew up in Singapore before making California his home. His dish, “Curry and Quail with Ingredients My Mother Said Were Healthy,” drew on memories of eating Indonesian fried chicken and his mother’s insistence on including vegetables at family dinners. “I believe in the term happy food,” Lee explained. “There are no restrictions other than bringing joy to the eater and the chef.”.

Congratulations to all 10 chefs who competed, and best of luck to Chef Cacciato as she continues to work with her mentor and prepares to represent the United States at the 2027 Grand Finale in Milan. Follow her journey at @sanpellegrino_us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

In a recent development, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

It has been revealed that add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

Bond: The Business of James Bond

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This week, the internet is abuzz with news of the much-anticipated casting of the upcoming James Bond: Robert Pattinson, one of this year’s favorite leading men.
  • Pattinson’s arrival to the Bond franchise also marks the most luxury fashion-entrenched 007 actor yet.
  • Pattinson’s fashion affiliates were quick to stake their claim on the actor around the news of his casting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week, the internet is abuzz with news of the much-anticipated casting of the upcoming James Bond: Robert Pattinson, one of this year’s favorite leading men.

Pattinson’s arrival to the Bond franchise also marks the most luxury fashion-entrenched 007 actor yet. Pattinson has been a Dior ambassador for over 10 years, and has remained a key face for the brand since Jonathan Anderson took the helm in June last year. And in September — just two months before his Bond casting announcement — Pattinson was revealed as Swiss watchmaker Jaeger-LeCoultre’s new global ambassador. The announcement generated $1 million in media impact value (MIV) within 48 hours for the brand, according to Launchmetrics.

Pattinson’s fashion affiliates were quick to stake their claim on the actor around the news of his casting. Dior’s Anderson posted an image of Pattinson and ex-Bond Daniel Craig on his personal Instagram story, taken at Anderson’s first Dior men’s 2026 show last summer, complete with a heart emoji. (Anderson had previously cast Craig in Loewe’s Fall/Winter 2024 campaign, around the same time he worked with the actor while doing the costumes for Luca Guadagnino’s Queer.) Richemont-owned Jaeger-LeCoultre, meanwhile, has posted two stills of the newly minted global ambassador to its Instagram account since Monday morning’s announcement.

Pattinson may have the most pre-existing off-screen deals of any Bond, but on-screen, the franchise is a blueprint for mega-deals between brands and movies. Partnerships have been part of the 007 world since Sean Connery stepped into the role of Bond in the inaugural Bond movie Dr. No in 1962, which featured hatmaker Lock & Co. Bond has driven an Aston Martin since 1964’s Goldfinger, Bollinger has been Bond’s champagne of choice since 1979’s Moonraker, and Heineken has been a partner since 1997. The beer brand has reportedly spent over $100 million on Bond sponsorship. Swiss watchmaker Omega is Bond’s longest-running sponsor and has decorated the wrists of Bonds since 1995, while also developing Bond watches for sale. (Prior to that, Bond wore a Rolex.) Past-era Bonds have cycled through different suit brands: Pierce Brosnan wore Brioni suits (and later starred in a campaign for the brand), as did Craig in Casino Royale. For the rest of Craig’s tenure, though, he wore Tom Ford.

Recent findings suggest that the value of a Bond film has only grown. Spectre was estimated to feature $45 million in product placement; while the most recent Bond film — No Time to Die, Craig’s last — reportedly featured almost $100 million in brand placements and partnerships. In 2026, Bond’s on-screen value is immense. So much so that, last year, Amazon MGM Studios was stated to have paid $20 million for the franchise, plus additional payouts that could total up to $1 billion to take full creative control over the franchise.

Brand deals have evolved dramatically since the early days of Bond — and even since the last movie. “Five years ago, an ambassadorship primarily meant red carpets and campaigns, while the film was kept separate,” notes Krista Corrigan, senior retail analyst at EDITED. Now, they’re bleeding into the films themselves, whether by financially supporting films (and getting their clothes on-screen in the process), or inking deals with studios, as Dior recently did with A24. “Luxury brands give studios the aspirational quality that Bond depends on in return for a global marketing moment.”.

Daniel Craig celebrating 60 years of James Bond in 2022.

The landscape into which this new Bond is releasing is dramatically different from the No Time to Die days of 2021. That was pre-Barbiecore, well before the number of brand-film-product collaborations for a given movie surpassed the hundreds, and was a different era of film promotion, before A24’s embrace of fashion and merch developed into a playbook in and of itself.

It has been revealed that “What’s interesting about Bond is that there has always been that one iconic fashion moment or item everyone wants. Think Halle Berry’s orange bikini in Die Another Day,” indicates Adee Drexler, founder and CEO of communications agency ICA, who regularly brokers brand deals for clients. “These moments become part of pop culture and often live far beyond the film itself.”.

Industry observers note that the difference today, she argues, is that these moments can go viral overnight — which means the pressure to convert cultural relevance into commercial impact is heightened. “By aligning costume design, brand partnerships, and retail, the franchise can ensure that when an item captures the public’s attention, there’s already a way for consumers to buy into that moment,” Drexler says.

Will Pattinson’s be the most luxury-heavy Bond era yet? And how will the actor’s brand deals come into play?

Robert Pattinson in Dior for the Primetime screening in Venice.

Industry observers note that already, online chatter is bubbling about the impact of Pattinson’s current brand ambassadorships on the films. Puck’s Matt Belloni reported in his newsletter on Tuesday that Pattinson’s test deal didn’t address the actor’s current brand deals with Dior and Jaeger-LeCoultre, and that these will now need to be ironed out. One Redditor worried that Pattinson’s existing brand deals could delay filming. Most respondents expected not.

It has been revealed that still, it raises questions about how an actor’s off-screen brand ambassadorships influence their on-screen outfitting. “This is the first time in recent memory that a new Bond has been cast with a major luxury relationship already in place,” Corrigan indicates. “While brands have historically attached themselves to the role, this time it went to an actor already tied to Dior. With release expected in 2028, Dior —if involved — has plenty of time to design menswear around the film, which I’d expect to see over the next few seasons.”.

It has been revealed that corrigan wouldn’t be surprised to see Dior on-screen come 2028, particularly given the brand’s recent embrace of the film industry and Anderson’s many costume designer credits. On November 12, Dior sent an email to US customers presenting Anderson’s cruise 2027 collection — shown in Los Angeles — as an exploration of the house’s Hollywood history, she notes.

In a recent development, even if Dior isn’t integrated into the films themselves, the brand still stands to gain, Drexler says. “The press tour, premieres and cultural conversation create an enormous opportunity for Dior to own those fashion moments and translate that visibility into real commercial impact.”.

Robert Pattinson in Dior, again, at the Latest York premiere of Die My Love.

Bond’s watch may be a different story. Jaeger-LeCoultre may have been posting Pattinson, but Omega wasted no time in staking its own claim on the Bond franchise. The brand got ahead of Pattinson’s casting by launching new models in its Seamaster diver’s watch collection, the James Bond and Spectre, in October. Omega will host an Art Basel Miami dinner to celebrate the Bond-themed timepieces. And on Tuesday morning, less than a day after Pattinson’s announcement, the watchmaker posted an image of its Seamaster Diver 300M James Bond Edition watch. Commenters were quick to pick up on what they expect to be a “battle” between the two Swiss watchmakers.

It has been revealed that it may be a case of the highest bidder, and Omega is one of the largest watchmakers in the world (though Richemont CEO Johann Rupert recently told investors that Jaeger-LeCoultre was up 17% in the most recent quarter). Or it may be an on-screen, off-screen split. Some brand ambassadorship contracts include non-exclusivity clauses for filming. That mentioned, when films know an actor is an ambassador for a given brand, producers will sometimes request to borrow clothing from that brand, given the existing relationship. For a moneyed franchise like Bond, though, no lending will be necessary. Instead, it’s a question of which brand will be Pattinson’s official outfitter.

In a recent development, plus, for a role like Bond, the character the actor plays on-screen does become synonymous with the actor off-screen, particularly given how long the actor remains in the role. (Pattinson has a three-film deal.) One couldn’t imagine Craig donning Omega watches on-screen, while shilling non-Omega watches off-screen. In fact, the actor was — and still is — an official Omega ambassador.

Sources indicate that whichever brands do fill out this next iteration of the Bond world, they’ll have even more work cut out for them than in eras past, Drexler says. “It’s about moving beyond traditional product placement and creating partnerships that can capitalize on cultural moments in real time, without compromising the authenticity of the Bond universe.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No holiday table—or really any dinner table, for that matter—is truly complete without a substantial side of creamy, buttery mashed potatoes. While it may seem like simple, classic comfort food, there are a few ways to take mashed potatoes from good to great. That's why we retested this recipe again and again until we achieved potato perfection.

Recent findings suggest that what People Are Saying:"So good! I don’t typically like sour cream on its own but it was a huge improvement for basic mashed potatoes. Will definitely be making this again." – PurpleStrawberry.

In a recent development, "Easily my go-to mashed potato recipe. I've made it for Thanksgiving, and got requests to make it again. It's so good, doesn't even need gravy." – kitkat123.

It has been revealed that really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

Industry observers note that now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

Then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for a max of 3 to 4 days. With all of our recipes to transform your creamy leftover mashed potatoes—like fried mashed potato balls, potato rolls, waffles... we doubt they'll even last that long.

#31159. Denis Villeneuve on Finishing ‘Dune,’ Casting James Bond, and Why ‘Reality Is Unbeatable’

Denis Villeneuve on Finishing ‘Dune,’ Casting James Bond, and Why ‘Reality Is Unbeatable’

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the last days of the making of the Dune trilogy take place on an unassuming Hollywood side street in September, in a dark, mostly silent room.
  • Sources indicate that villeneuve, the director and cowriter of Dune, Dune: Part Two, and Dune: Part Three, is tall, slender, and bearded, with deep-set eyes.
  • In a recent development, today, Villeneuve and his cinematographer, Linus Sandgren, are at the postproduction facility Company 3, where they have been the past weeks and months, color-timing—the process of adjusting and balancing a film’s many colors and contrasts—the 150 minutes of Dune: Part Three.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the last days of the making of the Dune trilogy take place on an unassuming Hollywood side street in September, in a dark, mostly silent room. “We were about to have a quick look at reel one because they did some adjustments, and it’s without sound,” Denis Villeneuve says, apologetically. “So it’s a way to discover the film that is a bit brutal for you.”.

Sources indicate that villeneuve, the director and cowriter of Dune, Dune: Part Two, and Dune: Part Three, is tall, slender, and bearded, with deep-set eyes. He has a disarming effect. Many directors of Villeneuve’s stature—Christopher Nolan or James Cameron—lead their productions with a kind of remote but dazzling competency: They can do everything better than you and are used to the deference that comes with that fact. Villeneuve’s charisma is closer and more mischievous: He speaks quietly and playfully, in Quebecois-accented English, and commands loyalty via the protective instinct he inspires in nearly everyone he meets. His method is emotional; his instructions are conveyed with sincerity and praise. When presented with the results he is seeking, he will let you know with an almost childlike enthusiasm: I deeply love it. Or: Wow.

In a recent development, today, Villeneuve and his cinematographer, Linus Sandgren, are at the postproduction facility Company 3, where they have been the past weeks and months, color-timing—the process of adjusting and balancing a film’s many colors and contrasts—the 150 minutes of Dune: Part Three. For my sake, and because there is still work to be done on it, they have started, once again, at the beginning of the film. “So here we could have fucked up the Warner Brothers logo if we wanted,” Villeneuve notes, gesturing at the screen at the studio’s iconic WB, “but we are nice guys.”.

Then he leans forward: “No, but seriously, without joking, are they too rich, the colors? A little bit? Or is it the original to your eyes?” Sandgren—a calm Swede in Birkenstocks—and Matt Wallach, the film’s colorist, chime in to agree and to tone down the blue. “Their logo is a little cartoonish,” Villeneuve says, still staring at it. “It’s not their best work, I will say. But that feels better. Thank you, Matt.”.

Villeneuve and his wife, Tanya Lapointe, who is a producer and second-unit director on Dune: Part Three, disagree on how long they have been working on Dune: Villeneuve tends to say nine years, and Lapointe indicates 10. (It’s 10.) Frank Herbert’s Dune books, which are notoriously complex and hard to adapt, have stymied directors as talented as David Lynch and Alejandro Jodorowsky. But Villeneuve seems to have found a way. The first two Dune films—Part One came out in 2021—have grossed over a billion dollars, been nominated for 15 Academy Awards, and helped make stars of Timothée Chalamet (who plays Atreides, the film’s complicated messiah figure and main character) and Zendaya (who plays Chani, a native Fremen warrior and the lover of Atreides) while still capturing the uniquely strange and surreal texture of Herbert’s novels. (Multiple people in the Villeneuve films imbibe what one character describes as “worm piss.”).

Industry observers note that right now Villeneuve is feeling the last decade acutely. “I’m at that stage of the process where all my body hurts,” he says. On Dune: Part Three alone, the production shot for nearly a hundred days, in three countries: Hungary, where the film’s main stages were; Iceland; and the Liwa Desert, in the United Arab Emirates, which doubled for the sand planet of Arrakis. They wrapped last November, and Villeneuve went directly into the film’s edit and postproduction process. “It’s a feeling of some kind of deep melancholia to finally come to the conclusion of this long journey,” he says. “Because it has been nine years of my life dreaming about Arrakis, about sandworms, about the adventures of Paul Atreides. I’m pretty emotional about that.”.

Industry observers note that in the history of Hollywood, there have been only a handful of directors who have had the ability to work, again and again, at the highest level of the art form while also connecting with audiences at the widest possible scale. Villeneuve is one of them. His signature films—2015’s cartel thriller Sicario, or 2016’s science fiction film Arrival, which was nominated for eight Academy Awards—are knotty and severe and not always easy to follow; they are also beautiful and seem to play well anywhere, whether on an airplane, in an HBO rerun, or at an IMAX theater. Villeneuve’s reward for all his success is his next project: the 26th James Bond film. “It’s a blessing,” Villeneuve states. “Because to leave Arrakis, I need some kind of strong rocket, something that will grab me and pull me away from the orbit of that planet. I’m leaving a childhood dream. I need something so powerful to pull me away from it. And Bond is the one that will do it.”.

In the dark screening room, Wallach lets the first minutes of the final Dune film play. We watch soldiers on a dimly lit warship prepare themselves for battle. Sandgren and Villeneuve discuss trying to bring out one of the actor’s features more concretely. “I guess what we’re fighting is we could have lit him more,” Sandgren says, “but also what Denis really wants here is the realism and the sort of incidental light—like he just happens to sit in a shitty light here, and gets what he gets, which adds to the realism, which is nice. But you still want to see him. So it’s a balance.”.

“What Linus says, in a very polite way, is that it’s my fault,” Villeneuve says, smiling, while Wallach finds a little more detail in the actor’s face.

“I deeply love it,” Villeneuve pronounces, when he is done. “Thank you. The scene is at the beginning, and becomes claustrophobic. In French, we say they are chair à canon.”.

“Cannon fodder,” someone supplies.

“Cannon food, we call it in Sweden,” Sandgren says.

In a recent development, villeneuve watches his own film as it plays on. “Wow,” he notes. “Fantastic. Fantastic. That’s beautiful. Nice work on the highlights here. Thank you, guys. Wow. Great work. It looks real now. Wow.” His voice is full of emotion as he turns to Sandgren: “It’s beautiful, my dear friend.”.

In the Dune movies, you can feel Villeneuve’s desire to go deeper into the desert, to shed all the significant, loud machinery of his own films, and to get to the places out near the horizon. This is one of the reasons his trilogy works where others have failed: Despite Villeneuve’s talent for spectacle—his Dune is full of menacing, chromed-out oblong shapes and eerily familiar war machines—his true gift is finding the uncannily quiet spots in the worlds he creates, the lonely places where his characters are tested against themselves.

According to recent reports, “That was the main condition when I agreed to make these movies,” Villeneuve states, about the way all three Dune films were shot in the desert, on location. “I remarked that it was deeply important for me to shoot it in the real environment.” The Liwa Desert was so mind-bendingly hot while shooting Dune: Part Three that the director had to incorporate a midday break into the crew’s daily schedule. Robert Pattinson, who joined the cast for the third film, has talked about the set being so intensely warm that he basically disassociated for most of shooting. But being there is one of the main things Villeneuve is after. “I love reality,” he says. “I love to be in the environment. It’s like a pleasure that I give to myself to be in the crew with a camera in the desert. I feel that there’s all these shots that we did, the realism, that I think you cannot achieve otherwise. And you cannot feel the power of the desert if you’re not there. There are some shots you can cheat sometimes. But in general, reality is unbeatable.”.

Villeneuve on the set of Dune: Part Three with Timothée Chalamet.

Villeneuve and Zendaya on location in the Liwa Desert, Abu Dhabi.

Sources indicate that villeneuve, 59, grew up in Gentilly, Quebec, a small town right next to a river. From that place he emerged with “a relationship with horizon and silence,” he says. “I was in contact since my birth with incredible gigantic skies, very dramatic, operatic skies. And colors as well. I grew up in a world that has a black-and-white winter, which has a tremendous, beautiful, precise palette of black and white and blue and grays.”.

According to recent reports, villeneuve likes to point out that the two main structures in his town were a church and a power plant. “I grew up melancholic, a child that was dreaming significant alone in his corner and fascinated by the engineers that were working in that nuclear power plant,” he says. “I was raised as a Catholic, and I was raised going to the church, and those chants and the passion of religion [are] all that mixed together with incredibly powerful grandmothers. I think that’s the background of Dune right there.”.

It has been revealed that villeneuve was a reader, a dreamer. It was only as an adult, when Villeneuve became a documentary filmmaker, that he began to discover a larger world outside his own mind. “I think that there’s something about Paul Atreides in the way he’s introduced at the beginning, the way he is like a kid that has been protected in a small bubble all his life and suddenly finds himself confronted to a new reality where he has to consolidate his identity in another culture,” Villeneuve indicates. “I think it’s something that I, at the time when I was a kid, I really connected with. And early on when I became a young adult, I traveled a lot, a lot. I went a lot to Asia and was spending a lot of time there doing small documentaries and being in contact with so many perspectives, so many points of view on reality.”.

In a recent development, villeneuve made his first feature, August 32nd on Earth, in Canada in 1998. He would go on to make three more films in French, before making his first English-language film, Enemy, in 2013. “I consolidated my identity as a filmmaker,” Villeneuve says about the time before he came to Hollywood “through documentaries and movies with less commercial pressure where I was free to express myself and find my own voice.” Partially, he learned by failing. “I will say that I don’t see my first feature films as...they had some clumsiness in them. I was a beginner. I learned my craft. I made mistakes and I learned from those mistakes, a lot more than from my successes.”.

Villeneuve, as a young filmmaker, was wary of Hollywood, even as he was pointed at it like an arrow. “Hollywood has always had that kind of dichotomy, to be a paradise for a filmmaker and hell at the same time,” he indicates. “Since the birth of Hollywood there has been a struggle between the art of cinema, the idea that you want to express yourself—and for that you need a lot of money, and somebody will write the check, and you have a responsibility. Since the birth of cinema, it has been like that.”.

In 2012, Villeneuve found himself facing a rare opportunity: He had two films greenlit at more or less the same time. One was Prisoners—an in-demand Hollywood script about the abduction of two children and the vigilante efforts of one father to get them back. The other was a coproduction between Spain and Canada called Enemy, about a college professor who becomes obsessed with another man with whom he appears to be physically identical. Both were English-language films, which Villeneuve had not yet done. Both films starred Jake Gyllenhaal. But to Villeneuve, they were very different propositions: Enemy was a deeply personal film about identity and the unknown nature of the self. And Prisoners, which also starred Hugh Jackman and Viola Davis and which would be largely distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures, represented Villeneuve’s first true chance to make a real Hollywood film.

Recent findings suggest that villeneuve decided to make both. But he made Enemy first. “I did convince the studio, Alcon”—the producer of Prisoners—“to wait a few months for Prisoners because first I wanted to make a first film in English in a smaller environment. And the real reason is that I wanted to make sure that I will shoot something that will be so close to me that if ever I was smashed and destroyed by Hollywood, there will be something. If people say, ‘What’s that? Oh, Denis’s there. He’s flying over there.’ Because I did feel that I was afraid.”.

In a recent development, I remember watching Enemy in a small screening room the year it premiered, in 2013 (the movie was distributed in the United States by a then upstart studio called A24), and being increasingly unsettled and haunted by the film. Sometimes, in quiet moments, the final shot of Enemy still comes to me, unbidden. Who is this guy? I wondered then.

According to recent reports, enemy and Prisoners were both stylish, morally ambiguous films that highlighted the extremes of human behavior without ever venturing into sadism or pure spectacle, and this style of filmmaking—brutal, unresolved, lush, and heartbreaking—would become Villeneuve’s signature as he made progressively bigger, and bigger-budget, films in Hollywood: 2015’s Sicario, 2016’s Arrival, 2017’s Blade Runner 2049. “I always did projects I [felt] ready to do,” Villeneuve indicates. “I was ready to do Dune after Blade Runner. I would have not been ready to do Dune after Prisoners. I slowly learned my craft one step at a time—my skills with actors and then to work with more and more background action and increase the technical difficulty slowly. I just felt secure. And when I started Dune, I knew I could not go in front of people and ask them to invest $200 million [until I was ready]. I need to feel deep inside me that I can do that.”.

Recent findings suggest that villeneuve indicates he only recently stopped feeling like a tourist in Hollywood. “I think that feeling of having the right to be here in some ways came from other filmmakers, colleagues that wanted to reach out and share thoughts about cinema with me or some friendships that began and that I accepted,” he says. He’s coy about who exactly he’s talking about. But part of it, surely, has also been the acceptance of the films, which despite their increasing size and scale and sometimes exotic source material are consistently deeply personal.

“My work is all about me,” Villeneuve claims, helplessly. “If you don’t like Dune, the movies, I’m 100 percent responsible because I made every single decision. I brought them to the screen, and they are very personal films. Even for me, it’s like—scope is not something that is contradictory with the ownership of a movie. These movies have been brought to life by me, and I say that without arrogance. I mean, I’m the one who brought them to life. And yeah: It’s my Dune.”.

It has been revealed that A few weeks later, Villeneuve and Lapointe, who is shorter but equally warm and charismatic, are at the North Hollywood warehouse of Legendary, the production organization behind the Dune films. The warehouse is full of costumes from past productions: Pacific Rim, Crimson Peak, Godzilla. In the back, transported from another continent entirely, is one of the ornithopters—a helicopter-like vehicle—from Dune: Part Three. Soon this prop, which is the size of an actual helicopter, will join a bunch of others in an upcoming exhibition of work from the Dune films. But right now it is here, in a parking lot under the glaring Los Angeles sun. Its paint—an homage to the specific color of a 1981 Porsche—glows in the light. “The last time I saw this vehicle, it was in a deep desert,” Villeneuve says, looking on. “We had brought it to Abu Dhabi, and it was, I remember vividly, at the top of a cliff of sand. This thing I’ve seen a lot. It’s like an old friend.”.

Recent findings suggest that later in the day, Villeneuve tells me he is set to approve a final handful of effects shots. And then Dune: Part Three, and the director’s work on the trilogy, he claims, will cease. “I do feel that I have to stop,” he reflects. “I don’t think I should spend another minute on it. Because I’m still curious, I’m still alive, and I do it for artistic reasons, not because I see that I’m comfortable or I see that it’s going to be good business-wise or for my career. I think it’s good for me to stop artistically.”.

According to recent reports, as Villeneuve’s star has risen, he has increasingly had to think through the question of how to remain an artist at the very high tier of the business that he’s in. “In the past 25 years, there’s a tendency to try to find the perfect formula to make a film, and to try to reproduce, reproduce, and make sequels,” Villeneuve says. “I’m responsible. I just made three Dune movies. I’m about to make James Bond 26. So I’m a sinner. But the idea is that as an artist, I feel that there’s an urgency, and you feel it in the young filmmakers, which I deeply love—the idea to bring upcoming stories, original stories to the screen. It’s very crucial. And that we have to try to, at the end of the day, we need to take risks.… I want to say that we, as humans, as artists, if we want to be better than AI, we have to be unpredictable.” Only humans, he says, “can step into the unknown and go deeper into the dream. That is the strength of a human being. And I think that no computers can do that.”.

According to recent reports, it’s the end of September, and the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger is about to close. “I think that consolidation, I mean, less players in the business is never a good idea,” Villeneuve says. “Those studios are historical studios. And I hope, I truly hope, that the people in power will have the wisdom to protect the legacy of both studios. There’s a limit to profit. I mean, if the only goal is to make money, it’s really sad. Those things are historical gems of American culture and they have a duty to—I hope and I pray that they understand the responsibility that they have and that they will take care of both of these entities.”.

Villeneuve, for his part, is already turning his attention toward Bond—another character, and another world, he grew up fascinated with. “I adore James Bond,” he notes. “I adore Sean Connery, the Sean Connery years, the verve of James Bond, his panache, his drive, his charisma, his unapologetic way of living the strength and what it says, good and bad, about masculinity. There’s something about James Bond that deeply inspires me.” He says the previous producers of the franchise approached him with the idea of directing the film a few years ago, right as he was beginning Dune: Part Three. Villeneuve says he hung up the phone and actually screamed out loud when they offered the franchise to him. Then he told them they’d have to wait. “I said to them, ‘Yeah, I’m up for it, but I have something before called Dune: Part Three. I’m shooting in two weeks.’ And the only way I can do things in life is to fully commit to something. So I said to them, ‘If you want to work with me, you will have to wait many months because I will be entirely focused on Part Three.’ And so that’s why I’m sorry for everybody, but it took more time for the casting because I’m busy.”.

Industry observers note that now we know: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. Villeneuve’s decision, albeit in consultation with his producers and the studio. He is incredulous that I am even asking. “I am the director!” he says. And then softens a bit: “I’m doing cinema because I love to share the creative process,” he says, about the conversations that led to Pattinson. “Otherwise, I will do ice sculpture in my basement. I love the idea to share creativity. But when it comes to casting, it’s something that—I’m doing the casting. But, of course, it will need to be accepted and approved by a ton of people, including you, the pope, my mother, my brother, who has a strong opinion about who should be James Bond.… I think Donald Trump wants to be James Bond. Everybody talks about James Bond. So yes, I will choose James Bond with my friends, producers, and hopefully everybody will.…” He pauses. “You know what? At the end of the day, the truth is, no matter who I choose, some people will be excited and others will be disappointed.”.

In a recent development, now Villeneuve has a gleam in his eye, talking about what he was looking for in the part. “The first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer, because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin,” he indicates. “I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It’s not everybody who has that. I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that when he comes into the room, everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma and someone that has a lot of sensuality as well and that people are attracted to and that someone who expressed some kind of pleasure, someone who has width, sometime who has dark humor, sometimes that has pleasure into being in deep shit, someone who is not afraid to put his hand in the mud. I need someone that is strong, muscular, someone that is a force. And someone, of course, who has a deep intelligence in the eyes, someone that is always ahead of us.”.

Industry observers note that he is grinning. You can feel Lapointe, in the nicest possible way, willing him to say less. But Villeneuve, as is typical, is swept away. “Every time I’m thinking about James Bond,” he states, “there’s an electricity that goes into my vein that is the electricity of pleasure. It’s like: For me to do that is just a pure cinematic pleasure. Incredible pressure, stress, yes. But the pleasure is bigger.” ✦.

Latest Update: I Tried The Great British Bake Off’s Most Controversial Recipe—Here’s How It Went

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The “technical challenge,” a blind-baking test where contestants receive the same recipe and ingredients, often with minimal or deliberately sparse instructions, is a staple of The Great British Bake Off.
  • After bakers argued that an hour wasn’t enough, Paul noted, “There’s plenty of time.” But fans, critics, and former bakers alike have been plenty vocal about their feelings.
  • Industry observers note that with all the controversy, I was curious to see if the challenge was even possible—so I tried it myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “technical challenge,” a blind-baking test where contestants receive the same recipe and ingredients, often with minimal or deliberately sparse instructions, is a staple of The Great British Bake Off. And contestants have seriously struggled with it over the years. But according to Paul Hollywood, this season’s challenge featuring blue cheese and roasted grape flatbreads was the worst yet. After 60 minutes of kneading, grape-roasting, and undercooking, the bakers produced trays of thick, raw flatbreads that Paul and Nigella could barely eat.

After bakers argued that an hour wasn’t enough, Paul noted, “There’s plenty of time.” But fans, critics, and former bakers alike have been plenty vocal about their feelings. The popular opinion? The bakers were set up to fail—and also that the flavors seemed a little weird.

Industry observers note that with all the controversy, I was curious to see if the challenge was even possible—so I tried it myself. While I purposefully did NOT watch the episode before my attempt, I did print the full recipe from the GBBO website. This recipe was definitely WAY more helpful than the one the bakers were given, and I followed it to the letter.

Here’s how it went: the good, the bad, and the very ugly.

Sources indicate that the beginning? Very smooth. I put the grapes in the oven (the online recipe told me to roast them as a whole bunch rather than cutting them up) and made the bread dough, kneading it for the five minutes specified before letting it rest.

Sources indicate that as soon as I set the dough aside to rest, I discovered how absolutely torturous technical downtime is. I was at an absolute loss. I had nothing to do…except read the recipe over and over again and make sure I knew what 8 cm and 23 cm looked like.

Interestingly enough, the bakers on the show didn’t have this downtime; they were busy cutting and roasting their grapes by then. That said, I don’t think that order was necessarily better; with the time spent slicing the grapes, they wouldn’t have had much time at ALL to roast—and not nearly enough to cool.

The grapes came out of the oven. They weren’t very roasted—as one of the bakers mentioned, they just looked like “raw grapes”—but the recipe said 20 minutes and gave no indicators for how roasted they should be (and also I knew they needed to cool before stuffing), so I just went with it.

Industry observers note that I dumped out the dough (a rude awakening after its 15-minute rest) and chopped it into eight pieces. Immediately, I realized I should have weighed the larger ball and divided it by eight so I could make sure all the pieces were equal, but I didn’t have much time to fuss, so I tried to make them roughly the same weight and moved on.

The recipe noted to roll out each portion of dough into an 8 cm circle, fill it with five roasted grapes and one-eighth of the blue cheese, lift the edges of the circle up to pinch them together, then turn the little ball seam side down and roll the whole thing out into a 23 cm circle.

I ran into problems immediately.

To begin, I cut my dough into wedges from the larger ball, and it was hard to roll them out into a circle to fill. But that was nothing compared to the problems I had rolling out the filled dough. First, the dough wasn’t rested enough, so it kept springing back at me as I tried to roll it out. But the bigger glitch was the grapes. Since they were still pretty juicy, they started bursting as I rolled out the flatbread, flying to the edges and tearing holes in the dough as they oozed out.

After over 15 minutes of stuffing and rolling, my workstation was littered with burst grape guts. None of my flatbreads were 23 cm wide (I think the widest they got was 18?) and I still had three to roll out, but I also knew I needed to start cooking or I was going to have eight totally raw flatbreads at the end of time.

In a recent development, cooking the flatbreads wasn’t a total disaster—I guess—but grape juice oozed out of the holes where they burst and left black patches of burnt sugar on the pan, which I had absolutely no time to clean out since I was still racing the clock. Fortunately, the flatbreads didn’t seem to need the full 90 seconds per side. In fact, they seemed to need constant attention to prevent them from burning, which was bad news since I was still trying to roll out the remaining three flatbreads on the side.

Sources indicate that time was up, and I had five cooked (burst) stuffed flatbreads on my sheet tray, three totally raw ones on the countertop, and a smoking pan. I now know how the bakers feel at the end of such challenges: slightly insane and utterly defeated.

Looking back on the challenge, I can honestly say that it was difficult and somewhat impossible. Ultimately, I couldn’t get all the flatbreads cooked in time, even though I was rolling them out much thinner than the bakers were. But while timing was definitely a problem, the bigger issue was the impossible stupidity of stuffing juicy grapes inside a flatbread and then trying to roll it out without the grapes bursting out and ruining the dough.

It has been revealed that since I managed to cook five flatbreads, I could (unlike Paul and Nigella) taste the finished result—but honestly, I wasn’t a fan. The blue cheese was WAY too strong, and the grapes felt like random pockets of juice in an otherwise savory flatbread. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend trying this challenge yourself—unless you want to be scrubbing the burnt bits of grape sugar off your pan for the next week.

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

Sources indicate that “Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner indicates. “It could be any language.”.

It has been revealed that the idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix says was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across Upcoming England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”.

Sources indicate that phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor states. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”.

Industry observers note that in an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director mentioned.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

Sources indicate that when I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he notes. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”.

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

In a recent development, preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Sources indicate that whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Recent findings suggest that arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a substantial pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

According to recent reports, this is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying. Stagnancy, he’s quick to clarify, is different from stillness. Stagnancy is like a fetid pond; stillness is meditative. Baraghani seems to be at risk of neither.

It is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen. He is about to make me scones—salty-sweet ones with dates and lemon zest, an offering under development for his forthcoming café Ditto. But first, we’ll need to pop out for cream.

Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he claims.

Recent findings suggest that he lives just a few blocks from the Union Square Greenmarket, where niche pepper varieties are currently splayed in colorful fractals across folding tables. We have just completed a ground floor tour of the apartment that the chef-cum-writer-cum-chef shares with his husband, Keith Pollock. Now he moves across the kitchen and pauses at the Crittall-style window. It gives me 30 seconds to take inventory of his countertop alliums.

These details feel important. Baraghani has become a sort of standard-bearer for exquisite seasonal produce and the exquisite life one can lead preparing such stuff. I clock a couple of shallots, which sit in a Swid Powell bowl beside five heirloom tomatoes. It occurs to me that even onions are more beautiful in Baraghani’s universe.

“Oh,” he claims casually, following my gaze. “Torpedo shallots.” As if all of our countertops look like this.

In the decade or so since he became a household name for a certain set of a certain era (food-obsessed aesthetes who love an acidic drizzle and a hard, salty cheese), as a video star for a certain magazine—okay, this one—his fandom has only continued to explode.

His debut cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be, was a Latest York Times bestseller and the recipient of a James Beard Award. He has more than 370,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok. He’s been called “the Internet boyfriend of our dreams.” Vogue covered his wedding. The New York Times published his ideal Thanksgiving menu. In the last 24 hours alone, Baraghani has been busy beating out creative director Terrence O’Connor for a Best Body prize at the podcast How Long Gone’s inaugural “Goneies” Award Show, (Baraghani was asked to remove his blazer to reveal a formfitting Dario Vitale–era Versace pink tank top) before running into David Tanis while shopping for groceries.

When Baraghani unveiled he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. Still, he says, few have pushed him on the true meaning of the name Ditto. Perhaps they were too busy trying to keep up.

Baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. I inquire about his cortisol levels as he juggles opening Ditto a few blocks away, the second cookbook he has just shot in this apartment, and now the remodel below us.

Industry observers note that baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”.

He has spent the last 10 years peppering his recipes with caveats. “I know that my food may be a touch too lemony for some,” he writes in The Cook You Want To Be. “And that I use what has been called a ridiculous amount of herbs.”.

According to recent reports, his background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. The piece ended with an admission: “So as nice as it would be for this story to end with that Iran feature or getting my dream job at Bon Appétit, the truth is that I’m still trying to figure things out. It’s not always steady progress.”.

Since I had a baby six weeks ago, I have been walking around floored that the adults in my life could have ever been children, but with Andy, I don’t have to work too hard to picture it. He has a particularly cheerful sense of wonder. When I ask about it, he states it comes from his upbringing. His parents were political activists. Andy’s mother worked as an aesthetician (yes, he established his famous skin-care routine early). He grew up surrounded by a diverse community of immigrants who would invite his family to their celebrations and into their homes, where a young Baraghani got to taste dishes from far-flung places. After he landed in New York, he would take respite in stints abroad, traveling from hostel to hostel so he could eat his way across Vietnam, Lebanon, and Turkey.

It has been revealed that now, though, Baraghani says he is done footnoting his vision. In the intervening years since that essay, Baraghani has written and cooked and tasted at warp speed. He was bound to self-actualize in the same timeframe it took the rest of us to figure out how to style barrel-leg pants. Or perhaps it’s the reality of having to reckon with what he can’t change: In 2024, after a battle with small-cell lung cancer, his beloved father passed away. Baraghani tells me that before it was stagnancy, his greatest fear was losing a parent. He has since learned that loss isn’t something to solve, but a tremendous void one must learn to live with.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see [at Ditto,]” he says. The dishes will weave together all of the threads of Baraghani-ism: seasonal vegetables prepared deftly with Persian flourishes, blending tart and sour and aromatic with a firm point-of-view. If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.).

It has been revealed that literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in Latest York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with plans for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

In a recent development, the goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was important for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the plan is breakfast and lunch.

Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

Sources indicate that the sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.).

Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

Recent findings suggest that as we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he indicates simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

Later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”.

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

In a recent development, and for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

Industry observers note that from intricate braids and gravity-defying knots to elaborate, architectural chignons, the red carpet has seen plenty of sculptural hair looks as of late. Leave it to Hunter Schafer to offer a decidedly cool-girl interpretation of the trend.

Attending the London premiere of Blade Runner 2099 on Tuesday evening, Schafer—styled as always by Dara—wore a custom ivory Celine ensemble comprising a strapless satin bustier dress, with a dramatic train trailing behind her, layered over tailored tuxedo trousers for that nonchalant elegance. In a recent development, it’s another clever beauty moment in what’s proving to be an excellent press tour for Schafer. At the Los Angeles premiere last week, Ganzer paid homage to Daryl Hannah’s replicant character Pris in Ridley Scott’s original Blade Runner, creating a dramatic, futuristic strip of gunmetal eyeshadow across her eyes and nose. Calhoun fashioned her hair into a disheveled updo, with flyaways escaping at the back for a cyberpunk heroine to red carpet look.

Then there were the hair-matching fuzzy earmuffs from Undercover’s fall 2007 collection, which Calhoun incorporated into a double-ponytail hairstyle. Working alongside Dara and Ganzer, Schafer has been having enormous fun with beauty references that are both deeply considered and playful, often drawing on the sci-fi world of her forthcoming series and beyond.

In a recent development, the up-do renaissance is firmly upon us. At this year’s Golden Globes, Audrey Nuna, Mia Goth, and Jenna Ortega were among those experimenting with interesting shapes and structures, while Anya Taylor-Joy recently sported a sleek knot at the LACMA Art+Film Gala.

What’s so great about Hunter Schafer’s latest look is its restraint. While everyone else is twisting, sculpting, and shellacking their hair into elaborate works of art, Schafer makes a case for something more low-key. Sometimes the most interesting beauty detail is the one you almost miss.

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:.

According to recent reports, what People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot.
