The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

According to recent reports, time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

It has been revealed that slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

According to recent reports, time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Sources indicate that save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

Recent findings suggest that to be sure, there’s no shortage of quaint, storybook villages in any part of the Alps—but over on the French side, tucked away in the Haute-Savoie region, there’s something special about Megève. “I’ve been coming for years; I enjoy it just as much in summer as in winter,” says Vogue France’s Head of Editorial Content, Claire Thomson-Jonville. “I love that it still feels like a small, cozy village. It’s postcard-perfect with a family-friendly atmosphere; it’s discreet, not flashy, with incredible nature.”.

According to recent reports, while the hiking—and generally stunning landscape—is a great draw for year-round tourism, travelers in the winter really have one reason to visit: the skiing. Thomson-Jonville has her routine down: “One of my favorite things to do is to take a moniteur de ski for the day and head into the mountains, around Mont d’Arbois.” (On her more adventurous days, she’ll brave the challenging pistes a little farther out at Mont Blanc.) In between stints on the slopes, she’s developed a list of local favorites, for everything from designer fashion to where you can find the best raclette; ahead, she offers us a peek into her Megève address book.

It has been revealed that for a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Allard is a classic—a Megève institution. It’s on the square beside the church, the maison behind the original ski fuseau created in the 1930s. It’s a lovely place to find a beautiful sweater. Blu&Berry is where I go to find something more unexpected; they have pieces from The Row and Celine. Major Boss is another Megève institution, with a great skiwear selection. It’s one of those shops that everyone who comes here regularly knows.

For a worthwhile investment piece: The Hermès store in Megève is particularly well-stocked, and the Loro Piana boutique in the center of the village is great for après-ski shopping!

According to recent reports, for unique souvenirs: Again, Allard for something classic that feels connected to the village. For something more unusual, there’s Max et Isa; it’s great for antique jewelry, vintage Murano lamps, and decorative objects. It’s a good address to browse for an unusual gift or a special piece for your chalet.

For the magpie: Guilhem Joaillier is my favorite jewelry store in Megève. I’ve picked some meaningful pieces here over the years; it’s a solid gift shop, too. Someone always has a birthday when we’re in Megève, and, of course, there’s always Christmas.

For your next great read: Scarlett Megève has a good curation of art books, as well as fun decorative objects. It’s a good place to buy gifts. The Maison de La Presse in town is the place we all go to buy magazines and novels; it’s super simple but you’ll always bump into someone you know there. Megève is a small place!

In a recent development, for the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: I spend a lot of time in the Pharmacie de la Tour on Place de l’Église—it’s full of little treasures. I love an après-ski French pharmacy haul. Vitamins, moisturizers, supplements, hair masks… I love trying out new products when I’m in the mountains.

For a pick-me-up treat: Le Hibou Blanc is a great address for brunch or a coffee. It’s in the center of town with a massive, heated terrasse to sit outside with a cappuccino and watch the world go by.

For a luxurious lunch: L’Idéal 1850, up on Mont d’Arbois, for a lunch break between runs with a beautiful mountain view. It’s very social; wear a great ski outfit the day you book a table.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Le Vieux Megève. It’s a cheerful, traditional spot in the village—it’s noisy, yummy, and so much fun. Book early to share a raclette or fondue with family or friends. It’s my favorite spot in Megève—in fact, everyone in my family loves it there. It’s a unanimous favorite.

For a different kind of evening, I love Kaito at the Four Seasons. The sushi is delicious, and it’s a bit of a scene. Dress up and people watch!

Sources indicate that for a post-slope spa day: I always love to try upcoming places, but to me, Les Fermes de Marie has the best spa in Megève. The facials are great. The Susanne Kaufmann spa at Les Chalets du Mont d’Arbois is also good for bodywork.

Sources indicate that for an apéro.. or a nightcap: The bar at the Fer à Cheval. It’s cozy and welcoming—a perfect place to settle by the fire after a day in the mountains, plus it’s in the center of town. The bar at the Four Seasons after dinner is also a vibe for the people watching.

According to recent reports, for your packing list: My mountain packing list is tried and tested: One ski look, one puffy ski jacket, a (fake) fur coat, cashmere joggers, and substantial sunglasses. I also pack UGGs and cashmere socks for warmth, plus some great earrings to liven up a low-key dinner look.

Maple Pumpkin Overnight Oats

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast.
  • Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.
  • Sources indicate that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Sources indicate that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

It has been revealed that whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health.
  • Sources indicate that according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease.
  • Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

Sources indicate that according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, claims.

It has been revealed that dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

Recent findings suggest that “It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”.

It has been revealed that that concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the new study.

According to recent reports, the study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

Sources indicate that "I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy.".

So while I don’t initiative on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “Antwerp is a small city with so many substantial stories,” states Charlotte de Geyter, co-owner of Bernadette, the Antwerp-based fashion label she founded with her mother, Bernadette. The best way to see it all? Slowly; and if you’re anything like the mother-daughter duo, by bike.

Sources indicate that A hub of creativity, the Belgian city has real fashion bonafides; it counts Ann Demeulemeester and Dries Van Noten among its graduates, the best-known of whom are the subject of the current “Antwerp Six” exhibition running at the MoMu Fashion Museum through January 2027. There’s never been a better time to visit; come winter, the city slows down and gets even cozier. “One thing that embodies the Antwerp spirit to me is its quiet confidence,” continues Charlotte. “The city has always been home to incredible fashion designers and artists, and I think that creativity still defines Antwerp today.” Below, read Charlotte and Bernadette’s recommendations for where to eat, shop, and souvenir hunt in Antwerp—plus, what to pack for a trip to town.

According to recent reports, for a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Expect a strong focus on high fashion and directional pieces at Renaissance, a boutique known for championing emerging designers and young brands, all curated with a distinct point of view. And no trip to Antwerp is complete without visiting the iconic Dries Van Noten store. Decorated by Gert Voorjans, the interiors feel both theatrical and deeply personal, true to the spirit of the brand.

For vintage gems: Rosier 41 is a long-standing vintage designer store where you’ll discover an exceptional selection of second-hand Belgian fashion. Antwerp has a deeply rooted fashion culture, and the store reflects that, full of unique archival pieces and rare finds.

For a worthwhile investment piece: The destination in Antwerp for established luxury designers and international fashion houses is Louis. I would invest in Belgian designers like Margiela.

For the magpie: Go straight to the diamond district in Antwerp, near the station.

For your next great read: Eric Tonen Books in Kloosterstraat for art books, and the bookstore inside the fashion museum MoMu for the best fashion books.

For stylish home goods: We love the smaller boutiques like St Vincents, as well as antique shopping in Kloosterstraat.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Take them to buy Christmas ornaments in Christel Dauwe for a truly unique experience.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: Le John is a go-to for a low-key dinner. Quiet, simple, and consistently good food; the kind of place you keep returning to. Order the pumpkin tortellini, a delicate handmade pasta filled with sweet pumpkin served with rich sage butter, with a good glass of red wine.

Decorated by Axel Vervoordt, Sir Anthony Van Dijck is an Antwerp institution that has a timeless atmosphere and remains one of the city’s classic dining rooms. Go for the seasonal menu, featuring refined Belgian-French dishes made with fresh ingredients (and a great tarte tatin).

For a bakery treat: The “Een Strik” from Dellafaille is a go-to—it’s a bow-shaped pastry made from delicate, flaky puff pastry, with a golden, caramelized exterior and a light, buttery crunch.

For the art-lover: My partner, Ben Sledsens, works with the Tim Van Laere gallery. They truly put the artists first and host new exhibitions almost every month. We also love Cour Space, a young, more conceptual gallery showcasing emerging artists and contemporary practices. The space feels intimate and understated, with carefully curated exhibitions that attract Antwerp’s creative crowd.

Recent findings suggest that for an apéro.. or a nightcap: Tango Bar is a favorite. It’s a newer, trendier restaurant by two young entrepreneurs, with interior design by Cami Verborgh. Expect a more fashion-forward crowd here.

For your packing list: There’s a deep sense of history; you feel it most while slowly wandering through the old streets on a quiet weekend, surrounded by beautiful, historic buildings. In the winter, this means you’ll need a good raincoat, and boots for lots of walking (A.F. Vandevorst is a classic Belgian option). Don’t forget a comfortable pair of jeans and a warm cashmere sweater.

  • The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux.
  • According to recent reports, what’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

According to recent reports, what’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

A 1972 advertisement for the Pogue.

Sources indicate that one of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

In a recent development, when it comes to healthy breakfasts, free yourself to eat more than plain yogurt and granola bars. And honestly, those $19 acai bowls from the smoothie shop aren’t that nutritious. A truly healthy breakfast has plenty of carbs for energy (this includes fiber-rich ingredients like whole grains, berries, legumes, and seeds); muscle-and-bone-supporting protein; and plenty of healthy fats for nutrient absorption. Many of these recipes can easily be made ahead and doled out from the freezer, so before you swing by the drive-through for bland egg muffins, consider these more flavorful options. Here are 23 of our favorite healthy breakfasts.

When it comes to healthy breakfast ideas, my mind immediately goes to oats. Also chia seed pudding. So the newest edition of my column Good for You is a chia seed–overnight oat hybrid, which also uses up a can of pumpkin purée (I bet you have one in the pantry).

Frozen or fresh berries work great in these accidentally vegan pancakes (thanks, silken tofu!) from Good for You. A good drizzle of maple syrup is all they need for accompaniment, but since I’m not vegan, I enjoy them with a swipe of Greek yogurt.

Another Good for You hit is this speedy, protein-and-collagen-rich soup, which is something in between Italian stracciatella and Chinese egg drop soup.

Industry observers note that okay, after this one, I’ll stop shamelessly promoting my column. But seriously, don’t sleep on this hydrating mixed berry smoothie, especially if you’re lukewarm on eating plain cottage cheese.

This tricked out avocado toast is loaded with hot smoked salmon and creamy scrambled eggs.

You maybe haven’t seen an omelet filled with sliced apple and cheddar, but I recommend trying before knocking.

Industry observers note that oatmeal is an ideal choice in the morning for carbs and fiber. I like to slowly stir in egg whites while it’s simmering on the stove for extra protein and top it with ground flaxseed.

A great option for weekend mornings. You could top it with feta or yogurt, dunk whole wheat toast in the sauce, or spoon it over rice, anything goes.

Nothing hits quite like a breakfast burrito, but I can’t buy one every day and still pay rent. DIY to the rescue: I line the tortilla with salsa or hot sauce and sometimes add leftover refried beans if I have them.

The texture of chia seed pudding took me some time to get used to, but now I’m obsessed. Strange how the body adapts! I love that this recipe makes enough for a workweek of breakfasts. Head here for our favorite matcha powders.

If you don’t have time to make the hot honey mixture, these simple breakfast tacos are great with any hot sauces or chile-based condiments that happen to be in the fridge.

Recent findings suggest that this Persian egg dish is similar to a frittata, which means it makes for great meal prep. It takes awhile to wash all the herbs, so make sure you have time, but leftovers will last a few days in the fridge. I like it cold with a swipe of Greek yogurt, but you do you.

Sources indicate that meet the bran muffins you’ll actually crave. Squidgy dates and chopped chocolate make these more like a hearty breakfast cake than the dense pucks you may have eaten in the past.

If it’s not heirloom tomato season, opt for smaller cherry or Campari tomatoes in this recipe—your taste buds will thank you.

To bulk up this green smoothie into a filling meal, add some nut butter and cottage cheese or plain yogurt, plus a scoop of protein powder if you have it.

It has been revealed that leftover cooked quinoa mocking you in the fridge? Stir it in to these blueberry muffins. Win-win.

Speaking of leftover quinoa, if you’re looking for a savory option instead of sweet, throw together this morning salad with a few boiled eggs and smoked trout.

While I personally love mushy porridge, I understand that cakey is a more pleasant texture for many. If that’s the case for you, baked oatmeal is the solution.

In a recent development, serving brunch to a crowd? Make this breakfast casserole. Just grab a nice loaf of sourdough to slice alongside.

If you haven’t yet tried fried eggs that were based with turmeric oil, now is your moment.

For the savory oatmeal fans out there, try simmering with instant dashi powder and salt-softened vegetables.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Vogue’s 16 Best Hotels in the Alps, From Chic Chalets to Design-Forward Boutique Stays

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Alps have a particular hold on the imagination.
  • Across France and Switzerland, the region’s hotels run the gamut from storied grand dames and old-world mountain inns to contemporary retreats where thoughtful architecture and considered design take center stage.
  • Industry observers note that les Fermes de Marie, a hamlet above Megève, was put together in 1989 by Jean-Louis and Jocelyne Sibuet from Savoyard farm buildings dismantled elsewhere and carted here, stone by stone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Alps have a particular hold on the imagination. There are the snow-dusted peaks, naturally, and the villages tucked into their folds, with timber chalets, candlelit restaurants, and views that could make even the most committed city dweller reconsider their priorities. But the pleasures of an Alpine escape extend well beyond a day on the slopes and unlimited raclette.

Across France and Switzerland, the region’s hotels run the gamut from storied grand dames and old-world mountain inns to contemporary retreats where thoughtful architecture and considered design take center stage. Some trade in old-school glamour, others in rustic charm or a welcome degree of seclusion, but the best are worth giving up a powder morning for and staying in. Whether you’re here for serious skiing, fireside dinners, or simply the pleasure of waking up to a panorama of peaks, these are the Alpine hotels in France and Switzerland worth planning a trip around this winter.

Industry observers note that les Fermes de Marie, a hamlet above Megève, was put together in 1989 by Jean-Louis and Jocelyne Sibuet from Savoyard farm buildings dismantled elsewhere and carted here, stone by stone. The result is a welcome abundance of old timber, antiques, wool, plaid, and animal skins, with fires burning in the appropriate places. (The Sibuets also run La Bastide de Marie in the Luberon and Villa Marie in Saint-Tropez, but this is their grande dame; no small thing from a family this good at hospitality, especially where children are concerned.) Here, they are dispatched to Le Hameau des Enfants, a free club with its own children’s concierge, where 5-to-10-year-olds are kept busy with cooking and ski lessons.

According to recent reports, breakfast, served in the heart of the hotel, in the main restaurant with an enormous fireplace, is not to be slept through (on the menu: homemade jams, Alpine cheeses, farm butter, and exceptional bread). From 2 to 6 p.m. the lounges and library put out homemade Savoie cakes, whipped-cream waffles and the house hot chocolate, after which the bar moves on to wine with slates of local cheese and charcuterie. By evening the main dining room settles into traditional Savoyard cooking by the fire, including a house pâté that has earned its permanent place on the menu. Downstairs, the hotel’s stube is given over entirely to cheese—fondue included—though for dinner in town, the family also owns Le Vieux Megève, a Savoyard institution in the village with as many locals at its tables as guests. The spa’s outdoor hot tubs are best used in falling snow, when the hamlet looks sealed inside a snow globe, and the terraces come heaped with sheepskins and blankets for an evening apéritif under the heat lamps.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pool, kids’ club, shuttle, on-site ski rental.

Editor’s tip: Stop by L’Épicerie de Megève, the Sibuets’ grocery in the village. The breakfast jams are on the shelves, as is honey from the hotel’s own hives and wine from the family’s Luberon estate, all of which makes for a perfect souvenir.

Address: 163 Chemin des épis, 74120 Megève.

The Saint-Georges is the latest addition to Megève’s hospitality scene. Located right in the center of Megève, a few steps from the pedestrian rue Charles Feige and a short walk from the lifts, the old building has been reimagined by the English designer Luke Edward Hall as a kind of Alpine fairy tale, complete with all the decorative flourishes that the genre demands.

Savoyard folklore provided the starting point, but the 29 rooms take the idea in a cheerfully eccentric direction: Pierre Frey fabrics, painted and patterned headboards, boldly colored bathrooms, floral tiles, deep carpets, and hand-painted murals jostle against carved wood and antiques. On weekend evenings, there’s live piano beside the fire in the bar, lending the place the air of an old mountain inn in which one might reasonably expect a wolf, a princess, or at least a particularly off-kilter uncle to appear before dinner. Le Trappeur, the hotel’s bistro, serves classic French cooking with a few Savoyard dishes, while the spa takes a more elemental approach, built around hot and cold contrast therapy. Families are well catered to, with dedicated rooms and activities for children who may find themselves rather more at home here than in the usual hushed Alpine palace.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bar, kids’ club.

Address: 159, Rue Monseigneur Conseil, 74120 Megève.

Recent findings suggest that le Coucou occupies a large wooden chalet on Méribel’s Belvédère, beside the Rond-Point des Pistes, arranged so that the windows look out over the slopes and a blue run begins just beyond the ski room. It is ski-in, ski-out in the fullest sense: Staff are on hand to unbuckle your boots, lest the final indignity of the day prove too much.

It has been revealed that on arrival, one encounters a domed ceiling painted by Matthieu Cossé with owls perched among trees against blue mountain peaks, which establishes the level of seriousness with which the decor is to be taken. Pierre Yovanovitch designed more than 130 pieces of furniture and lighting for the 55 rooms and public spaces—including teddy-shaped armchairs—and set them among terracotta walls, sheepskin, and upwards of 160 artworks, Calder and Chillida included. The bar, done up in yellow, blue, and cream, looks directly onto the pistes through floor-to-ceiling windows. There are indoor and outdoor pools, a Tata Harper spa, and two children’s clubs, should the adults require a little peace. For dinner, Biancaneve serves Italian food; Le Fumoir seats sixteen around a fireplace for fondue; their flagship restaurant Beefbar extends onto a terrace. The whole enterprise is unapologetically theatrical; and though one might reasonably ask how much theater a ski holiday requires, the answer, apparently, is quite a lot.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, bar, pools, kids’ clubs, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental.

Address: 464 Route du Belvédère 73550 Les Allues Méribel.

Industry observers note that courchevel has never been short of hotels willing to make a spectacle of luxury. Saint Roch, opening in December on the Bellecôte piste, is Maisons Pariente’s case for the opposite approach, one the family already made persuasively in Paris with Le Grand Mazarin and Méribel’s Le Coucou. Architects Virginie Friedmann and Delphine Versace have recast a longstanding hotel as something closer to a well-traveled aesthete’s chalet, its 37 rooms dressed in dark wood, mohair velvet, agate and onyx by way of Russian dachas and Persian interiors. Pierre Mesguich’s mosaic frescoes and Atelier Toporkoff’s stained glass do more for the place than any amount of gilt would. The living room alone, with its deep sofas and fireplace, makes a decent case for skipping the afternoon session.

Recent findings suggest that come evening, visit Prunier, the Parisian caviar house’s first alpine restaurant. To unwind further, head downstairs, where you’ll find a ceramic-tiled pool and Tata Harper treatments that take their cue from Ottoman hammams.

Amenities: Spa, pool, ski shop, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental.

Address: Piste de Bellecote, 73120 Courchevel 1850.

Opening in December from Chapitre Six, the group behind Megève’s Saint-Georges, Bourbon Hotel seems to have concluded that the last thing the resort needs is another chalet. Instead, it takes its cues from a London members’ club, with dark woods, deep velvets, and low lighting. It sits in Courchevel’s Golden Triangle, with direct ski-in, ski-out access to Les Trois Vallées, which is useful, though the more interesting offerings involve what happens after a day on the slopes.

Industry observers note that simonetta, the hotel’s Italian restaurant, will be led by Simone Zanoni, whose Paris credentials include Le George at the George V; this will be his first restaurant in the mountains. The bar pairs cocktails with vinyl sessions, a combination that suggests the après-ski hours here are to be taken at least as seriously as the skiing itself. Below ground, a spa built around contrast therapy offers the usual opportunity to repair the damage before heading out to do it all again. There are 28 rooms and three suites, and pets are permitted on request. Whether Bourbon can make the London-club formula work at altitude remains to be seen, but it is at least a departure from the expected wood-and-antler routine.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bar, ski-in, ski-out.

Address: 286 Rue Park City, 73120 Courchevel.

Sources indicate that les Airelles occupies the Place de Neige, where the village meets the mountain, with direct access to the pistes and the Solaise and Olympique gondolas, as well as a large sun terrace for watching skiers descend. Its 41 rooms, suites, and penthouses have been conceived in the spirit of a medieval Alpine residence, furnished with antiques and artworks drawn from a collection of more than 4,000 pieces. Each has a balcony or terrace, and the penthouses come with their own butler. The Bernard Orcel ski room takes care of the business of getting dressed for the mountain, and, on one’s return, offers hot drinks and crêpes. Dinner can be had at Matsuhisa or Palladio, followed by a stint in the Guerlain spa—the largest in Val d’Isère–or the private cinema.

Children have a grotto-like pool of their own, while dogs receive monogrammed mats, personalized collars, and a dedicated walker to take them out while their owners ski. There is something delightfully over-the-top about a hotel that provides more elaborate arrangements for a dog’s afternoon than most people make for their own, but Les Airelles has never been especially interested in the modest pleasures of Alpine life. Its particular talent is to turn every practical inconvenience into an occasion for service, and every stay into a small performance of aristocratic excess.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pools, cinema, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental.

Address: 145 Rue de la Poste, 73150 Val d'Isère.

Recent findings suggest that the skiing is serious in Verbier, but so is the après. Experimental, the Paris group that built its reputation on cocktail bars, chose its first Alpine hotel accordingly, opening a chalet a short walk from the lifts and directly above Farm Club; otherwise known as the nightclub that has kept the village awake since 1971.

In a recent development, for those who have come to ski, the village shop Les Ruinettes delivers rentals to heated lockers downstairs, and a shuttle takes guests to the lifts. The 39 rooms, designed by Fabrizio Casiraghi, favor warm wood, deep colors, and clean lines over the typical heavy chalet style. This ethos extends to the food: Saint Bernard, the restaurant beside reception, gives Alpine classics a lighter touch. Upstairs, the Experimental Cocktail Club draws a mixture of hotel guests and outsiders, while the outdoor hot tub at the Biologique Recherche spa looks directly into the bar, allowing one to order a cocktail through the window without ever getting out of the tub. Starting this November, the bar is introducing a vinyl listening room built around Klipsch speakers, where record selectors stand in for the usual resort DJ.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bars, nightclub, hot tub, ski lockers, shuttle.

Editor’s tip: On certain weeknights, guests can bring their own records to play in the fresh listening bar.

Address: Route de Verbier Station 55, 1936 Verbier.

Industry observers note that welsh brothers Grant and Craig Maunder, who have been part of Adelboden since Grant first came here in the late seventies, own two hotels in the village; the Brecon, named for the Brecon Beacons, is the smaller, quieter one, housed in a timber building dating to 1914 at the more peaceful end of town. Its interiors look to the ’50s and ’60s, with leather, wool, stone, and crazy-paved Welsh slate underfoot. (Continuing the nod to the owners’ home, you’ll also find Welsh wool blankets lie folded on the beds.).

Each of the 18 rooms and four lofts are television-free; a decision that might once have seemed a little severe but becomes easier to defend when you realize the Adelboden massif occupying the entire window offers a much better thing to stare at. Grant’s wife, the American ceramicist Andrea Anderson, has thrown more than 950 pieces of pottery by hand for the hotel, a level of commitment to the breakfast table that seems almost unreasonable until one sees the results. The Brecon is adults-only and all-inclusive, organized around an open kitchen, with a sauna facing the mountains. While it’s not ski-in, ski-out, a free shuttle runs to the lifts, and a heated Art Deco pool awaits on your return.

Amenities: Restaurant, sauna, pool, shuttle.

Editor’s tip: As an all-inclusive adults-only property, food, drinks, and spa access are included in the room rate.

Address: Dorfstrasse 88, 3715 Adelboden.

Industry observers note that at Kleine Scheidegg, beneath the Eiger, the Mönch, and the Jungfrau, the day ends when the last train leaves. The pass is accessible only by the Wengernalp railway, and once the final service has departed, the guests of the Bellevue des Alpes have the mountain largely to themselves.

The inn has stood here for generations: Christian Seiler bought it in 1840, and his descendants, the von Almens, still run it, with Andreas von Almen and his wife Silvia (a flutist), representing the fifth generation. The hotel was last extended in 1948, and little in the public rooms seems to have felt an urgent need for improvement since then. There is the grand piano, the old furnishings, and a bar dating to 1929, its swing door hung with photographs of the climbers and guides who used the hotel as a base camp for attempts on the Eiger’s north face. Guests would watch their progress through telescopes on the terrace, a rather more compelling form of entertainment than anything likely to appear on a hotel television. Clint Eastwood filmed The Eiger Sanction here in 1974, though the mountain itself has never needed Hollywood to establish its credentials. Skiing begins at the front door, and the setting is so imposing that the usual question of what else the hotel offers seems faintly beside the point.

Amenities: Restaurant, bar, terrace, ski-in, ski-out.

Address: Kleine Scheidegg, 3823 Wengen.

Klosters acquired its Hollywood connections after the war, when American soldiers interned in Switzerland returned with their families and friends, and the film business followed. Greta Garbo, Gene Kelly, and Rex Harrison all appear in the guest book at the Chesa Grischuna, which earned the nickname “Hollywood on the Rocks”. The Guler family opened the hotel in 1938, and since 2022 it has been run by Zurich entrepreneurs Astrid von Stockar and Clemens Gregor. The entire building is a protected landmark, listed on Switzerland’s national register of historic places.

Industry observers note that the thirteen rooms are furnished with antiques and local woodwork, and the old piano bar, whose walls are painted with winter scenes, is now a pasta bar—the natural gathering place after a day on the slopes. But the hotel’s best surprise lies below: a two-lane bowling alley painted by Alois Carigiet, the Swiss illustrator best known for A Bell for Ursli. Raclette is served in the adjoining tavern, which seems an entirely sensible way to recover from an evening of competitive bowling. One can understand why the Hollywood contingent came back: The Chesa Grischuna offers the sort of atmosphere that no amount of set dressing can quite manufacture, and has managed to preserve it without turning its history into a theme park.

Amenities: Restaurants, bar, bowling alley.

Address: Bahnhofstrasse 12, 7250 Klosters-Serneus.

Sils Maria has attracted writers and painters for well over a century. (Nietzsche among them: His summer house stands directly across the road from Chesa Marchetta.) The village lies between the lakes of Sils and Silvaplana, just fifteen minutes from St. Moritz, though it belongs to a rather different tradition of Engadin life—one more interested in contemplation than conspicuous consumption.

Chesa Marchetta occupies four connected farmhouse buildings dating to the sixteenth century. Artfarm, the hospitality company founded by Swiss gallerists Iwan and Manuela Wirth, whose other projects include Scotland’s Fife Arms, spent four years restoring the property before reopening it in January. The architect Luis Laplace retained the original sgraffito—the intricate scratched-plaster decoration that distinguishes the old houses of the valley—and furnished the thirteen rooms with traditional Engadin furniture, antiques, and work by local artists and artisans. Art, in other words, is not an accessory here so much as part of the building’s grammar.

In a recent development, upstairs, the library and bar form the social heart of the house, a richly layered room where books, beautiful works of art and carefully chosen furnishings make for an atmosphere closer to a collector’s private residence than a conventional hotel lounge. It is the sort of place that invites you to linger over a drink, surrounded by objects with their own stories, without ever feeling overly designed. Downstairs, the restaurant draws on seasonal recipes, an Italian-Swiss mixture that makes good sense in a valley whose geography has never entirely respected national borders. Lake Sils is a fifteen-minute walk away, while Corvatsch is the nearest skiing.

Address: Via da Marias 88, 7514 Sils im Engadin/Segl.

Sources indicate that there are luxury hotels, and then there are institutions whose very existence has helped define luxury. Badrutt’s Palace, which opened in 1896, belongs rather emphatically to the latter category, having spent more than a century establishing the terms of alpine grandeur. Its unmistakable tower rises above the center of St. Moritz, overlooking the lake and the expensive little theater of Via Serlas, where the international winter set gathers each year to perform its familiar rituals of consumption.

Inside, the atmosphere is grand hotel in the fullest, least apologetic sense: chandeliers, imposing public rooms, formal service, and interiors that understand the importance of making an entrance. The original rooms remain reassuringly traditional, and the lake-facing ones are the ones worth asking for (Hitchcock, for his part, kept Suite 501). The Serlas Wing, opened in 2025, offers a contemporary counterpoint, its 25 rooms and suites by Antonio Citterio and Patricia Viel finished in local stone, oak, and Loro Piana Interiors wool. A three-minute walk from the property leads to Chesa Veglia, a 17th-century farmhouse housing several restaurants and bars, including beloved favorites, like Pizzeria Heuboden, the Carigiet Fondue Stübli and the Polo Bar, among others.

Back in the Palace, Matsuhisa occupies what was once Switzerland’s first indoor tennis hall, which is set to debut a reimagined design this winter by Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, while a latest bar designed by Milanese designer Giuseppe Porcelli will welcome guests in Le Grand Hall. Up on Corviglia, Paradiso, the hotel’s mountain restaurant, trades chandeliers for panoramic views, Alpine fare, and a livelier après-ski scene. The Renaissance Bar is where the evening tends to end, preferably with a whisky, a cigar, and a seat by the fire. The spa’s glass-walled infinity pool looks straight out at the lake; even the business of doing very little ought to come with a view.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, bars, pool, shuttle, on-site ski rental.

Address: Via Serlas 27, 7500 St. Moritz.

Founded by Johannes Badrutt in 1856, the Kulm helped establish St. Moritz as a winter resort. Set above the village with sweeping views across the Engadin, the hotel balances its sporting heritage with a distinctly contemporary appetite for reinvention. Many of its 150 rooms and suites have been refreshed by Pierre-Yves Rochon, while the restaurants range from Amaru, Claudia Canessa’s Peruvian-inspired restaurant dressed in contemporary whimsy by Luke Edward Hall, to Mauro Colagreco’s Kulm Country Club, housed in a neighboring building with its own ice rink. Sunny Bar, a St. Moritz institution in its own right, remains essential for a drink and a dose of local history.

It has been revealed that the latest addition is the Alpine Sports Lounge & Boutique, designed by Foster + Partners for winter 2025. Clad in fragrant Swiss stone pine, it reimagines the conventional ski room with private fitting areas, specialist equipment, a ski concierge, and a pantry serving healthy snacks and energy shots. The idea is to get guests from suite to slope with rather less fuss, and considerably more style.

Amenities: Restaurants, bars, ice rink, shuttle, on-site ski rental.

It has been revealed that address: Via Veglia 18, 7500 St. Moritz.

Sources indicate that few hotels have so thoroughly shaped the identity of the place they inhabit as Gstaad Palace has shaped that of Gstaad itself. Rising above the village like a white castle, it belongs to an older conception of luxury, when glamour required a little grandeur and there was an art to knowing exactly who was in the room (and that they may prefer not to announce themselves). Behind its turreted façade are ninety rooms and suites, five restaurants, a sprawling spa, indoor and outdoor pools, and the GreenGo, the legendary nightclub that has entertained generations of international society. Its corridors have absorbed the passing of royalty, financiers, and film stars.

Industry observers note that one comes here, presumably, for the mountains, the service, and the fondue that’s served in a former wartime bunker. But one also comes for the sense of entering a world that has long since ceased to exist anywhere else—except, somehow, on this hill above Gstaad, where the old rituals of privilege continue to be performed with magnificent, almost theatrical conviction.

Amenities: Restaurants, spa, shuttle, on-site ski rental.

Address: Palacestrasse 28, 3780 Gstaad.

Gstaad has always done luxury in a particular, old-money key, and The Alpina carries that tradition forward with a more contemporary hand. The 55 rooms are fitted with carved ceilings, timber walls and Swiss farmhouse cupboards, and even the leather straps once used to hang cowbells turn up as decoration. Meanwhile, above the main staircase is a hand-painted ceiling made in southern Europe around 1780 and painstakingly restored. Fresh executive chef Francesco De Bartolomeis oversees the hotel’s entire food offering, so dinner can be Japanese at Megu or Bernese at the Swiss Stübli, with a cellar of 1,700-plus labels behind either. It isn’t ski-in, ski-out, but a shuttle runs to the lifts and the hotel sorts passes and rentals. The Six Senses Spa is vast, and its menu runs from Tibetan healing to bio-hacking therapies, such as their hyperbaric oxygen chamber.

Amenities: Restaurants, spa, shuttle, on-site ski rental.

Address: Alpinastrasse 23, 3780 Gstaad.

Recent findings suggest that suvretta House occupies a rather different corner of the St. Moritz universe. Opened in 1912, it sits away from the village center, surrounded by mountain scenery and woodland, in a position that feels deliberately removed from the main procession of boutiques, champagne bars, and other seasonal distractions. Its fairytale exterior and grand interiors are unapologetically old-world, retaining the grandeur and traditions of the great Alpine hotels, but with a more secluded, sporting character. This is a hotel for people who regard a ski holiday as something that ought to involve actual skiing: It has direct ski-in/ski-out access to the Corviglia slopes, its own ski facilities, and a long-standing connection to the mountain that sets it apart from properties in the village.

For lunch on the slopes, there’s Trutz, near the top of the Suvretta lift, while Chasellas, down at the base, is the place to stop for a hot chocolate after skiing. Back at the hotel, the Grand Restaurant offers an altogether more formal expression of Alpine luxury, with elaborate interiors, traditional service and a culinary repertoire that combines French influences with international touches. Among its most famous dishes is spaghetti with caviar, a luxurious yet understated signature that reflects the Grand Restaurant’s timeless elegance. Afternoon tea and a swim in the pool within the hotel’s expansive, freshly renovated spa complete the experience. Suvretta’s particular appeal lies in this combination of grandeur, sporting heritage, and seclusion… with a hotel shuttle to bring you into town in a matter of minutes whenever you’re ready to rejoin the scene.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pool, ski-in, ski-out, shuttle, on-site ski rental.

Address: Via Chasellas 1, 7500 St. Moritz.

Latest Update: 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day.
  • Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns.
  • Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

Sources indicate that I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety concerns. The tech giant paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow organization food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such complications can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the concerns found overseas!).

In a recent development, sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

Industry observers note that more recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

According to recent reports, substantial Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety challenges over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

According to recent reports, the Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

According to recent reports, wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

According to recent reports, perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

It has been revealed that even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

  • So why not make some kicks for the people who can tell you exactly which artisanal mill produced their selvedge?
  • It has been revealed that social Status is a North Carolina-based sneaker and streetwear boutique owned by the Whitaker Group, the same organization behind A Ma Maniére.
  • According to recent reports, social Status’s take on the AJ1 Low starts with the classic ‘Chicago’ color palette.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menswear guys love Japanese denim. Menswear guys also love sneakers. So why not make some kicks for the people who can tell you exactly which artisanal mill produced their selvedge? That seems to be the thinking behind the new Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko.’.

It has been revealed that social Status is a North Carolina-based sneaker and streetwear boutique owned by the Whitaker Group, the same organization behind A Ma Maniére. Over the years, it’s worked with Nike on everything from milk-inspired Dunks to Air Pennys. The shop’s last proper Jordan collab was an extremely hairy Air Jordan 6 from 2019, but now the pair are back with something a little easier to wear.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’.

According to recent reports, social Status’s take on the AJ1 Low starts with the classic ‘Chicago’ color palette. The toebox is white, the overlays are red, and the Swoosh and collar are black. But rather than keeping everything box-fresh, Social Status has roughed up the leather so it arrives pre-scuffed, as though you’ve owned these shoes for years.

The massive switch happens across the sidewalls. The usual white leather panels have been replaced with mismatched patches of indigo fabric covered in white sashiko-style stitching. Sashiko is a traditional Japanese embroidery technique used to reinforce, repair, and extend the life of clothing. It’s particularly associated with vintage workwear and denim, which is why these Jordans look like they’ve been mended using a very expensive pair of jeans.

There’s also an old-school nylon tongue, a slightly aged sole, and a custom shoebox wrapped in the same blue pattern.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’.

While you might normally expect this sort of big Jordan release to land on the High, it’s nice to see the Low silhouette get some love. Some dudes prefer it, after all—it’s less bulky around the ankle and works better under wider trousers. You still get all the bits that make an Air Jordan 1 instantly recognizable, only without half the collar.

According to recent reports, the Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’ is set to drop on December 18 for $155 through Social Status, with a wider release via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists expected to arrive later on. Japanese denim guys, get your credit cards ready.

A version of this story originally appeared on British GQ.

Tech Report: Too Busy for Breakfast? Make These Pumpkin Overnight Oats

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
  • Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

Sources indicate that I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Humans have been on the planet for hundreds of thousands of years and our ability to thrive simply isn’t rooted in whether we eat first thing in the morning. In fact, the cliché is barely a century old, stemming not from nutritional science but good old-fashioned advertising.

Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.

It has been revealed that yet today breakfast is one of the most commonly skipped meals. So instead of wagging my finger at you about missing something so “vital,” I think it’s worth asking: Why did you miss it in the first place?

Industry observers note that on a jam-packed holiday like Thanksgiving, there are plenty of reasons. You have a turkey to roast. The table has to be set. Someone needs to pick up the wine. And oh, there’s still the pie dough to roll out! Maybe you even want to “save room” for the glorious feast you’re putting so much effort into.

But skipping this meal does come at a cost. Even if you aren’t ravenous, it’s metabolically valuable to eat in the morning. Breakfast stabilizes energy, and studies have shown that forgoing it leads to a reduced consumption of vital nutrients like fiber, potassium, iron, and calcium, often found in morning staples like fruit, whole grains, and dairy. Without some food to start the day, you risk an energy dip, brain fog, and downright hanger. Which, let’s be honest, we don’t need in a kitchen overflowing with dirty dishes and extended relatives.

I have an easy solution. Making breakfast on Thanksgiving (or any day, really) doesn’t have to be a last-minute hassle. It can be quick to assemble and still feel special—like you’re really taking care of yourself, because you are. Take this overnight oats–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes the night before you plan to eat it.

Open up a can of pumpkin purée—odds are you bought extras that didn’t become a pie. Mix it with oats, maple syrup, and whichever milk you have in the fridge. A scoop of chia seeds adds bonus nutrition and prevents the oats from turning gluey as they hydrate overnight.

The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you. It’ll keep you full and firing on all cylinders for a day of turkey roasting, potato mashing, and vibe managing. It may not be the most vital meal of the day—at least on Thanksgiving—but it will be delicious.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are headed right into the thick of ski season; when warm, wool knitwear is the uniform du jour, and the temperature is the kind of cold that’s completely inexcusable unless accompanied by plates of melty raclette at après-ski. This is your sign to book your winter getaway in advance. And while there are tons of great ski resorts you could jet off to, nothing quite beats an Alpine retreat—whether freeskiing in Zermatt or trialing bunny slopes in Megève, you have options. The best Airbnbs in the Alps, from Austria to France to Italy, are the perfect place to stay if you need more flexibility and space than a hotel.

It’s a vast region—the Dolomites alone are an 18-peak range—so there’s a lot to choose from. Go for stately chalet elegance with a multi-bedroom option if you’re traveling with lots of friends and family; book something closer to a cozy cabin if you prefer a low-key holiday. These 15 options span the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps, as well as a range of prices and styles. Your next decision? Which Fair Isle sweater will make it into your carry-on.

In a recent development, those in search of the most traditional of Alpine vacations will find everything they’re looking for in this peaceful chalet—right down to the Savoyard pottery. It looks out onto the Aravis mountains, just five minutes away from the Croix-Fry ski resort and 40 minutes from the busier spots of Annecy and Megève. It has a wood-burning fireplace that’s ideal for relaxing after a day on the slopes, and a spacious balcony for those brave enough to wrap up and take their coffee outdoors in the winter chill.

Sources indicate that situate yourself in the heart of one of the most sought-after ski resorts, close to all of Gstaad’s main shops. The apartment, which can sleep up to six, has heated underground parking and a ski cellar to facilitate winter trips. The interior is simple but well-appointed—the dining table being a major plus for cozy dinners—but the real draw is the balcony. Head outside for gorgeous mountain views whenever you want them.

If you’re not looking for a fully remote stay, this charming mini-chalet gives you a taste of quaint mountain village life. Renovated in 2024, the updated amenities list includes a pizza stone oven, walk-in shower, and hypoallergenic bedding. (Your booking also comes with a Beatenberg guest card, a perk inclusive of a free bus pass for travel back and forth to Interlaken for when you want to explore the alpine area.) This has all the cozy touches you’ll want for a weeklong vacation, plus one important extra: The wraparound balcony has storybook views of both Lake Thun and the Eiger, Mönch, and Jungfrau peaks.

Recent findings suggest that not all alpine retreats are stuffy, rustic cabins; some are luxurious, light-filled homes that expertly blend old and new. This spot is a perfect example. The 18th-century farmhouse right in the historic center square of Scuol was recently restored, keeping its old-world charms (that wood paneling!) while making some necessary updates. Sleek chrome furniture, a chef-grade kitchen, and whitewashed walls bring light in.

There’s no television in this mountainside cabin; all the better to truly unwind with. Instead, occupy yourself with a forest hike or a day on the slopes (the Airbnb is in the La Tzoumaz resort, by Verbier in the Swiss Alps). Wind down by candlelight, whether that’s with a warm meal served family-style at the dining table overlooking the tall trees or a game of Hearts by the fire.

It’s pretty hard to beat these views. This restored barn looks out onto Mount Pelmo in the Dolomites, with a key highlight being the covered balcony; you’ll want to take every meal there to soak in the mountain views. It can fit up to seven guests—great for a large family or group—and you’ll each have plenty of space to stretch out in.

According to recent reports, this charming cottage in the Valais town of Ayer puts you right near all the top ski resorts: Grimentz, Zinal, St-Luc, and Chandolin are all about a 15-minute drive away. The combined dining-living space is charming, with windows that look out onto snowy hills in the winter and green pastures (plus the occasional cow) in the summer. Four bedrooms offers plenty of space for a massive friend trip.

From the outside, surrounded by snowy pine trees, this chalet looks like a fairytale cottage; inside, it’s outfitted with all the contemporary amenities to make your stay a luxurious one. A Bose Bluetooth sound system, HDTV with all the streamers, and state-of-the-art kitchen appliances bring a modern element to the wood cabin. A private sauna and hot tub only add to the five-star feel.

In a recent development, it’s an easy drive to the alpine lake and mountains of the Salzkammergut region from this Airbnb, which sits on a spacious property surrounded by forest. Sweat out the day in the sauna or gather around the fireplace to listen to a vinyl or play a board game—both are provided by the host.

Sources indicate that with Montblanc in the distance, this 19th-century cottage offers picturesque views from the balcony. Take your morning coffee there before heading out to the slopes or nearby hiking trails, returning home to soak in the tub, whip up a home-cooked meal, or crack open a upcoming book in the glass-walled (and, crucially, heated) reading room.

Industry observers note that expect charm at every turn with this farmhouse, which dates back to the 15th century. Located in the Kaiser Mountains of the Eastern Alps, this sprawling property features wooden ceilings, terracotta tiled floors (with partial underfloor heating), and beautiful murals painted throughout—there’s even an original stove in the dining room.

Industry observers note that this rustic mountain hut located in a secluded part of the Italian alps is actually a working farm and apiary: Those with a fear of bees, plan accordingly. A breakfast basket is provided each morning, with the freshest of ingredients you can enjoy outdoors or in the open-air kitchen in the warmer months, or by the fire in the winter. You’ll need a car to access the property—it is properly remote—but its isolation is part of the charm.

Sources indicate that this French Alps home is ideally built for family holidays. Child-friendly features, from a travel crib to fireplace grates, will make your stay more comfortable; several separate bathrooms give everyone their own space; upscale amenities, like heated flooring and optional catering, make every day feel like a treat. It’s just south of Lake Geneva, if you want to rent a car and take a little day trip.

Recent findings suggest that avid skiers, this one’s for you: This ski-in/ski-out property puts you right on the slopes, at the foot of the Mont d'Arbois ski area. You’re within walking distance to ski lifts and the ski school, and will be staying in one of the six apartments that make up the larger Chalet Griffin—so you have access to communal amenities, but with more privacy than a hotel. The space itself was recently renovated in 2022, and includes luxe amenities like a functioning fireplace and chef-grade kitchen.

This apartment in the Dolomites is deceptively spacious: It sleeps up to six, with soaring A-frame ceilings giving the illusion of even more space. The theme appears to be, simply, wood. From the exposed beams to the built-in furniture to the floor-to-ceiling cupboards, the whole space is designed with rustic cabins on the brain.

Joseph Zada of The Hunger Games Is Still Getting Used to Being a Movie Star

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joseph Zada is doing “very, very, very good,” he tells me, with a heavy emphasis on the third very and an audible exclamation mark.
  • His much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week.
  • Sources indicate that in the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joseph Zada is doing “very, very, very good,” he tells me, with a heavy emphasis on the third very and an audible exclamation mark. And why shouldn’t he be?

His much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week. Zada and I spoke the morning of his Upcoming York City premiere, while he was being shuttled from one press obligation to the next, already go-go-go before actually hitting the red carpet Monday night in custom Louis Vuitton, punctuated with a pair of gold-toed cowboy boots from Pharrell’s first collection for the brand.

Sources indicate that in the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy. When asked about the movie, the 21-year-old Australian demonstrates palpable care and excitement, even a bit of sadness that it’s over. “I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes,” Zada says. “And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.”.

Since being cast, he’s barely had a second to stop and reflect on joining one of the biggest franchises in the world—and this comes right on the heels of East of Eden, too, in which Zada played another haunted young man. He laughs when I note the comparison: “I guess I just pride myself on my ability to show my vulnerability.”.

Below, read our full conversation with the emerging star as he reflects on his Hunger Games journey, talks red carpet style, and shares his thoughts on Robert Pattinson playing James Bond.

Joseph Zada: Yeah, I wonder if I’ll be nervous.

Recent findings suggest that maybe towards the start. It doesn’t get old… but it gets familiar.

Well, I did SiriusXM this morning, and then, I mean, it’s basically just been like, "Hey, do press all day and then go to your premiere." So there’s not much time for a ritual, so I guess I go a little bit nonverbal and half-dissociate.

According to recent reports, no, it’s so much fun. I have a lot of fun at these premieres. It’s always like a crazy, crazy crowd. The way they’ve set it up has just been otherworldly, and I’m not sure if I’ll ever have it again, but I distinctly remember each stop and the feelings that I’ve had thus far, and it doesn’t get old. It’s always crazy to see this many fans and the passion they have for this project. I mean, it’s not every day that you get to step into something with a built-in fan base where people are already coming out and supporting it before they’ve even seen it. So it’s a really special experience, and I don’t know when I’m going to be able to get that again.

It has been revealed that where did I have the most fun? I had a lot of fun in London because my little sister was there, my little sister and my brother’s girlfriend, so I got to hang out with them and I haven’t seen them in a while. And Mexico. Mexico was the craziest event that we’ve had. There were literally thousands, several thousands of people there. The reception was incredible.

According to recent reports, am I allowed to drop this? Oh, yes, that is what this [interview] is for. I’m wearing a Louis Vuitton suit—custom, custom—that Jason [Bolden] and I have worked together on, and I’m a substantial fan of the boots. The boots are pretty dope.

You know I have some serious stompers.

I feel a lot more comfortable in these clothes nowadays, and it’s actually become a lot more enjoyable to put them on. And it feels like more of an armor and less of a scary thing, and it feels like I build a lot of confidence being able to do this.

My red carpet style, I think... I don’t know. Just whatever Jason puts me in for the night.

Yeah, I think just doing it so often and finding different looks and just being able to wear all the different brands and find what I’m comfortable in.

Recent findings suggest that I pride myself on my ability to have vulnerability. I think as a young man, that’s what I find interesting in these performances of these young men coming of age, and I think that was really what I was just looking for in my early career. I modeled my career on people like Timothée Chalamet and Lucas Hedges, and I love the way that they kept their heart on their sleeve and how they feel like an open nerve. I love being able to portray that in my performances.

I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes and really, really felt like I was there every single day and just had the most incredible support in terms of my cast mates and my directors and my producers. And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.

In a recent development, I guess everything just kind of changed just like that. Everything just changed in one quick second, and it feels like... I guess I haven’t really thought about what it was like before. I’ve just kind of been trying to ride the wave. I’m sure being able to go back home for Christmas, I’ll have some time to reflect, but right now it’s just—what’s the day ahead of me? And just making sure I’m ready for all of that.

In a recent development, I’m just excited to be at home every single day and watch movies with my mom and my siblings and see all my friends. That’s what I’m really excited for. I’m just excited to also just turn off my phone for a little bit, maybe go on a little road trip down to South Australia and get a little beach house and not bring my phone and have six days where I’m just off the grid.

That’s a great question. I’ve got Apocalypse Now on 4K Ultra HD on my projector that I bought at home, and I cannot wait. I feel like people ask me what was the best part of my year, and I just start naming all the movies that I’ve watched. And genuinely the happiest that I ever am is when I’m watching a film, which is kind of sad but also kind of cool.

I think... I don’t know. I loved Wild Horse Nine. That’s a favorite I’ve watched in cinemas. I loved Primetime too, because I love Rob Pattinson. I love Skyler Gisondo.

Sources indicate that I did just see the Bond casting news! I am chuffed. That is so exciting. That is beyond exciting. He is just the most phenomenal actor, and he really just makes the most interesting choices. And I think him in that role, the stoicism that he’ll bring along with those really interesting choices, it’s going to make that character so interesting. He’s a really special actor. It feels like every young male actor that I speak to feels like that is a person to look to right now and a person’s career to emulate in terms of the risks and the commitment to his craft and all these roles that he’s churning out.

Sources indicate that I don’t know. It’s so ridiculously helpful to have a book with you because it’s just so much information, and I love preparing for roles and having a book because it’s just an internal monologue, which is what you should be doing for every character. You read a scene, and you should be writing what is going through your character’s head. And when you have a book, it’s all done for you, or at least you have a good foundation.

I hope I get to do as many book adaptations as possible, but I think what I’m really looking for is just a great director and a great script. I’m not sure what’s [next]. I’ve got a fresh slate right now, but there’s a couple of things floating around.
