#31128. Latest Update: Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)

📅 14 Mar 2018 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3022 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)

📅 14 Mar 2018 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as notable to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale.
  • In a recent development, another bonus of a kitchen scale?
  • It has been revealed that scales aren’t just for bakers, either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as notable to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale. Bon Appétit’s Test Kitchen team agrees, which is why you’ll see gram measurements in the baking recipes on our site.

In a recent development, another bonus of a kitchen scale? In most cases, you can kiss measuring cups and spoons goodbye, which means far fewer utensils to clean once your bakes are in the oven.

It has been revealed that scales aren’t just for bakers, either. They make portioning burger patties and meatballs easier, streamline meal prep, and keep your Sunday morning pancake routine cleaner.

I’ve tested 16 models over several years and consulted Shilpa Uskokovic, former BA senior Test Kitchen editor and co-owner of Hani’s Bakery, to find the best kitchen scale for home cooks. The winner is just $27.

Recent findings suggest that new in this revision: I tested the new version of the Oxo Good Grips 11-Pound Digital Kitchen Food Scale. While it was easy to use and I appreciated the pull-out display, it was less accurate than the Escali—and over double the price. You can read my full review below.

Size: 8.5 x 6 x 1.5"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: 4 minutes 30 secondsPower: AA batteries (included).

It has been revealed that this Escali Primo has held the top spot in our testing for over six years and has been a favorite in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen for far longer than that. “This scale has been with me for more than a decade of my career, staying faithfully by my side through 12-hour shifts in pastry kitchens, bouts of religious recipe testing, and weekly sessions of casual baking,” notes senior Test Kitchen editor and resident baking whiz Shilpa Uskokovic.

It’s durable, accurate, intuitive to use, and affordable—pretty much everything we could ask of a kitchen scale.

What we love: The Escali Primo is lightweight, comes in a variety of fun colors, and has a simple two-button interface to turn it on, tare it, and toggle between ounces, pounds, and grams. In testing, it was responsive and precise, quick to tare, and delivered accurate readings every time. Its 4.5-minute auto shut-off is among the longest of any model we tested, so you won’t lose your measurements mid-bake. Plus, its 11-pound capacity is large enough to accommodate any task a home cook might ask of it.

According to recent reports, performance aside, the Escali Primo has several design features that helped it stand out. For one, the fact that the weighing platform is elevated and offset from the base means you can easily read the display or use the buttons even when measuring into a large, wide mixing bowl. The plastic body and sealed control panel make it a breeze to wipe down after a floury baking session and also keep stray crumbs from getting stuck in any crevices. Another detail we like? The four rubberized feet keep it stable on your kitchen counter.

According to recent reports, the Escali Primo has proven quite durable as we’ve continued to test it long-term, another reason why it’s a perennial favorite among our Test Kitchen editors. Shilpa again: “It’s compact and easy to store, it’s easy to wipe clean, it toggles between grams and ounces seamlessly, and it’s reliably accurate.".

According to recent reports, what we’d leave: The Escali can only measure in 1-gram increments. While this was typical of most scales we tested, those looking to use their kitchen scale for dialing in their coffee routine will want something more precise (though coffee scales are kind of their own thing). Unlike some pricier models, the Escali’s display is not backlit, but we didn’t find this to be an issue. It’s also worth noting that the Escali is not a touchscreen device, so you’ll need to use a bit of pressure on the buttons.

Size: 8.3 x 7 x 1.3"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: NAPower: AAA batteries (included).

Amazon Basics products are not consistent across the board, but this scale is a certifiable hit. At about half the price of the Escali, it’s a good option if you’re not positive about this scale thing and want to spend as little as humanly possible to do so.

What we love: There are a lot of similarities between the Amazon Basics scale and the overall winner. The Amazon Basics scale has the same two-button setup, a similar elevated weighing platform that makes it easy to see the display, and the same 11-pound maximum capacity. It’s made of plastic with a stainless-steel platform that’s easy to wipe down and is just a touch larger than the Escali at 7 inches across.

In testing, I was impressed by the Amazon scale’s accuracy, considering its price point. It responded to weight addition or removal almost as promptly as the Escali and provided an accurate readout about 99% of the time. That 1% weight change inaccuracy happened when someone repeatedly added weight or switched back and forth between units of measurement, and when it did happen, the reading was off by a minor amount. The problem could be fixed by removing what was on the scale, taring it, and starting over. For $10 (at the time of writing), you’d be hard-pressed to find a better model.

Sources indicate that what we’d leave: Unlike the Escali, the Amazon scale’s buttons lack any kind of laminated sealing to prevent crumbs or liquid from entering the crevices around them. As mentioned, this scale isn’t quite as accurate as the winner and it tended to overshoot an item’s actual weight at first (before correcting itself relatively quickly). And last, the stainless-steel platform is more prone to scratching or smudging than Escali’s plastic one.

You’ll notice there aren’t any other scales marketed as coffee scales on this list, and that’s because the Fellow Tally was the only coffee scale we thought could plausibly work as an all-purpose model too.

What we love: The Fellow Tally is one of our favorite coffee scales (especially for pour-over) thanks to features like a built-in timer and a “brew assist” that directs you on the proper ratio of coffee to water—but its 5.5-pound maximum capacity means it works for most home baking projects too. If you’re the kind of person who likes to nerd out over your brewing and baking techniques, this is your best bet unless you want to invest in two separate scales.

According to recent reports, in testing, we quite liked the Tally’s design for its tactile controls and easy-to-read OLED display, and appreciated its ability to measure grams, ounces, pounds, and milliliters (that milliliter measurement is calibrated for water, so one milliliter equals one gram; if you're measuring a heavier liquid like milk it will be slightly off). The elevated 6-inch platform is large enough to comfortably hold a mixing bowl while allowing easy visibility of the display.

Calibration weight accuracy test.

To find out how accurate each scale was, I used a set of calibration weights. I tested each scale’s ability to give an accurate reading for the minimum amount of weight it claimed to be able to accommodate (usually 1 or 2 grams), and its ability to detect small changes when there was already weight on the platform. I also placed weights in various places on each scale’s platform to determine whether they could give an accurate reading regardless of whether the weight was in the center or at the edge.

In a recent development, I coated each scale in a mixture of flour, water, and oil and let them sit overnight. I cleaned the residue off and noted which scales were easy to clean and resistant to any scratching or staining.

I distributed winning scales to staffers to see how they fared after long-term use in our homes and in the Test Kitchen and added any long-term testing notes to reviews as they came in.

In a recent development, I looked for consistently accurate measurements and a short response time when adding and removing items of varying sizes and materials from each scale. I took into account how weight distribution affected the readings, looking for scales that delivered spot-on results regardless of where on the platform we placed the weights. I also took note of how precise each scale could be in its measurements, but found our favorite all-around options tended to measure in 1-gram increments.

I looked for scales that were intuitive to use without picking up a manual.

I tested scales with weight capacities ranging from 1.65 to 16 pounds, but found that a maximum capacity of 11 pounds was more than enough for the tasks one might try to accomplish in a home kitchen.

I wanted a scale that felt durable, well-made, and stable on the counter and was also designed to be easy to clean.

Unlike a stand mixer, a scale isn’t the kind of kitchen gadget most home cooks are looking to keep permanently on their counter. Lightweight, compact models that could be easily stashed in a cabinet were better.

I took into account the relative price of each scale. After years of testing, we’ve found that you really don’t need to spend much to get a high-quality, highly accurate kitchen scale, so any models that were pricey needed to wow us with their design or extra features.

These scales didn’t quite make our list of top picks, but they still impressed us in testing and might fit your needs depending on what you’re looking for.

Recent findings suggest that this is another scale from the makers of our top overall pick. It’s sleeker and slightly more advanced, with a four-button control panel that includes the typical on-off, unit change, and tare functions, plus a “hold” feature that keeps your measurement on the screen rather than automatically shutting off after a given amount of time.

We ultimately didn’t think the added feature and upgraded design merited spending an extra $10, but this is undoubtedly a good scale (and the rainbow of colorways available makes it easy to find a match for your kitchen decor).

Industry observers note that this Oxo scale is a favorite among professional chefs for its easy-to-clean stainless-steel weighing platform and handy pull-out display design (great for measuring into extra-large bowls). I liked it a lot, but found it was often off by 1 gram, especially when the weight was placed in one of the platform’s corners. I ultimately didn’t feel its performance merited its price tag, which is more than double that of the winning Escali at the time of writing.

Industry observers note that true to its name, this precision scale from Etekcity provides measurements in 0.1-gram increments as well as the option to measure in milliliters and fluid ounces (along with the typical grams and pounds/ounces). That remarked, we didn’t love that the instructions recommended using this scale with only the included plastic bowl and found that the stainless steel weighing platform scratched easily.

Etekcity Luminary Smart Nutrition Scale.

In a recent development, this rechargeable digital kitchen scale seemed promising, with its 22-pound maximum weight, easy-to-clean weighing platform, Bluetooth-enabled app connectivity, customizable auto-off function, and host of premium features. However, it was one of the least accurate scales we tested: Our 5-gram nickel weighed in at a low of 2 grams and high of 6. For that reason, we don’t recommend it unless you’re buying a scale primarily for meal tracking reasons.

Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale.

In a recent development, the Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale was another promising option. It’s rechargeable via USB cord and has a sleek, buttonless design and 22-pound capacity. However, it wasn’t as accurate as we’d have liked, and despite how cool it looks, the lack of buttons turned out to be frustrating. We also disliked how the tab that switches the units of measurement is located underneath the scale.

MyWeigh KD-8000 Bakers Math Kitchen Scale.

This scale is heavy-duty. It’s got a 16-pound max capacity, it can be charged with a plug-in A/C adapter, and it’s the size of a small kitchen appliance. It works well (and even allows you to measure using baker’s percentages), but unless you’re in a professional bakery setting, it’s overkill.

Greater Goods Digital Pocket Scale.

Recent findings suggest that at less than 3-by-3 inches, this scale is truly tiny. It’s an impressive little kitchen tool, able to provide measurements in 0.1 gram increments, but its maximum capacity of 1.65 pounds is just too small for most cooking or baking projects besides making coffee.

Cuisinart KML-KO3B Precision Chef Bowl.

This scale from Cuisinart has a glass weighing platform and removable stainless-steel bowl, but we ultimately didn’t love the idea of the bowl adding yet another piece of clutter to our kitchens. Besides that, this scale was less accurate than our top picks, had a short, 1-minute auto-off time, and was nearly double the price of the winning Escali.

Sources indicate that this scale lost for a couple reasons: It was less accurate than our winners and one of the most difficult scales to clean in our most recent round of testing. The display panel was prone to trapping crumbs and bits of flour, and the scale itself required intensive scrubbing to remove leftover residue.

Joseph Joseph TriScale Compact Folding Digital Kitchen Food Scale.

Like many of Joseph Joseph’s products, this scale has an interesting design. It’s made up of three prongs that fold into a small rectangle, making it easy to stash away when not in use. That said, this scale struggled in testing; it couldn’t detect small amounts of weight and was prone to reading the weight of your finger when you tapped its buttons.

Ooni Dual Platform Digital Scales.

According to recent reports, I had high hopes for this dual platform scale from the makers of some of our favorite pizza ovens. It’s got a sleek, low-profile design, wide capacity range (0.1–22 grams if you take into account both platforms), and handy light-up display. Unfortunately, we found both the small and big platforms inaccurate: The small platform struggled with picking up small changes and was often off by multiple tenths of a gram, and the big platform was inconsistent, often fluctuating between two readings or off by a couple grams.

KitchenAid Dual Platform Digital Kitchen Scale.

We noticed inaccuracies and inconsistencies with both of the KitchenAid’s platforms. The small scale is meant to be precise down to the hundredth of a gram, but it struggled to detect our .02-gram calibration weight and fluctuated between .19 and .20 when we weighed a 0.2-gram weight. The significant scale was decidedly more inaccurate, off by 3–4 grams when we tested it with a 100-gram weight.

Smeg Contemporary Kitchen Scale.

Like all of Smeg’s products, the brand’s take on a kitchen scale is very cute. Unfortunately, while the design is aesthetically pleasing, it didn’t prove to be very functional. The scale is very bulky because of the built-in bowl, which can’t be removed from the base (though the stainless-steel bowl insert can be removed for cleaning). The scale’s base itself is sensitive to weight, which means pressing on the buttons with force can cause a temporary spike in the reading—and, more crucial, if you drop any ingredients on the base, the weight of mentioned ingredient will be added to the total. We also found that this scale struggled to accurately report small (1- or 2-gram) changes in weight.

ThermoWorks Gravitas Precision Kitchen Scale.

I was very excited to test this scale from the brand behind our favorite cooking thermometers, but unfortunately it failed to impress me enough to merit a recommendation. The scale boasts the capability to measure down to the tenth of a gram, but according to ThermoWorks' product description, it does so with ±0.7 g accuracy. In testing, I found this to be true—readings were rarely accurate to the exact tenth. After testing the scale in his home kitchen for several weeks, senior commerce editor Noah Kaufman also noted that readings came in on the slow side, which made measuring ingredients that pour out promptly (like flour or liquids) tricky. I did appreciate the detachable display (helpful when using a large, wide bowl that might otherwise obscure the screen), but it wasn’t enough to outweigh the negatives—and besides, I’m of the opinion that there’s no reason for the average home cook to pay $120 for a scale when a $25 one performs incredibly well.

We also tested the Ozeri Pronto, Etekcity Multifunction Food Kitchen Scale, and GDealer Tempered Glass Kitchen Scale, all of which have been discontinued.

How do you use a kitchen scale?

Recent findings suggest that to use a kitchen scale, you’ll have to familiarize yourself with the concept of “tare.” Taring a scale allows you to reset the weight back to zero when you already have something on the weighing platform. This is particularly useful if you want to measure ingredients into a bowl (just place the bowl on the platform, click the tare button, and go on adding your ingredients), or if you want to measure multiple ingredients into that bowl without needing to add or subtract the existing weight in your head.

What should you use a kitchen scale for?

According to recent reports, baking is the obvious answer here, but the use cases for kitchen scales go far beyond the world of flour and butter. Use a scale to perfectly portion out meat for meatballs or burgers, aid in your meal prep for the week, or for any recipe where precise quantities are of the utmost importance.

It has been revealed that alaina Chou: Alaina has been testing products at Bon Appétit for over three years, which means she’s used dozens of air fryers, toasters, rice cookers, and—you guessed it—kitchen scales. She’s an avid baker who’s been a proponent of measuring by weight for the better part of a decade.

It’s no secret that Japan has perfected the art of, well, a lot of things—design, cuisine, wellness, hospitality, and craft, to name a few. A trip to Japan offers a glimpse at living with intention and elegant restraint, from the traditional tea ceremonies to the ritual of long soaks in an onsen. In its populous capital, slowing down might feel like a contradiction, but the best Airbnbs in Tokyo offer travelers respite from the bustle.

Industry observers note that winter is an especially beautiful time to visit. The crowds thin out and the city is illuminated by trees glowing with little white lights—it feels like your own personal winter wonderland. Those visiting around Newly introduced Year’s celebrations, or Shōgatsu, can participate in a long list of traditions, from visiting temples and shrines to eating a bowl of buckwheat noodles in warm broth, to ensure luck for the year ahead. Whether you’re looking to explore Shinjuku’s narrow alleys lined with tiny bars or prefer to spend your time in Shimokitazawa’s bohemian district amidst the cafes and vintage shops, these Airbnb rentals will situate you in Tokyo’s most compelling neighborhoods.

This design-forward spot starts with a lofty living room and just gets better. Recently renovated in August 2026, the unique property used to be a sign shop before it was converted into an inviting vacation rental. From the exposed wood beams to the rustic pottery that lines nearly every available surface, it’s a perfect reflection of the city’s creative energy. It also fits up to 10 guests; if your trip to Tokyo is part of a significant group holiday, this is the place to book.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, TV, crib, AC.

Natural materials and muted colors create quite the calming spot—though hints of playfulness, like a fish decal in the bathroom, ensure it’s not devoid of personality.

Ideal for larger groups, this four-bedroom home offers a serene spot of respite in the city, complete with a zen garden, a rooftop terrace, and a soaking tub. (For those craving something livelier, the National Stadium Plaza is not far away.).

Amenities: Balcony, bathtub, washer and dryer.

Its location puts some of the city's most significant sights, such as the Tokyo Skytree and the Sensoji Temple, within easy walking distance; if it’s your first time in the city, this is a convenient home base.

Amenities: Elevator, balcony, bathtub, washer, AC.

Sources indicate that clean lines, a restrained palette, and geometric motifs await in this elegantly pared-back house, which feels more minimalist case study than typical vacation rental. With three bedrooms and three bathrooms, there’s ample room for groups to settle in. The interiors are elegantly pared back, reflecting the timelessness of Japanese design, and the oversized square tub makes for the perfect antidote to a long day exploring the city or browsing the shops of nearby Nakano Broadway.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, movie theater, balcony.

Experience penthouse living in this stylish home just three minutes from Shibuya station. The two-bedroom property’s star amenities include the four-person stone bath as well as a spacious tatami room, where you can unwind after a busy day of sightseeing.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, heating.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, waterfront.

For those in search of a break from the city’s fast-paced energy, take note of this calming rental. Traditional design details such as paper door panels and light fixtures also help cement a tranquil atmosphere.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, AC, heating.

Taking the bones of a 60-year-old wooden Japanese house, the Superhost owners of this lovely property kept relaxation top of mind when giving it a modern refresh. Both the dining room and living area are spacious enough for six people to spread out and unwind, and high-quality bedding, toiletries, and furniture ensure a supremely comfortable stay.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, smart lock.

This lovely two-story house was completely renovated in 2024 and offers modern design touches and lots of natural light. House plants are also peppered throughout the space, and the Simmons mattresses are there to ensure guests have the snuggest sleep possible.

Amenities: Washer, high chair, smart lock.

Situated on a peaceful street in trendy Sangenjaya near central Tokyo, this home features plenty of natural sunlight, a handmade wooden staircase and other traditional Japanese carpentry finishes. Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, dishwasher, outdoor dining area.

Located in the “Little Kyoto of Tokyo,” this brand new home offers easy access to major attractions such as Shinjuku, Shibuya, and Ginza and is within walking distance of the train station. Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, heating, free parking, private balcony.

With its garden (a rarity in Tokyo) and Japanese artworks guests can actually buy, this home goes above and beyond to provide guests a distinct experience. Request a car service for pickup from Haneda airport for a smoother check-in; when here, you can also request other luxury amenities like a private chef. Whether you’re unwinding in the living room on the curved sofa, or savoring a meal at the long dining table, a stay here is the perfect high-end experience.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, AC, heating, backyard with furniture, smart lock.

Sources indicate that in the heart of Tokyo just a two-minute walk from Yoyogi Park, this four-story home is cozy and spacious. All of the bedrooms are aglow in soft light, lending a zen-like atmosphere perfect for falling asleep. Plus, the private balcony comes with outdoor furniture for pre-dinner canapés and cocktails.

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, high chair, private patio with furniture.

Robert Pattinson, I’m Begging You For a Quirked-Up James Bond

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our long international nightmare is finally over: two-time Meme of the Year nominee Robert Pattinson has been chosen as Daniel Craig’s James Bond successor, bringing an end to an exhausting series of “reports” and “leaks” about Amazon’s search for a new 007.
  • In the hands of another (read: more limited) actor, I’d never suggest such a risky swerve.
  • 20 years ago, Casino Royale was a refreshing reset and a crucial corrective to the overflowing ridiculousness of the Piece Brosnan era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our long international nightmare is finally over: two-time Meme of the Year nominee Robert Pattinson has been chosen as Daniel Craig’s James Bond successor, bringing an end to an exhausting series of “reports” and “leaks” about Amazon’s search for a new 007. Finally we can stop the debates and fan-casting and let Patts and Denis Villeneuve cook until they’re ready to present their new vision. But that would require a level of restraint that the internet doesn’t typically exercise. Immediately after the protracted process of casting Bond concluded, the internet moved on to naming its dream picks for Bond Girls and Bond Villains (sometimes, to brilliant effect.) I can’t say I have a dog in either fight, at least not right now. My Bond WishList is of a different magnitude altogether: can we make James Bond silly again? Just a little, even, 15 percent goofball?

In the hands of another (read: more limited) actor, I’d never suggest such a risky swerve. But the best thing about Pattinson is his range. Sure, if Villeneuve and co. want to render Bond as the stoic and taciturn gentleman he’s generally been this century, Rob has proven he can do that, as every Tenet truther has been gleefully preaching for the last 24 hours. But more often than not, Pattinson is keen to get weird, whether that’s going Full Freak, as he does in Primetime, or approaching certain archetypal parts with a silly, goofy mood (like his conniving suitor in The Odyssey). He can do a “voice” (Mickey 17), he can do scumbag grime (Good Time), he can do hapless screwball (The Drama). Why not make what’ll be his biggest role to date a little cocktail of all his best elements? (Okay, he can leave the Mickey 17 voice behind.).

20 years ago, Casino Royale was a refreshing reset and a crucial corrective to the overflowing ridiculousness of the Piece Brosnan era. But in the past two decades, the pendulum has swung back—the gritty reboot has become studios' stock-in-trade. I feel the same way about Batman; the actual risky choice would be to make something less like Nolan’s series that, instead, hewed a little closer to, say, Batman Forever, or even the gothic camp of Tim Burton’s two films.

Of course, Robert Pattinson was at the center of a Batman reboot as well, and the result was a movie that felt more like a spiritual cousin to David Fincher’s Se7en; audiences ate it up so much that the hunger for a sequel persists even after endless delays. When it comes to franchises as high-stakes as Batman or Bond, you can’t trust these increasingly sauceless execs to make anything but the basic choice. There’s no reason to expect Jeff Bezos isn’t texting Denis screenshots from Skyfall for reference from his megayacht at this very moment.

According to recent reports, but if there’s anybody capable of putting a little English on the handle while still giving the mainstream what it wants, it’s Big Bob Pattinson. He could easily make his James Bond a little off, or he could go full seductive cad who smiles like Neil Tenet, has a ki with Q, and charms women with some playful banter instead of simply brooding them into submission. I’m not looking for invisible cars and sharks with lasers, or a Lothario like Roger Moore who speaks in puns. All I’m asking is that we give camp a chance. Because ultimately, the most exciting thing Villeneuve and Pattinson can do to set their Bond apart would be to loosen him up a little.

The 18 Best Hotels in Tokyo, From Modern Ryokan to Boutique Hideaways

📅 09 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that millions of visitors flock to Tokyo every year to explore the organized chaos that is one of the world’s most populous cities.
  • In a recent development, let’s take it one step at a time and start with where to stay.
  • According to recent reports, one thing to note for winter travelers: Keep in mind that Newly introduced Year is Japan’s most important holiday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that millions of visitors flock to Tokyo every year to explore the organized chaos that is one of the world’s most populous cities. Whether it’s the tantalizing food scene, trend-bending fashion, or rich history, the Japanese capital entices every type of traveler. Quite frankly, you could spend months here and barely skim the surface. And choosing your hotel can be just as overwhelming as deciding what to cram into a short visit.

In a recent development, let’s take it one step at a time and start with where to stay. To help you navigate the thousands of options, we’ve narrowed the list down to some of our favorites; they vary in neighborhood, from frenetic hubs to quieter residential enclaves, so the discerning traveler has a lot to pick from. Some are brand new, others are tried-and-true institutions. Many are from familiar international brands, but a few are the dreamy results of home-grown talent.

According to recent reports, one thing to note for winter travelers: Keep in mind that Newly introduced Year is Japan’s most important holiday. While temples and shrines remain open (and are at their busiest), most businesses and cultural sites are closed for several days—even in a city like Tokyo. If you’ll be in town at the start of the year, it’ll be more important than ever to pick the right hotel to keep you entertained.

With that in mind, here’s our guide to the best hotels in Tokyo.

With just 57 keys—making it the second most intimate property within the Four Seasons portfolio after Naviva in Punta Mita, Mexico—the brand’s exemplary service is brought to the next level here. From Sézanne, the hotel’s lauded French restaurant now under the helm of chef Stephen Lancaster, right down to the reception staff who greet guests by name, you’ll be well looked-after.

In theory, a beautifully textured facade made from salvaged tile fragments should catch the attention of wide-eyed wanderers in a neighborhood that is otherwise modern; after all, we’re talking about Ginza. Here, where the goal is typically to shop until you drop, the last thing you’d expect to come across is a ryokan-inspired hotel hidden away on one of the area’s busiest streets. But that’s exactly what gives Fufu Tokyo Ginza that “if you know, you know” badge of honor.

Recent findings suggest that the hospitality brand is known for its intimate onsen retreats in some of the country’s most popular countryside destinations; this is its first urban outpost. There are just 34 rooms, all of which feature furnished balconies dotted with vegetation and hot spring–fed tubs filled with water ushered in from Atami, the birthplace of Fufu Japan. (Either amenity is hard to come by in this city, but both is simply unheard of.) It only gets better when you head to the lush rooftop terrace, where semi-private banquettes hover above a foot bath. Like with any ryokan, half-board options are available and are worth booking. Dinner features either a sushi omakase or a seasonal kaiseki; and as for the breakfast, it’s easily one of the best in Tokyo.

For its inaugural debut in Japan, 1 Hotel set up shop in Tokyo’s Akasaka district, a central hub for business, entertainment, and dining just a stone’s throw away from other popular enclaves like Azabudai Hills and Roppongi. The brand fresh property opened this past March, with a whopping 211 accommodations that look out to either Tokyo Tower, the Imperial Palace gardens, or the city skyline. In keeping with the brand’s sustainable sensibilities, single-use plastic is non-existent, filtered water taps are installed in every room, and glassware is made from recycled wine bottles. There’s even a farmstand in the lobby featuring fresh fruit that’s deemed “too imperfect” by farmers to sell at local markets—though it looks fairly flawless by this plebeian’s standards—along with more than 1,500 live plants throughout the entire hotel, including the moss that lines the hallways.

It has been revealed that gin fans will delight in the gorgeous lobby bar, where you can choose from nearly 100 locally crafted varieties under a ceiling that’s inspired by karesansui (Zen gardens). At NiNi restaurant, vegetables are the star of the breakfast spread; the rest of the day calls for French Riviera cuisine with a Japanese twist, like a kabocha pumpkin soup de pistou. And if you have time for a dip, you’ll find an indoor pool with a beautiful outdoor terrace just next to the spa.

In a recent development, every few years there’s a hotel that garners so much attention it becomes an icon before it even opens. In 2024, that title belonged to Janu Tokyo. The flagship of Aman’s long-awaited sister brand, Janu Tokyo trades in zen and serenity for a more energetic approach to hospitality, perhaps best exhibited by the property’s whopping eight food and beverage venues. The hotel also offers a robust wellness center that spans four floors, housing one of the city’s largest gyms, a 25-meter pool, and an extensive spa. Once you’re ready to retire, spacious rooms with largely monochromatic interiors welcome you with soaking tubs and balconies in most instances.

Bookended by action with the heart of Shibuya on one side and Harajuku at the other, there’s a lot happening around Trunk(Hotel) Cat Street. In addition to its stellar location, this lifestyle boutique property has managed to capture the zeitgeist, turning it into a favored haunt for the neighborhood’s effortlessly cool inhabitants. The lobby lounge, with a café by day and bar by night, doubles as a co-working space and is quite the scene at nearly all hours. Upstairs are just 15 accommodations ranging from cozy rooms to residential-style suites, all accented with custom Japan-made adornments utilizing upcycled materials.

The hotel offers two on-site restaurants—one that serves Japanese-inflected international fare, the other a yakitori (skewered meats and vegetables) spot—and its own version of a convenience store with locally sourced bites and a curated selection of sustainable products.

In a recent development, remote destinations have been a part of Aman’s ethos since its inception—the opening of the Tokyo property in 2014 marked the brand’s first true city project. Resident architect Kerry Hill’s minimalist approach to the group’s luxury-defining properties arguably plays the most natural role in Japan, a country where less is more. The vaulted atrium in the lobby, which is a hot spot for afternoon tea, has become an icon of sorts within Aman’s portfolio, as has the stone-clad, 30-meter pool overlooking the city. Its bright and airy rooms are some of the largest in the city (the smallest coming in at 71 square meters), and are characterized by light wood and low-profile furnishings. Slide the shoji screen back to reveal a stone bathroom, complete with a window-side ofuro tub with uninterrupted views.

Hotel Groove Shinjuku offers a more approachable price point than its sister property Bellustar Tokyo while still benefiting from the same shiny new tower and prime location. Entry-level rooms are cozy, but there are plenty of larger options (at relatively reasonable rates) like the Japanese Suite, which features a tatami-mat floor spacious enough for multiple futons, making it highly popular with families. Colorful carpets accent the otherwise neutral-hued accommodations while the artist-designed suites up the ante on personality. And if you’re here for a lengthier stay, the on-site coin-operated laundry is an unexpectedly wonderful touch.

Top-floor occupancy of a high-rise is commonplace for luxury hotels in Tokyo; it’s no different at the Four Seasons’ second outpost in the city. When you exit the elevators on the 39th floor, you’re greeted by a tranquil water feature that draws inspiration from the Imperial Palace’s moat. In fact, the royal residence (and the sprawling metropolis’ skyline) can be seen from various points throughout the hotel, including the lobby lounge, where afternoon tea is served, and many of its 190 rooms. Speaking of accommodations, they’re spacious here, as to be expected from a Four Seasons, with floor-to-ceiling windows offering plenty of natural lighting and panoramic views. And if you’re looking to set your eyes on Tokyo Skytree, head down to the heated indoor pool for a couple of laps, then cool off in one of the mist chairs.

When hunger strikes there are a few on-site dining options to choose from, including the all-day Italian restaurant Pigneto (the hand-tossed Neapolitan pizzas are the highlight); but the crown jewels are Est and Virtù, both of which are worth visiting even if you’re not a staying guest. At the former you’ll find refined take on contemporary French cuisine with a commitment to sourcing nearly all ingredients from around Japan and a seasonal menu. Meanwhile, the French-Japanese love affair continues at the latter in the form of cocktails, where spirits from both destinations are the star. The Smoked Ume Fashioned is a prefect representation of the concept, which uses a homemade brandy umeshu with plums that have been aged for at least six months, as is the Yuzu Nagi, where yuzu gin meets cognac in a bright, citrus-forward tipple. (Make sure to ask for the seasonal cocktail menu, where you might just find a kakigori-inspired drink, and order the lobster okonomiyaki, an elevated take on the Japanese classic.).

Back in 1962 when Japan was in the midst of an economic boom, the Okura was one of Tokyo’s preeminent hotels, playing host to a number of dignitaries during its tenure. So when it announced its closure in 2015 with a full demolition in tow—on par with the Japanese affinity for rebuilding rather than renovating, as exhibited with the country’s holiest shrine, Ise Jingu—the decision caused quite the stir amongst locals. Nevertheless, the Okura was reborn in 2019 with two glitzy fresh towers. Some of its history was preserved, like the original mid-century modern chairs that have since been reupholstered, the signature pentagon-faceted lanterns, and kumiko lattice woodwork seen throughout the property.

The main building, dubbed Prestige, is largely geared toward business travelers. The other (the Heritage Wing) appeals more to leisure travelers. All accommodations are suites with sumptuous, oversized bathrooms, complete with a jet tub and private sauna. Some even boast balconies—a rarity in the city. While you’re here make sure to check out Yamazato, a high-end Japanese restaurant with dedicated sushi and tempura counters, along with a visit to the spa for what is arguably one of the better massages in the city.

Recent findings suggest that in a city ruled by skyscrapers, finding some greenery in the middle of Tokyo is like a glass of ice water on a hot summer day. That’s what you get at Takanawa Hanakohro. Part of the larger Prince Hotels compound near Shinagawa Station, the ambiance is set by a classic garden complete with a koi pond, over 200 sakura trees, and the hotel’s very own temple. And while Takanawa Hanakohro occupies one of the complex’s three towers, what makes it particularly special is its 16 ryokan-style suites. Characterized by tatami floors, shoji screens, and large bathrooms with a tub, they’re about as traditional as you get, with courteous service by kimono-clad staff to match. A stay here comes with unfettered access to all of the four executive lounges, including Oh-Sai, which is reserved only for Hanakohro guests, along with a dedicated spa. And while breakfast is usually served at Oh-Sai, you can also request an in-room delivery; the best option, if you’re staying in one of the garden view rooms.

The business district of Otemachi is perhaps one of the most unsuspecting locations for a ryokan, but that’s what makes a tranquil retreat like Hoshinoya Tokyo even more special. Upon entering, the cacophony of the bustling metropolis instantly dissipates and is replaced by a relaxing aura. You’re greeted by a diligent attendant who stores your shoes in one of the bamboo and chestnut cubbies lining the walls, welcoming you to walk barefoot on the tatami mat floors.

According to recent reports, with the exception of the restaurants (which includes a recently added sushi bar), the hotel is strictly reserved for guests. And while there are 84 rooms in total, each floor only has six accommodations, creating a sense of intimacy as though every level is its own mini ryokan, along with a shared ochanoma lounge that’s stocked with complimentary snacks like onigiri and an array of seasonal teas. Enjoy spacious digs with low furnishings, deep soaking tubs, and traditional Japanese design elements like shoji screens, but while you’re here make sure to head up to the rooftop onsen and soak in the healing properties of the natural hot spring.

Hoshino Resorts has several brands under its umbrella—including the uber-luxe Hoshinoya—but at the opposite end of the spectrum is OMO, a more budget-conscious collection of hotels that feature compact but well-appointed rooms. At OMO5 Tokyo Gotanda the accommodations start at 200 square feet; ideal for solo travelers who want something more comfortable than a hostel without breaking the bank. Suites are just a little over 600 square feet. Most have sofas by the window so that you can enjoy the city views in comfort, and there is also a bunk-style room that’s great for families or a small group of friends.

But the real highlight here is being immersed in the lesser-explored Gotanda district, where you’ll find culinary gems like tonkatsu institution Tonki, famed reservation-only izakaya Shokudo Todaka, and stand-up udon bar Oniyanma (this particular store is arguably better than its other locations in the city).

Sources indicate that ginza has no shortage of luxury hotels to complement its high-end stores. Just north of the city’s most glamorous shopping district is relative newcomer Bulgari Hotel Tokyo, which opened in 2023. Set directly across from Tokyo Station, the glitzy 98-key property blends its roots with its newly introduced environs through contemporary Italian design and time-honored Japanese craftsmanship. Bulgari fans will also appreciate overt nods to the brand in the form of framed sketches from the archives, the jeweler’s 1970s Mount Fuji brooch on display in the gallery, and the house’s signature eight-point star inlaid in the black granite floor of the reception area.

It has been revealed that the mark of any stellar city hotel is when it’s enticing enough to keep you indoors despite an exciting metropolis waiting to be explored, and Bulgari Hotel Tokyo delivers. To start, the accommodations are incredibly spacious, starting from 51 square meters. And while there are plenty of luxe touches—throws crafted in Kyoto, hand-brushed gold ceilings, Bulgari-branded bathroom amenities—the automatic blinds are the winner, opening every time you step into the room to reveal panoramic vistas of the city and, in some cases, Mount Fuji on a clear day. Looking for even more dramatic views? Head up to the 45th-floor rooftop lounge, where you’ll be met with Venetian terrazzo flooring and a beautiful glass mosaic wall of birds and trees behind the sleek bar, flanked by lush terraces with plenty of seating looking out to a seemingly endless skyline.

But whatever you do, don’t forget to carve out some time for the spa. There, you’ll find a 25-meter pool clad in reflective green and gold tiles, surrounded by daybeds and floor-to-ceiling windows.

Industry observers note that just blocks from Harajuku and Omotesando Hills, the Aoyama Grand Hotel is arguably one of the most underrated gems in Tokyo. Joining the latest crop of stylish boutique hotels to pop up in the city, the property features plush rooms with mid-century modern decor and punchy patterns that add a quirky character. It offers guests a host of amenities that aren’t even found at hotels commanding double its price tag, such as a complimentary minibar inclusive of alcoholic beverages and snacks as well as bicycles to explore the surrounding area. And while there are a handful of on-site dining concepts, the two standouts are Shikaku, a countertop restaurant serving comforting Japanese fare, and the Top, an alfresco rooftop lounge with a DJ every weekend.

Industry observers note that while Shibuya is known for its frenetic energy, things slow down a bit just north of the station in Tomigaya. The trendy neighborhood has been popular for quite some time amongst well-heeled locals, but it’s now drawing in discerning jet-setters thanks to Trunk(Hotel) Yoyogi Park. In stark contrast to its lively and cool sister hotel on the other side of Shibuya, this new property is serene and understated, providing an urban sanctuary just a stone’s throw away from one of Tokyo’s most exciting enclaves. Japandi interiors are the shared work of Keiji Ashizawa Design and Copenhagen-based Norm Architects, setting the stage for a relaxing stay. Its crown jewel, though? The pool club. Open only to guests, the heated infinity oasis looks out at the lush treetops of Yoyogi Park and is complemented by a jacuzzi, sunken fire pit, and oyster bar.

Sources indicate that crowning the fresh 47-floor Tokyu Kabukicho Tower—where you’ll also find a cinema, nightclub, arcade, and yokocho-style food hall amongst other facilities—Bellustar Tokyo is the perfect hideaway for those who want to be in the thick of Shinjuku without feeling like they are. It’s just steps from the buzzy district’s famed attractions like Golden Gai, a grid of narrow alleys filled to the brim with tiny bars and restaurants, but once you’re whisked up to the sleek lobby, chaos softens into tranquility.

Spacious, minimalist rooms are outfitted with deep tubs and floor-to-ceiling windows to capitalize on their sky-high position (the view alone is worth spending the night in). When it comes to the penthouses, enjoy the benefits of a butler service, a fully equipped kitchen, and access to a dedicated lounge stocked with champagne and small bites. Sora, the largest, also boasts an en-suite spa.

According to recent reports, topping Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower, the Mandarin Oriental is the neighborhood’s premier address. The luxurious group’s signature aesthetic of rich hues and supple fabrics carries over to its Tokyo property with the addition of Japanese design elements like paper lamps and traditional kimono patterns. Spacious accommodations are outfitted with luxurious bathrooms, oversized windows, plush beds, and a bonsai tree for a welcomed touch of greenery. Service, like at any MO, is attentive, and the four-handed massage might be the best way to beat jet lag. While you’re here, explore the immediate area. At the hotel’s doorstep, you’ll find centuries-old businesses still in operation today, a brilliant launching point for discovering Japanese traditions and souvenir shopping.

The Peninsula Hotels has accrued quite a loyal fanbase for its top-notch service, luxurious accommodations with spa-like bathrooms, and its incredible fleet of Rolls-Royces. You can expect all of this at its Tokyo outpost, where doormen donned in the group’s signature white uniform greet you with doors wide open. Rooms nod to Japanese craftsmanship with ajiro ceilings and tochinoki wood doors, and are extremely spacious, with walk-in closets and bathtubs. Beat jet lag with a few laps at the 20-meter pool or make use of your in-room yoga mat and foam roller. Then, head down to the lobby for an unforgettable breakfast. In addition to Japanese and Chinese sets, there’s also a plant-based option inspired by shojin ryori, a Japanese Buddhist cuisine. All three are phenomenal and some of the best in the city.

Upgrade Your Basics: Best Undershirts for Men in 2026

📅 05 Jun 2019 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, just because you don't see a building's foundation doesn't mean it isn't holding everything up.
  • It has been revealed that and while they're certainly good for some added warmth in the winter, there's a common misconception that they can make the wearer too hot.
  • Recent findings suggest that an undershirt is an undershirt is an undershirt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, just because you don't see a building's foundation doesn't mean it isn't holding everything up. In much the same way, the best undershirts for men are the humble base layer of countless great outfits. Many GQ staffers, in fact, wear-test theirs daily, and yet they're often overlooked, even though they've long-perfected their role: to be the protective layer between your gross body and your steezy, attention-hungry shirts and polos.

It has been revealed that and while they're certainly good for some added warmth in the winter, there's a common misconception that they can make the wearer too hot. In fact, lightweight, moisture-wicking undershirts made from fabrics like modal, or cotton blends can actually transfer the sweat away from your body, speeding up your cooling down. All that's to say: Undershirts are more than just men’s underwear. They’re the cornerstone of a hall-of-fame fit.

Recent findings suggest that an undershirt is an undershirt is an undershirt. If you want the most straightforward version, the kind that you’re picturing in your head is most likely from Calvin Klein. It’s a classic crewneck undershirt that’s made of a lightweight jersey that’s 100% cotton which has a smooth, very slightly brushed hand that feels worn-in in the best way possible. The slim fit won’t cause any weird bunching or bulging and it’s got enough length to stay tucked even when you’re out on the town cutting rugs.

My colleague, GQ senior commerce editor Avidan Grossman, has been wearing CK's genre-defining undershirts since his high school years. (He could do without the logo at the hem, but has made his peace with it, given that you never see it once it's tucked.) Otherwise, he prizes Calvin Klein's riff for its simple, pared-down design and blessed lack of modern-day frills. After all, not every shirt needs to moisture wick or odor block. If you just want an undershirt that gets the job done, don't overthink it.

Sometimes, sleeves are just too much undershirt. That’s where tanks come in. Also known as A-shirts, the humble, sleeveless tank has been rocked by every heartthrob and neighborhood grandpa as far back as anyone can remember. And while the low neck and lack of sleeves means you’ll practically never see them underneath a button-up, the irony is that they look great shown off with an unbuttoned camp shirt or on their own.

According to recent reports, for the money, we think Hanes takes the cake with their multipack of undershirts. The stretchy ribbed jersey is made of 100% cotton and fits snug with a low neck that’s slightly squared off compared to most tanks. They may cost just under twenty bucks for a pack of six, but they look like a million bucks. “I’ve had buyer's remorse over many a menswear garment over the years,” explains GQ editor Jordan Bowman, "but the one thing that has never let me down is the humble tank top from Hanes. They nailed the fit and the material, and the great thing is, you can buy a pack just about anywhere.".

If every part of your wardrobe has to be fit for a king, down to the most basics of basics, then CDLP is what we’d recommend, my liege. The reality is that most luxury tees don’t offer much more than the regular stuff. It’s diminishing returns after a certain price point, but CDLP is the notable exception. My colleague, our contributing editor Louis Cheslaw, has put his same CDLP cottons through the ringer year after year, and says they still haven't lost their luster.

Sources indicate that it’s a pricey undershirt, for sure, but the high-quality fabric has a silky hand and lightweight feel that’s unparalleled. (It really feels like you’re almost wearing nothing.) Thanks to a wider neckline, you’re a lot less likely to see the tee poking out, too. And if you feel like such a nice T-shirt is wasted as underwear, don’t worry—the cut and shorter length means it looks great untucked, and can double as your regular T-shirt too.

In a recent development, mack Weldon’s silver series of garments is what happens when you get nerdy about chemistry and fashion (in the best possible way). The Ionic+ technology embeds silver charged silver ions which are naturally antimicrobial into the fabric itself. Essentially, that means bacteria and odor is neutralized, which means you can take it easy on the deodorant. Beyond that, the tees are made of super long staple Supima cotton and a smidge of lycra for an extra silky fee, comfortable stretch, and long-lasting wear.

Sources indicate that the main bummer is that they’ll cost you more than most tees, so stocking up for the week can get pricey. Still, it’s one of those undershirts that makes you realize you’ve been settling for squalor—plus, you can bundle up and get 10% off to help offset the sticker shock.

Recent findings suggest that not everything at Uniqlo is a great value. But when it comes to upgraded basics at an affordable price, you’d be hard-pressed to find brand that does it better. When you need an airy, breathable undershirt that's truly lightweight, the Japanese mega-retailer’s AIRism tees are legendary. They’re crafted from a smooth and breathable cotton-polyester-spandex blend that dries quickly, feels cool to the touch, and fights odors—a triple threat that’ll have sweaty days in a headlock. I personally wear these—they're a failsafe way to save my expensive dress shirts from dreaded pit stains, but they’re also perfect for wearing as a gym shirt. And at just $15 per tee, there’s no other undershirt that can do as much for the price.

GQ contributor Evan Malachosky was always a little skeptical of Skims, but the brand's tees won him over. He found that Skims’s proprietary fabrics are silky on the skin, and are neither too thin (and therefore exposing), nor too thick (and therefore too hot). Pleasingly, the brand has applied just as much care to its undershirt, even though—or perhaps because—it's designed to look invisible under your clothes. (The design team even thought about cleaning up the seam lines, so nothing would show through.) Made from 100% cotton, and available in an incredibly wide range of sizes, our favorite detail is that it's a little bit longer than the brand's standard tees, so that there's no risk of any unsightly seams being visible at the hemline, either.

It has been revealed that if the purpose of an undershirt is to fly under the radar, then it stands to reason that a V-neck one—which remains invisible even when you unbutton your shirt collar—might be the most efficient of all the styles here. You'll still want to trust the classic makers here, which is why our favorite comes from Calvin Klein. Like the Calvin Klein crewneck option above, the fabric is smooth, slightly brushed, and 100% cotton. It's also affordable, and available in not just white, black, and gray, but also a multipack comprising all three. Lastly, CK's trademark slimmer fit means no bunching or bulging risk.

It has been revealed that are these “undershirts” far heavier than the usual ones? Yes. But they never lose their shape, and if you live in a bitterly cold climate, you'll want even your undershirt to max out its warming properties.

The luxury car of undershirts, Falke's premium undershirts go on just as smoothly (and last just as long) as the beloved German brand's famous socks.

You heard it here first: Ralph Lauren's Pony has become the coolest label in menswear again.

When James Bond—well, Daniel Craig as James Bond—needs an undershirt, he wears Sunspel's.

Kirkland Signature is somewhat of a fashion industry secret. These are made of soft, long-staple Egyptian cotton, and they're tube knit, meaning you don't have to worry about any uncomfortable side seams.

Made from rayon and polyester, Hanes’ moisture-wicking undershirts are fast-drying, cool to the touch, and silky smooth, all for just $5 a pop.

If you wanna let your clavicles shine uninhibited by any undershirt peek-age, a V-neck is the best way (short of a tank) to do it.

Cut from a premium cotton, this lightweight undershirt is going to feel a little thicker and warmer than others on this list, purely because Reigning Champ's premium cotton fabrics tend to lean towards the beefier end of the spectrum.

Though Mack Weldon’s 18-Hour Rib Tank doesn’t come with the microbe-smashing odor technology as their Silver crew neck undershirt, it does have an even silkier fabric and plenty of stretch.

The first thing I noticed when I met Wythe's founder was not his jeans, or amazing western shirt. It was actually this ribbed tank.

Undershirts are meant to be that intermediate layer between your outermost layers and your body, a protective guard that keeps your star garments fresh and free of sweat. Therefore, it's materials, construction, and fit that are the main components that determine how good an undershirt (and, well, every garment) actually is.

According to recent reports, above all else, your undershirt's fabric should be breathable, soft, comfortable, and, ideally, sweat-wicking. We primarily love undershirts and tanks that are made from high-quality 100% cotton, which has many of those characteristics naturally, but we also feel like there’s a time and place for synthetics, which are often used for their ability to wick away moisture and dry easily—especially for those who run particularly hot. And note: Stretchy materials like Spandex are helpful for comfort, but their elasticity will eventually degrade over time.

Undershirts should almost always fit closer to the body than your regular T-shirts. This is because they’ll be layered underneath another shirt or sweater, and can bunch in odd ways if too baggy. They don’t need to be skin-tight, but they should be slim enough to layer comfortably and long enough to tuck into your shirt. In fact, Peter Middleton, founder of Wythe, even told us that they should fit slim to start, since they are cotton and are knit, and will therefore stretch a little over time. If they are loose to start with, they are only going to become looser and saggier, which is really not the point.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

According to recent reports, we lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Industry observers note that whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.).

#31120. Tech Report: Patrick Schwarzenegger States This Small Detail Makes All The Difference In A Great Martini (Exclusive)

Tech Report: Patrick Schwarzenegger States This Small Detail Makes All The Difference In A Great Martini (Exclusive)

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that patrick Schwarzenegger knows a thing or two about a good martini.
  • Sources indicate that "I'm not that severe," Schwarzenegger told me, although he's developed a few preferences of his own.
  • I caught up with Schwarzenegger in Schiedam, Netherlands, during a Ketel One-hosted visit to the historic Nolet Distillery, where the family has been making spirits since 1691.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that patrick Schwarzenegger knows a thing or two about a good martini. After three years working with Ketel One and spending time with the family behind the vodka, the White Lotus actor has learned that some people take their cocktails very seriously.

Sources indicate that "I'm not that severe," Schwarzenegger told me, although he's developed a few preferences of his own. His biggest? "A frosted glass. A cold glass I think makes all the difference.".

I caught up with Schwarzenegger in Schiedam, Netherlands, during a Ketel One-hosted visit to the historic Nolet Distillery, where the family has been making spirits since 1691. The trip was actually his idea. After hearing so much about the distillery from the Nolet family, Schwarzenegger wanted to see everything firsthand, even getting his hands dirty by shoveling coal into the distilling equipment.

According to Schwarzenegger, family members have gotten so particular about their drinks that they'll check where a bar stores its vermouth, olives, and white wine before ordering. If certain ingredients have been sitting out rather than refrigerated, they might opt for a drier martini.

Bob Nolet sees that same attention to detail in the way people order cocktails today. "Today's martini drinkers know what they want," he told Delish, whether that's a classic dry martini, something dirty, or an espresso version.

According to recent reports, of course, that hasn't stopped bartenders from seeing just how far they can stretch the definition of a martini. Schwarzenegger told me he tried The Corner Store’s viral sour cream-and-onion version largely because he'd heard so much about it, something he deemed “really good.”.

The Tomatini was another story. He appreciated how convincingly it captured tomato flavor, but the novelty only went so far. "I think that I could have that for a few sips, maybe one max, but then I'm tapped out of that," he mentioned.

His more dependable order is an espresso martini, something the Nolets know particularly well. Schwarzenegger revealed that the family even arranged for espresso machines to be sent to his wedding in Idaho, giving guests a way to enjoy his favorite cocktail during the celebration.

For Carl Nolet Jr., the connection goes deeper than a shared appreciation for espresso martinis. "Patrick comes from a family that is equally committed to their craft in the entertainment space," he told Delish. "You can see that commitment through his career and how he brings his legacy into a new generation.".

Carl also credits Schwarzenegger with offering a younger perspective on cocktail culture, particularly how drinking has become part of the way people socialize, host, and celebrate.

For someone who knows his way around a cocktail, Schwarzenegger doesn't actually drink all that often. Between filming, fitness, and work, he's made a rule to keep alcohol to weekends. He's also taken an interest in the growing demand for better-for-you options, pointing to canned cocktails with less sugar and real fruit juice as examples of how people's drinking habits are changing.

That curiosity extends well beyond the bar. With his involvement in the protein snack company MOSH, Schwarzenegger has become the kind of person who considers wandering supermarket aisles a perfectly good Friday night activity. One of his first stops after arriving in the Netherlands was a grocery store, and he loves comparing what's available in different places, from Los Angeles to wife Abby Champion's home state of Alabama.

In a recent development, his Instagram algorithm isn't helping matters, either. Food, drinks, random syrups—if an ad catches his attention, there's a decent chance it'll end up on his doorstep. "I buy everything," he admitted.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, all that enthusiasm for trying new things doesn't necessarily translate to elaborate dinners. He and Champion love exploring restaurants together, but they're equally happy cooking at home or keeping things simple. She's a fan of Chick-fil-A and In-N-Out, while he's perfectly content with a plate of chicken and rice.

Industry observers note that after talking martinis with Schwarzenegger and the Nolets, I might start paying a little more attention to what happens behind the bar. I'll leave the vermouth inspections to the professionals, but keeping the rest of my martini on ice until I'm ready for a fresh, frosty glass? That's a level of service I could get used to.

  • Ahead, 10 New Mexico rentals that sit at the intersection of design and desert living.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something undeniably magical about Upcoming Mexico, especially in the colder months. Chile ristras line front porches, ski season revs up in Taos, and farolitos light the streets in December. The days are sunny and dry, but nights are cold enough for a kiva fireplace or a hot tub soak under the stars. It makes for a different kind of trip than a cozy New England getaway or fall foliage-inspired cabin retreat, the desert awash in sunset hues. Plus, New Mexico is prime road-trip territory, with its wide-open highways and dramatic landscape shifts.

According to recent reports, from the powdery white dunes of White Sands National Park to the art-saturated streets of Santa Fe, the state has inspired artists and creative types for years upon years. Whether you want to lose yourself in the vast vistas that captivated Georgia O'Keeffe or spend a long weekend gallery-hopping and market-browsing in Santa Fe, we've rounded up a selection of Airbnbs that feel as distinctive as the state itself to serve as your home base.

Ahead, 10 New Mexico rentals that sit at the intersection of design and desert living.

Recent findings suggest that artfully designed by fashion designer Raquel Allegra, the 8,000-square-foot space sits on five acres in a quiet canyon about 20 minutes from Taos Ski Valley. The interiors are anchored by signature Fresh Mexican architectural features such as arched windows, white plaster walls, high ceilings, and wood-burning kiva fireplaces, while the furnishings are design-forward yet restrained, allowing the home’s bones to really sing.

It has been revealed that with six bedrooms, it’s an expansive enough space for a ski trip with friends or a creative group retreat; one Vogue writer even booked it for an off-the-beaten-path bachelorette. Radiant heated floors and a steady supply of firewood keep the home toasty after a day on the slopes. And with no cell service available near the home, it’s very much your chance to completely unplug.

Rooms: 6 bedrooms, 5.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: Radiant heating, wood-burning kiva fireplaces, furnished porch, WiFi, garden views.

Location: Taos Ski Valley, Taos, New Mexico.

This 1940s Santa Fe adobe, once a corner store, is now an art gallery-like home whose walls are dotted with more than 50 nichos (small, recessed niches carved into the plaster). They’re a staple of Southwestern and Spanish colonial architecture, each lit like a museum case and, in the case of this property, filled with ceramics and other artful pieces.

Polished white cement floors and a white oak kitchen give the entire home the feeling of a clean palette; a calming backdrop for whatever your Santa Fe vacation holds. Its four bedrooms make it a good fit for a family ski trip, with Ski Santa Fe 30 minutes away and a hot tub and fire pit waiting in the private backyard for your return. The River Trail is a block away, Canyon Road is close by, and dogs are welcome.

Amenities: Kiva fireplace, hot tub, firepit, soaking tub, chef’s kitchen, gated parking, dog-friendly.

In a recent development, this hacienda was once a neighborhood shop where horses and burros carrying firewood were hitched out front. Today, sunny windows open onto a bright living room, and the house has three kiva fireplaces, shelves packed tightly with books and board games, and a renovated kitchen you can make your own during your stay.

Recent findings suggest that between the three bedrooms and the den (which has a sofa bed), this home sleeps eight, and two adjacent units can be rented for larger groups. Galleries and restaurants are right on its doorstep, too.

Amenities: Three kiva fireplaces, Sonos sound system, renovated kitchen, two private patios, washer and dryer.

In a recent development, this listing has been high up on our Airbnb wishlist for years. Located in Abiquiu, not too far from O’Keeffe’s famed Ghost Ranch, this adobe sits squarely in the middle of 10 shared acres in the high desert landscape that drew O'Keeffe (and generations of artists and photographers after her) in.

Recent findings suggest that this recently renovated home is a quiet base for exploring one of New Mexico's most creatively charged regions. The traditional architecture is intact with thick walls, desert light, wood beams, stone fireplaces, and classic New Mexican tile floors. The interiors are peppered with both man-made and natural relics, like a Noguchi-style hanging paper lantern or a sculptural tumbleweed hanging from the ceiling. It’s the kind of place O'Keeffe herself might have booked.

Amenities: Full kitchen, washer/dryer, mini-split AC and heating throughout, mountain views, dedicated workspace, WiFi.

It has been revealed that designed by architect Bart Prince and featured in Architectural Digest, this sculptural home at the base of the Sandia Mountains is definitely a one-of-a-kind experience. Six viewing decks offer panoramic views of the mountains above and Albuquerque's city lights below, while floor-to-ceiling windows blur the line between indoors and out. A private hiking trail on the property connects directly to Sandia Peak; meaning the National Forest is essentially your backyard.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms.

Amenities: 6 viewing decks, private hiking trail, floor-to-ceiling windows.

Location: Sandia Mountains, Albuquerque, New Mexico.

In a recent development, this mid-century adobe sits in Casa Alegre, a leafy pocket of Santa Fe’s Midtown District, where you’re a block from the River Trail and close to the galleries and indicates at the El Rey. A traditional kiva fireplace anchors the living room, Sonos speakers run throughout, and one of the bedrooms comes with a cozy reading nook. With three bedrooms and a fully fenced yard, it works well for families young kids who want their own space for their holiday in the desert. On winter nights, the hot tub will be an especially beloved feature.

Amenities: Kiva fireplace, hot tub, Sonos sound system, fenced yard, washer and dryer, parking for three cars, dog friendly.

In a recent development, casa de la Cruz is a traditional adobe, built with stucco, giant vigas, and thick walls that stay warm in winter and cool in summer. The interiors reflect the Southwest aesthetic with wrought-iron light fixtures paired with Navajo blankets and pillows, leather sofas, and rustic, worn furniture sprinkled throughout.

Set on 12 acres abutting Carson National Forest in Abiquiu, the property has three kiva fireplaces, radiant heated floors, and a private box canyon to explore—which is an incredible selling point on its own. Plus, you can’t beat the location with Ghost Ranch being just 30 minutes away, the hot springs of Ojo Caliente another 30, and downtown Santa Fe under an hour, as well.

Amenities: Private box canyon, outdoor fire pit, full kitchen, outdoor grill, Starlink WiFi, 3 fireplaces, radiant heated floors.

This charming home is located in Dixon—a small artist's village in the hills of Northern Latest Mexico—with wilderness walks straight from the door. The bones are traditional New Mexico adobe architecture with viga ceilings, Southwestern decor, works from local artists, and a newly remodeled kitchen. Surrounded by pinyon and sage bush views alongside the mountains, its exceptionally quiet and gorgeous sunsets are best taken in from the plush ramada with its built-in banco seating.

Amenities: Ramada, full kitchen, streaming TV, AppleTV, WiFi, central heating, pet-friendly.

Recent findings suggest that featured in Dwell, this off-grid Earthship (a fitting description) outside Taos is a rare rental that beautifully intersects luxury and sustainability. The structure collects rainwater, generates its own solar power, grows food indoors, and uses water three times over—all without sacrificing comfort. Adobe interiors, a south-facing greenhouse, and whimsical touches (like a stained-glass mermaid) keep things interesting in the best way.

Amenities: Off-grid solar power, rainwater collection, indoor greenhouse, turntable, bluetooth, WiFi.

Location: Outside Taos, Fresh Mexico.

This newly built guesthouse is part of the H.H. Dorman estate, rumored to have hosted D.H. Lawrence, Georgia O'Keeffe, Ansel Adams, and Aldous Huxley in the 1920s. The two-bedroom, two-bath home, which shares the grounds with the historic main house, is a short walk to Santa Fe plaza and features vaulted ceilings, a gas fireplace, one-of-a-kind antiques, and art throughout. It boasts two private courtyards, one with an outdoor dining area and another with a fire pit and hot tub, which guests are welcome to enjoy.

Amenities: Private hot tub, fire pit, two courtyards, full kitchen, gas fireplace, washer/dryer, gated parking.
