📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dedicating some counter space to a soda maker comes with several benefits. For one thing, these appliances are a great way to cut down on single-use plastic and other waste by eliminating the recycling bags full of bottles, cans, and cardboard boxes you inevitably accumulate with a regular La Croix habit. But they will also save you some money in the long run, as carbonating your own water costs less than buying premade fizz from the store. One standard-size CO2 canister, which should cost roughly $15, can carbonate around 60 liters of water. Considering the $3 cost of a 2-L bottle of Canada Dry, that comes out to around three times as much soda water per dollar.

After years of testing soda makers, I’ve found models that make it quick and easy to make zingy, fizzy drinks (including juice, wine, and cocktails) with the push of a button. Find our top picks below and scroll further down to see what I thought of the machines that didn’t earn a top spot.

New in this update: For this update, I tested two sparkling water makers by Drinkmate: the previously discontinued (and now recontinued) Drinkmate Spritzer and the Drinkmate Lux, which in between testing and publishing was subsequently discontinued and replaced with the new Sparkleup, welp!

Drinkmate Omnifizz Sparkling Water and Soda Maker.

Amazon (With 60-L CO2 Tank and Extra Bottle).

Home Depot (With 60-L CO2 Tank).

Height: 16.14"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Yes (size varies by retailer)Requires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years.

According to recent reports, over years of testing, nothing has surpassed the Drinkmate Omnifizz’s mix of versatility and affordability. It is, full stop, the most affordable sparkling water maker that can also do other “fun” carbonating, like wine, cocktails, tea, and (pulp-free) fruit juice.

What I love: The Omnifizz has a well-designed detachable siphon with fast and slow pressure release tabs. It carbonates fast, delivering maximum sharp fizz in around two seconds. This gives you more control when carbonating anything with a syrup or other sugars (wine or cocktails, for example), which fizz up a lot more than plain water. The siphon design also offers a much more secure connection than the machines that require you to pop and/or twist the bottle into the base, which diminishes the likelihood of an accidental soda explosion to the face (which happens to the best of us!).

What I’d leave: In addition to being kind of meh in the looks department (especially in a world where so many brands have placed a focus on the aesthetics of their soda makers), this carbonator is made of all plastic parts, so it doesn’t feel as durable as some others I’ve tested. It also screams like a banshee when its done. Depending on the retailer you order from, it may or may not ship with a CO2 cylinder, so be sure to read the product descriptions carefully.

Height: 16.9"Machine material(s): Stainless steelBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years.

Breville has cornered the market on high-end small kitchen appliances with its top-performing countertop oven, induction burner, toaster, and immersion blender. In 2024, the brand added a sparkling water maker to that list.

What I love: The Breville Infizz Fusion is a sleek, versatile carbonator, and like the Drinkmate Ominifizz, it will carbonate more than just water. The default setting on the carbonator cap is a slow pressure release that allows carbonation of fruit juice, wine, cocktails, and even creamy drinks if you’re feeling weird. You can manually release the pressure faster if you just need a bottle of fizzy water in a hurry. Unlike the soda makers I liked in the $100 to $150 range, which usually have all plastic parts, parts of the InFizz Fusion are made of durable, high-quality stainless steel, which is available in a variety of finishes, though options vary by retailer. It also comes with a handful of accessories (including a juice filter and silicone bottle brush) to enhance the experience of using and cleaning the machine and bottle.

According to recent reports, what I’d leave: Compared to the Drinkmate, this machine is slightly more fussy to operate. Not by much, but I prefer the Drinkmate’s quick click to Breville’s twist-and-lock design. Countertop soda makers are simple gadgets, and this is one of the priciest ones you can buy. If it’s worth it to you to pay for quality materials, aesthetics, and the ability to wow your dinner guests by transforming a bottle of bad rosé into something bubbly and palatable, you’ll likely be very happy with this (FWIW the Drinkmate can also sparkle bad rosé, it just wont look as nice doing it). But do keep in mind that the base model, which is $249 at the time of publishing, doesn’t ship with a CO2 tank, so you’ll either need to buy one or spend $30 more on one that comes with the tank.

Drinkmate Spritzer Portable Sparkling Water.

Height: 7"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years.

Sources indicate that what I love: When I first tested the Spritzer several years ago, it was my top pick. But then Drinkmate discontinued it, which was sad, but now, it’s back. At this point I can’t give it the absolute top spot (I’ll get into that down below), but in a more niche position of portable carbonator, I still recommend it.

Beyond that, the Spritzer takes up less space and is easy to stow away, and it is also cheaper than the countertop version.

What I’d leave: The Spritzer is designed to use smaller 10-L gas canisters rather than the standard 60-L size. Unless you source them directly from Drinkmate, the 10-L canisters are difficult to find, so you end up being reliant on its exchange program. The Spritzer will still work with a full size canister, but I wouldn’t recommend doing that because it doesn’t fit well in the carbonator and gets a bit unwieldy. Drinkmate also originally had a docking station for it the Spritzer, but unfortunately the brand got rid of it. Ultimately, the reason I don’t give this the top spot is that its design is such a departure from what most people expect in a soda maker it has a much narrower appeal.

With every update I look at the most popular and highly rated countertop sparkling water makers, taking into consideration availability, price, and customer ratings. Then, I judge them on the following:.

According to recent reports, I first assess how easy it is to use and assemble each machine. Looks matter too, but they aren’t everything. And if a machine can carbonate more than just water (what's up Drinkmate and Breville), that’s a huge plus as well.

In a recent development, I used each machine several times to get a general sense of how long the machine takes to carbonate and the fizz level of each batch. For the first few rounds I follow the manufacturer’s instructions. After that I try pushing the machine to its maximum capability (usually until I hear the hissing of excess gas escaping). If the machine can carbonate more than just water, I’ll do a few rounds with juice and wine.

Mysoda Woody Sparkling Water Maker.

In a recent development, this simple, stylish carbonator from Finnish brand Mysoda is made from renewable wood composite. It’s beautiful, sturdy, and, when it comes to the level of carbonation, performs as well as any SodaStream. And if you want an aesthetically pleasing, sustainably made, budget-friendly soda maker, you’ll be very happy with this purchase. But there’s a catch to that: Most soda makers ship with a starter CO2 tank, and this one doesn’t. New tanks, not tank trade-ins, cost $30 to $40. So when you factor that into the cost, the initial investment is more than the cost of our top pick, which did perform a little better anyway. If you want to stay under $100 all in, check out the Philips Sparkling Water Maker below.

Mysoda Glassy Sparkling Water Maker.

This Mysoda distinguishes itself from the others with a glass carafe. Anytime I encounter a soda maker that carbonates in glass, I'm suspicious, because I haven’t seen them work well in the past. This might be because soda makers that carbonate in glass tend to be designed with additional safeguards to minimize the possibility of the bottle exploding, and those safeguards are usually fussy. Often they take the form of some sort of cover that goes over the entire bottle during the carbonation process. In the case of the Glassy, the bottle is covered by a curved sliding door that you shut by hand, reminiscent of a changing room curtain or a shower stall.

To use the machine, you place the bottle inside and twist it onto the gas nozzle to lock it in place. Then you shut the door and press the top of the machine toward the front to inject the gas (the top is mostly one large button). After a couple of pumps, you’ll hear a hissing sound, which signals that it’s ready. You then press the top toward the back of the machine, which causes the door to fly open, presenting your carbonated water like a magician’s assistant doing a quick change magic trick. It’s all very dramatic, which is kind of fun.

As far as soda makers that carbonate in glass, this is the best I’ve tried. That mentioned, I'm not sure how key it is to be able to carbonate in glass, especially with the risk (however small) that it will explode into shards with you close by. You can always just carbonate in a plastic bottle and pour it into a glass vessel for serving.

Check out our full review of the Glassy here.

Recent findings suggest that the Philips Sparkling Water Maker is a handsome machine with a comparatively accessible price tag, and it’s easy to set up and operate with one button. More importantly, during testing, it made pleasantly sharp carbonated water. Like the Mysoda Woody above, it doesn’t ship with CO2, so you’ll still need to shell out for a standard screw-in 60-L CO2 tank. However, at the current retail price, even with the addition of a tank, it still comes in at just under $100.

The Aerflo is even easier to tae on the go than the Drinkmate Spritzer. There is a carbonator mechanism inside the lid, which you activate by pressing a button on the top. Instead of full-size CO2 canisters used for most sparkling water makers, it utilizes smaller capsules typically used for airsoft or BB guns. Because of the capsules small size, you will need to swap them much more frequently; one capsule has enough CO2 for about one day’s worth of sparkling water. It’s cool and convenient if you really prefer carbonated water over still. But this is a product for a smaller subset of people than a countertop soda maker. If it appeals to you though, go for it.

Check out my full review of the Aerflo here.

This is the model that came after the now-discontinued Aarke Carbonator II, and the main upgrades are materials. The Aarke Carbonator III has more stainless steel and fewer plastic parts than the II. Both models are highly aesthetic machines that are easy enough to use and make perfectly fine sparkling water. If you like the look of it, you’ll probably be very happy with it, but the Breville is in the same general price range and is more versatile. Plus, there are lower-priced machines that perform just as well.

Recent findings suggest that awa appears to be selling itself entirely based on aesthetics. Once you move beyond the body design though, this is a standard sparkling water maker with a single button for injecting CO2. It lacks a tilting nozzle or a slide-in lock, which makes it more annoying to use than the winning models. The build is also almost entirely plastic, save for a few metal details, which doesn’t really justify the premium price point. If you like how it looks, it will get the job done, but it’s not innovating on the form.

Fizzit Sparkli Carbonated Soda Maker.

Industry observers note that A frequent complaint people have about sparkling water makers is their reliance on plastic bottles, as many consumers are looking to avoid plastic entirely. The Fizzit is one of the few soda makers that uses metal bottles instead. Apart from that, its design and performance are similar to the other soda makers sharing the same standard design on the market. Were this the only machine on the market to carbonate directly into stainless steel, maybe that would be something, but Sodastream also offers stainless-steel carbonator bottles, and I imagine more brands will follow suit. Also sorry to Spärklï, but the branding on this machine is a bit of an eyesore. If you’re looking for a machine that comes with metal bottles and aren’t a fan of Sodastream though, this might be for you.

The Fritaire carbonator flipped the conventional soda maker design on its head. It’s the only soda maker I’ve tested so far that carbonates from the bottom up, with a fold-up gas nozzle that makes for a slightly more compact machine. The bottle is also different, with mechanical components built in at the bottom, and a wide curved carafe-style lip. Unfortunately I could not get this to produce a satisfyingly sharp bottle of seltzer, no matter how much gas I pumped into the bottle. Where other machines make a clear sound when the pressure has been maxed out, the Fritaire’s was not obvious. The instructions recommend pressing the button for three seconds until you “hear the sound of pressure building.” Each time I tried, the water came out under-carbonated. On top of that, the lid for the bottle dribbled water even when tightly screwed on. I really tried to give this machine the benefit of the doubt, testing and retesting to try and get it not to leak on me and to get a proper fizz, but each time I encountered the same problems no matter what I did.

In a recent development, smeg is known for its retro-futurist luxury kitchen products that really sell for their looks. This machine worked fine. You twist the metal dial clockwise to carbonate, a clever hidden feature that sets it apart from other carbonators, but it lacks the ability to tilt the nozzle, which makes screwing on the bottle more tedious. For a soda maker made almost entirely out of plastic, the price point is well beyond what it’s worth, but if you’re a Smeg collector, this is another piece to add to your collection.

It has been revealed that one of the few fresh electric sparkling water systems, the Carbon8 is quite different from other machines on the market. Instead of directly carbonating into the bottle, the Carbon8 has a refillable reservoir (much like a drip coffee maker) that instead, dispenses carbonated water straight into your glass. It has added flourishes, like a sanitizing UV light and a filter that remineralizes water while removing chlorine.

The brand implies superior eco-friendliness in their website copy because they don’t carbonate directly into a reusable PET plastic bottle; however, the reservoir and other parts of the machine are made of plastic, so I’m not sure they have much plastic-free ground to stand on. You could argue that since the plastic bottles of typical soda makers have to be replaced every couple of years, this system produces less plastic waste, but it’s a marginal difference in my opinion.

Industry observers note that as a premium machine this Carbon8 worked fine, but had one shortcoming: There seems to be no way to control the carbonation level of the machine, and when I tasted the finished product, I found the level of carbonation to be far less than what you’d expect from store-bought seltzer, or what you can produce with the winning machines. If the Carbon8 gave you control over how fizzy you wanted your water, it would make this a much better machine.

Recent findings suggest that ninja is among the most prolific small appliance manufacturers with coffee makers, countertop ovens, blenders, ice cream makers, juicers, toasters, air fryers—the list goes on and on and on. So it should come as no surprise that the brand is now in the soda maker business too. Like many of Ninja’s other offerings, the Ninja Thirsti is a bit gimmicky while still being kind of cool. Out of the box, this electric soda maker (yes, you have to plug it in) reminded us of a Nespresso machine. The water tank sits off to the side and the carbonation happens inside the machine before coming out of a little spout. There’s an opening on the front to add up to two proprietary flavoring cartridges, which you can put in your bubbly water individually or combine them both. Currently there are 30 flavors available and the machine shipped with four of them. The control panel on the front of the machine allows you to choose between still water or three levels of carbonation, and four drink sizes (6, 12, 18, or 24 oz.). After testing, I have mixed feelings about this machine. Overall, it seems like a bit much for something to have at home. It could maybe be a great addition to a teachers’ lounge or a small office. But keep in mind that the water tank does require chilled, cold water so you’d also need a fridge or ice nearby whenever you want to use it.

Glacier Fresh Sparkin Cold Soda Maker.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever dreamed of having a club soda tap in your kitchen, this is probably as close as you’re going to get without cutting into your countertops. Like the Ninja above, the Glacier Fresh Sparkin Cold Soda Maker carbonates water in the machine, not in a bottle. Unlike the Ninja, the machine chills the water for you (though the manual still recommends filling the reservoir on the back of the machine with cold water). Once it’s filled, getting your bubbly water from the “tap” is a three-step process. First, you push a button to send water from the reservoir to the bubbling (and presumably chilling) chamber, then you push down on a lever to carbonate it. Once it’s sufficiently bubbly, you press another little lever on the front to dispense the water into a glass. It’s less complicated than it sounds, but with an 88-square-inch footprint, most people will be better off with a bottle-style carbonator. I will also note that when moved from the counter to a nearby table with the CO2 canister in place and some water still in the chamber (ill-advised, perhaps), it began to make a weird squealing noise.

The SodaStream Art is marketed as the manufacturer’s premium carbonator, because of its retro-inspired body. Though it produces the exact same carbonated water as other SodaStream models, it operates a little differently: Instead of pushing a button to carbonate, you pull the lever and you can pull it up to six times for the bubbliest water. But it’s made of lightweight plastic that feels cheap. If you want something that looks good on the countertop, there are prettier options that are also sturdier.

Sources indicate that aarke carbonators are really easy on the eyes, and this “pro” version doesn’t skimp on materials. Instead of the typical plastic bottles, this one uses glass, and the top of the machine (which is available in a matte black, matte sand, or shiny stainless-steel finish) covers the top of the bottle in case you were to over-carbonate and cause the glass to explode. Unfortunately, it’s not very user-friendly. I had challenges getting everything to lock into place and ended up with an explosion—though, luckily, it was only water and not glass. I eventually got it to work, but for the price, it should be easier to operate.

I loved the sleek design of this soda maker in pictures, but in person, the materials felt cheap and flimsy. Also, because it’s so sleek and slim, the water bottles are really tall and didn’t fit into any shelves in a standard sized fridge.

In a recent development, instead of using a CO2 tank to produce carbon dioxide, this machine uses citric acid and baking soda. The mechanism is just way more high maintenance compared to the machines that utilize a gas canister, and I struggle to see why this method is in any way better than the industry standard.

At the moment, the Terra is SodaStream’s most basic offering, and functionally, it’s a lot like the original SodaStream, the Fizzi. However, instead of a screw-in CO2 cartridge, this machine uses the brand’s Quick Connect cartridges, which click in. Because the Quick Connect feature is proprietary, using this machine means being married to Soda Stream’s cylinder exchange program. With products like the Mysoda Woody or the Philips Sparkling Water Maker, you can and should get something with a universal connection.

It has been revealed that this style of carbonator is a relic of the 19th century, and while it has an abundance of charm, it’s more tedious, fussy, and impractical than its modern counterparts. It relies on small, single-use CO2 cartridges—which negates the whole eco-friendly argument for carbonating at home rather buying seltzer from the store— and you have to use two cartridges per liter if you like your seltzer extra sharp. Frankly, the only people I’d recommend this to would be that husband and wife on TLC who pretend they’re living in the 1950s.

According to recent reports, there is nothing inherently wrong with the E-Duo. Of the carbonators that use glass bottles, it is the easiest to use. It does require a few additional steps to lock the bottle safely into place (just in case that glass bottle explodes!), but I didn’t find the safety mechanisms to be overly fussy. However, as with the Ninja, this soda maker requires electricity. With so many excellent soda makers that function effectively without electricity, I don’t really see the need to use one that does.

A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Making it French Onion:Caramelizing the onions over medium heat helps them brown evenly and consistently. If the onions begin to stick or burn, add a splash of water to bring them back! Garlic, thyme, and black pepper are the aromatic unsung heroes in the onions, so you don’t want to skip them. Deglazing with white wine is essential in any French onion recipe, so use the one you’d sip! Once the wine has reduced, add some beef stock to impart meaty French onion soup flavor. The caramelized onions then get layered with torn croissants and Gruyère cheese, and topped with dollops of cream cheese.

Delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

Storage:The beautiful thing about a breakfast strata is that you can make it ahead. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 day and reheat until the internal temperature reaches 165°. This is also great to portion and store for breakfast at the office.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a upcoming pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

According to recent reports, scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that what People Are Saying:"Always a huge hit with friends and family!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The perfect mac & cheese will have you dreaming about its cheesy goodness for days after you eat it. Obviously, the cheese has to be top-notch, but the real secret to the best version is the perfect crunchy topping. My recipe delivers on all of that and more, so you won't even think about reaching for another mac & cheese recipe for the rest of your gatherings. From weeknight dinners to potlucks and holidays, this is the classic side dish everyone will be reaching for.

It has been revealed that what People Are Saying:"Always a huge hit with friends and family! This is my go-to if I'm bringing a dish to a holiday dinner with friends. I've rarely had leftovers to take home!" - Zafire_Shadows.

In a recent development, "This is exactly what mac and cheese dreams are made of. Love the gruyere funk and the mustard powder (so clever!)." - Pastagofer.

It has been revealed that first, you’ll boil the pasta. Start with a massive pot of salted water (and I mean super salty, it should taste like the ocean), then add your pasta and cook it until before al dente—I’m talking still-has-a-ring-of-hard-white-pasta-in-the-middle-when-you-bite-in uncooked. You want it to meld and absorb with your cheese sauce in the oven, not turn into mush. Undercooking now guarantees the perfect bite when you pull it out of the oven.

Then it’s cheese sauce time, and that means making a béchamel. You’ll start by melting your butter in a pan over medium heat, then sprinkling the flour over the top and stirring everything together until it starts pulling away from the pan slightly. You’re looking for what’s called a “blonde roux,” which has a slightly yellow tint and should smell a bit like baked goods. You don’t want it super dark (so keep an eye on the heat!), but you definitely don’t want it as light as it started.

Next, add the milk in slowly, stirring constantly so you don’t get thick lumps. Want to shortcut this process a bit? Heat your milk ahead of time to room temperature or even slightly warm. You’re going to cook it until it’s thick and bubbly (about 2 minutes), so having your milk warm will help you get there faster. It’s going to get a LOT thicker when you add the cheese, so if it’s still a little thin but you want to get on with it, that’s okay too.

Recent findings suggest that once you’re ready to add the cheese, it’s very vital to take it off the heat before so that the sauce doesn’t start to separate. That said, if you’ve been at it for a minute and are still having trouble getting your cheese to melt, pop your pot back on the heat for just a few seconds to bring the temperature up and help the process along.

Once it comes together, you can stir in the macaroni until every noodle is coated.

In a recent development, at this point, you could eat this mac & cheese right now, and it would taste wonderful. But! If you want exceptional mac & cheese, you’ve gotta bake it. So pour it into a pan, then get ready for the best part—the topping. To make it, you’ll combine some breadcrumbs and the remaining half cup of Parmesan in a bowl, then add the olive oil and mix it all up. Sprinkle it on top of the mac and cheese in the casserole dish.

Sources indicate that all you have to do is pop it into your preheated 375° oven and bake it until it's golden brown on top. Go ahead, snag a bite before it's fully cooled—you'll really be able to taste all your extra effort.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

If you’re looking to make this dish ahead of time, prepare the mac & cheese up until step 4, then cover it in your baking dish and refrigerate it up to 3 days (or freeze it up to 2 months). When ready to serve, add the Parmesan and panko mixture, bake, and serve. If baking from frozen, allow to thaw in the refrigerator overnight before baking.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for around 3 days.

  • Sophie Okonedo is one of those performers whose very presence can make a scene feel more alive.
  • Industry observers note that this winter, she leads two independent features opening theatrically after an international festival run: Clarissa, by brothers Chuko and Arie Esiri, and Mouse, by the husband-and-wife team of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson.
  • Mouse, out now, is a coming-of-age story set in 2002 Arkansas, in which the teenage Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer) develops a complicated relationship with her best friend’s mother (Okonedo) after an unexpected tragedy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sophie Okonedo is one of those performers whose very presence can make a scene feel more alive. The Tony Award-winning British actress projects both warmth and watchfulness, moving swiftly from humor to hurt, or authority to vulnerability, without announcing the shift. Even in a supporting role, she has a way of making you lean in.

Industry observers note that this winter, she leads two independent features opening theatrically after an international festival run: Clarissa, by brothers Chuko and Arie Esiri, and Mouse, by the husband-and-wife team of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. Though shot nearly a year apart, the two films are arriving within weeks of each other—a quirk of the release calendar that makes for an unusually timely double feature.

Mouse, out now, is a coming-of-age story set in 2002 Arkansas, in which the teenage Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer) develops a complicated relationship with her best friend’s mother (Okonedo) after an unexpected tragedy. Meanwhile, Clarissa—in limited theaters December 18—transposes Virginia Woolf’s novel Mrs. Dalloway to contemporary Nigeria, a project that brought Okonedo to a country she hadn’t visited in two decades. (Her late father, whom she was mostly estranged from, moved back to his home country when she was young.).

Sources indicate that filming in Lagos proved consequential in ways that extended well beyond the work itself. “The journey I had in Lagos was so immense, personally and professionally, that I remember thinking on the wrap day that even if nothing else happens with this film, I’ve already gotten everything I wanted,” she tells me.

In a recent development, both films were made on tiny budgets, and, as Okonedo points out, a conversation about one inevitably opens up a conversation about the other. So, we talked about both.

It has been revealed that vogue: Let’s start with Mouse. How did it come to you? What was it about your character Helen, or about directors Kelly and Alex, that made you say yes?

It has been revealed that sophie Okonedo: I didn’t read anything about them. I read the script completely cold. By the time I got to the end, I rang my agent and remarked, “I’m absolutely doing this. I don’t know who’s directing, I don’t know what’s happening with the film, but I’m doing it.” So he sent me their last film, Ghostlight. It’s such a brilliant film and it was made for pennies. These are two really interesting filmmakers who are talking about America in a way I haven’t seen—very quietly. There are no explosions, no big movie stars, and it’s deeply significant. Kelly’s writing is subtle and real. But films like this can slip by without anyone noticing. I have to galvanize everyone and get them behind it, because I think it’s so good.

Helen ends up mothering her daughter’s friend, Minnie, in a way that’s unnerving at times, as if she’s grieving and replacing her at the same time.

It’s totally inappropriate at times. She even notes it at one point: “Oh my God, I’m the adult here.” She uses Minnie to ease her own grief, then backtracks, then moves forward again. It’s a messy situation, but there’s hope in it. The film is funny, too. Kelly has that gift for finding levity in dark situations. But they never get you to play the comedy. You play the seriousness of it all and it’s funny as it goes along.

I realized after watching the film that the woman playing Katherine’s mother is her real-life mother. What was that dynamic like on set?

According to recent reports, she wasn’t even meant to play the part at first. Tara [Kupferer], her mother, is a theater actress. She runs a theater company in Chicago and was there as Katherine’s guardian. They’d cast a great local actor, but on the first day we realized it wasn’t right. By the second day, Tara stepped in. Everything was so homegrown. My baby in the film is actually Kelly and Alex’s baby. They removed all the blockers you normally have as an actor on a film, where you spend three hours in hair and makeup. Sometimes you need those things, but this film didn’t. You just rock up and start filming. It was very seamless.

Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Sophie Okonedo in Mouse.

According to recent reports, you shot on location in North Little Rock. Had you been to Arkansas before?

Never. I got there a little early to check it out because I was playing an outsider, but an outsider who’d lived there for 15 years, so I had to know the place and feel familiar with it. All the locations came from [O’Sullivan’s] childhood; you could ask her, “What happened here?” and she’d tell you. A lot of people with small parts in the film knew Kelly from high school and were now playing mothers. The dance we see at the memorial was one Kelly actually performed herself. We even brought back the dance teacher who taught her so she could teach it to the two girls in the film.

Does playing an outsider give you something to work with? You didn’t do the method thing, keeping yourself apart from everyone, right?

Sources indicate that no. I totally get that some people do, but I’m too shy to stay in character! I feel too silly. What I do is think very deeply about every single word I say in the script before I arrive. Because I’m theater-trained, the script is my bible. All answers will be there. I spend a long time thinking about everything I say and everything everyone else says, and I go through it many, many times. An internal world builds up inside me. I can’t really explain how it happens. When I get to set, I forget any notes or journals I’ve made. I drop it all, empty myself, and see what happens. I feel buoyant and flexible, not stuck in any particular way.

Mouse is so specific about 2002, down to the Michelle Branch music cues. I was a bit younger than the characters then, but it all felt right. What did setting it in that moment bring to the story?

It has been revealed that I’m older, but Kelly was that age in 2002, so she had all the references. She knew exactly what she was listening to, what she was thinking and feeling. The main difference is there were no cell phones back then. If you wanted information, it had to come to you through someone taking action. The jogger has to tell Minnie something, then she has to run to the house to see if it’s really happened, then she has to look for a phone book. Now it would just be someone posting “RIP Callie” on Instagram. It’s so much more interesting to film people taking an action than all these constant shots of phones and texts, which I see in movies all the time now. It’s so boring.

In Mouse, Helen and Minnie come from very different backgrounds. Class is also woven into Clarissa, where you play the titular role. Was that a connection you were conscious of while working on the two films?

Class is massive in Britain. We live and breathe it. It runs through every vein of everyone’s body here, probably more than anything else, so I’m very aware of it. But there’s another weird parallel between the films: Mouse is directed by a couple and one of them is the writer. Clarissa is directed by two brothers and one of them is the writer. With both, I had an instant, visceral response. I didn’t need to think about the whys and wherefores. It was just yes, yes, yes. With a lot of other work, I have to get myself into the right position or work it out. What’s also amazing is that the scripts for Clarissa and Mouse barely changed between that first draft and the start of filming—the same was true of Janet Planet. These are filmmakers who have thought deeply about what they’re writing. There weren’t a million drafts or endless revisions; all three films were already in a remarkably evolved state from the start. Even though Mouse looks improvised in places, I’m sticking to the script.

Industry observers note that but parts of Mouse were improvised, right? I’m thinking of the scene where Helen attends a grief group.

Sources indicate that it was a real grief group. I knew the man handing me coffee at the beginning was an actor, though by coincidence he was also in a grief group. I was just outside the room; they put two cameras in there and someone called action. I walked in, and during the scene it slowly dawned on me—someone had forgotten to tell me these weren’t actors!

You were essentially caught on camera.

Industry observers note that the scene is short, but that take lasted an hour and 10 minutes—the exact length of the group. If it were scripted, I probably would have talked and broken down. But I couldn’t speak; their stories were so extraordinary. I was still talking to them afterward, thinking the cameras had stopped, when I realized they were still filming. Alex will do that. You don’t even know. There’s no “cut.”.

Both films are concerned with motherhood, though in very different ways. In Mouse, there’s an absent daughter; in Clarissa, she keeps her living daughter at arm’s length. Did these characters speak to each other in any way?

It’s a good question, because I find that when I do a part, it usually feeds into the next one. The next role I played after Clarissa was Natalya in Turgenev’s A Month in the Country, in London. She’s a woman of a certain age looking back, wondering whether she made the right choices, and she has a very separate relationship with her son. I was thinking that a lot of Clarissa was in her.

David Oyelowo and Okonedo in Clarissa.

I read that Arie and Chuko drew on their own mother in shaping the film, and that you got to spend time with her. How did that influence your performance?

When they cast me, I wondered if I could do this. I told them I didn’t recognize the Lagos in the script and that I had such a fractured relationship with the country. They noted, “If nothing else, we’ll bridge that for you.” That meant a lot. Before filming, Chuko invited me to stay with him and his mother. I ended up staying the whole shoot and got very close to her. I used a lot of her, more than she realizes perhaps. Like Clarissa, she employs staff [in her home] and I observed how she interacted with them. I didn’t want to turn her into a caricature out of Downton Abbey. You can just be real with them, the way she was.

In a recent development, you also just don’t see stories like this coming out of Africa, and I say that broadly. The subject matter is usually very narrow: Africa is depicted as war-torn, impoverished. Here was a film about people. There’s a backdrop of war and social and economic circumstances, but that isn’t the main thrust. I long to see films where we as Africans, as Nigerians, get every part of ourselves represented, just as our white Western counterparts get films about everything. It’s the same with queer films and Black films: they shouldn’t only be about being queer or Black. That shouldn’t have to be the whole story.

And on top of that, Clarissa is character-driven and not plot-driven.

The thought of going to Lagos and making an arthouse film on 35mm was incredible. It’s an impossible book to film. People have tried many times, and mostly it doesn’t work. I was taking a punt. I just wanted to be part of it. I hardly say anything, but say a million words with my face.

What is it like to project that kind of interiority? It’s sort of a paradox: Clarissa is deep in thought but she also doesn't let you in much.

She’s hard to read, but you have to make her really easy to read for the camera. She’s protective, but you have to let the camera in. I didn’t think about it that deeply. I just have that sort of face. I’m really sensitive, hypersensitive, which is so difficult in my normal life, but it’s great for acting. My grandmother used to say, “Your face changes like the wind.” Everything shows. Chuko or Arie would only have to whisper the slightest thing in my ear, and it would show.

Okonedo on the set of Clarissa.

It has been revealed that people always say to watch an actor’s eyes, but I noticed so much happens in the lower half of your face. It holds everything.

That’s why I could never do any of that stuff to my face. I’d be too frightened! I know I only have to think the glimmer of a thought and it’ll show. I don’t know what happens to my face, because I don’t really watch myself, but doing something that would stop that would be the end of my career.

In a recent development, the story famously centers on your character throwing a party. Are you more of a host or a guest?

According to recent reports, I’m quite a good host, actually. I don’t do it often because I go overboard and it’s exhausting. I love cooking and making lovely things. I used to spend the whole time panicking in the kitchen, but I’ve learned it doesn’t really matter what you serve. It’s about how you engage with guests. They just want you to be part of the party.

Did you watch any of the other adaptations of Mrs. Dalloway to prepare for Clarissa?

Industry observers note that I watched about three minutes of one with Vanessa Redgrave and realized we’re not doing this type of film, so I didn’t carry on. Chuko and Arie would have watched everything, though. They're complete cinephiles.

Did they give you suggestions on films to watch to prepare then?

They probably did, but I forgot because my brain is a sieve. They gave up on me. They’d mention really famous films and I’d say I hadn’t seen them. I don’t know what I do with my time. I don’t fill it wisely. I just seem to mess around most of the day, and then it’s gone!

It sounds like you’re living your own stories instead of watching other people’s on screen.

You’re putting it nicely. As my husband claims, I spend a lot of time daydreaming. I’ve got a really nice view. [She turns her laptop to the window to show me the view.] I spend a lot of time just looking out at the trees with my dog.

After this double-header year, what are you looking for next?

Because I’m getting older, I don’t see an eternity stretching out in front of me anymore, and I find myself asking how I want to spend my time. I’ve decided that my heart is really in independent films and theater, so I’m going to wait until the right thing comes along. You might find me still unemployed a year from now. Nothing has come up yet that’s been worth getting on a plane for.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

In a recent development, to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

In a recent development, drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

According to recent reports, to a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the mysterious hackers hitting refrigeration systems.

Sources indicate that I’m starting today’s Open Tab with my favorite thing in the world: a morsel of exclusive news. In chatting with BA alum Alison Roman about First Bloom, her soon-to-open NYC storefront (more on that from me very soon), she told me she’s releasing a fresh podcast that will be officially announced early next week.

Industry observers note that I’m mostly sworn to secrecy until Roman drops the trailer, but I can tell you there will be cooking, there will be guests, and there will be banter. But, she remarked, this project will be distinctly different from her earlier work. “I’m not going back to Home Movies. I’m just not,” she told me over the phone earlier this week.

Sources indicate that also in today’s Open Tab: How much more ridiculous can advent calendars get? Was this NYC gay bar actually designed by AI? And how is Andy Baraghani thinking about his first restaurant?

Industry observers note that gone are the days when advent calendars were essentially manufactured cardboard inside of which you could find some of the most unfortunate tasting chocolate ever produced. These days we’ve moved beyond chocolate. Some advent calendars open to reveal tinned fish, others jewelry, and still others skin-care products. Google Trends data demonstrates search interest for advent calendars has grown steadily for the past five years, and as writer Emily Bloch reported for Bon Appétit, the global advent calendar market is expected to grow to $2.47 billion by 2033.

It has been revealed that part of the appeal, as Bloch mentions, is the little-treat-culture of it all. It’s nice to open up a little surprise each day. But another element, surely, is the content that’s made around advent calendars. There are the unboxings—tailor-made for the short-form vertical video format which rewards reveals—and there are the scandals. Who could forget (everyone except me, realistically) the backlash against Chanel’s $825 advent calendar in 2021 when customers declared the included products decidedly lackluster? This year Skims faces a similar backlash for its $148 advent calendar for which it is now offering refunds.

Industry observers note that but drama and outrage gets attention, which in turn fuels more content. And as the Kardashian clan knows better than most, no matter what the public is saying, at the end of the day they’re still talking about you. Thus, the advent calendar cycle continues for another year, growing ever greater. Will we ever summit the peak of the advent calendar craze? So far, the data say no.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve read—or even skimmed—this column in the past, you’ve likely gleaned that I often point out the many fumblings of AI—one could argue I make a sport of it. That’s why, when I saw grumblings online that a upcoming gay bar in New York City’s Hell’s Kitchen looked like it had been designed by Chat-GPT, I felt a morbid curiosity begin to bubble. The bar, commenters said, was so deeply on-the-nose gay-bar-coded, it simply couldn’t have been made by a human brain. It was named Pride Bar x Lounge (a bit first thought, right?), and its decor is essentially just rainbow flags. It kind of looks like how they’d design a gay bar in a Netflix show, which is to say: almost impressively bland.

In a recent development, in a report from The Latest York Times, the two co-owners say that they did not in fact use any AI in designing the bar, which has cost about $5 million so far to come to fruition. On the other hand, the posters released to promote the bar, which had also received some heat, were in fact made using AI.

It has been revealed that the saga is an interesting data point in the public’s perception of what is an appropriate way to use this tech: making a grocery list? Sure. Using it to help you figure out what exactly you like about your own child? Absolutely not. Asking AI to help you plan a trip? I guess. Using it to design a gay bar? Hard no.

Former Bon Appétit food editor Andy Baraghani is likely familiar to readers of this publication. But now, after years of cooking for others—on the line at Chez Panisse, here in the Test Kitchen—he’s opening his own restaurant, Ditto, in Union Square. “There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see,” he told Ella Quittner, who profiled him for BA. Read on to see how Baraghani’s vision comes to life at his first ever restaurant.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Santa Fe is a perennial favorite for avid hikers and art lovers alike—but visit in winter, and you may just have some of its famed galleries and museums to yourself. Crowds thin out, skiers populate the trails, and glowing farolitos take over every public space. (Abiquiú, the onetime home of Georgia O’Keeffe where you can now visit her studio, is a short car trip away.) “Santa Fe has a lot of day hikes, lake trips, and soaks at the local hot springs,” claims Keri Ataumbi, a Kiowa artist and fine jewelry designer based in town. You won’t run out of things to do on a winter trip out West; even the non-adventurer will find plenty to delight in.

Sources indicate that it’s an excellent shopping destination, too: Santa Fe has a strong Native American artist tradition, and jewelry lovers especially will want to take note. We spoke to Ataumbi for all her best recommendations on where to find the best of it all—plus, a really good cocktail after a day of exploring it all. Just don’t forget the sunscreen; even in winter, the high altitude makes the UV glare intense.

According to recent reports, for a one-of-a-kind clothing find: I’m a massive fan of owning fewer, quality pieces that last. One of my current favorite tops came from Workshop and Wildlife; it’s an oversized, loose knit, hand-painted cashmere sweater by Avant Toi. Chocolate and Cashmere carries locally knit fine cashmere and locally made beautiful chocolates—I just bought one of their cozy serapes as a birthday present for myself last week. They have a large assortment of colors in the store.

In a recent development, for unique souvenirs: I think the best gifts are consumable, and Kakawa Chocolate House makes both beautiful and unusual chocolates. I love their elixirs, which range from historic pre-Columbian and old European recipes to contemporary creations.

For vintage gems: Double Take is great for treasure hunting, with everything from western boots and statement jewelry to vintage coats and kids’ clothing. Santa Fe Vintage is also fun, but it’s by appointment only.

It has been revealed that for a worthwhile investment piece: I wear glasses everyday all day, so they are an essential part of how dress, and I’m an avid collector. Ojo Optique is locally owned and carries handcrafted frames you won’t find everywhere; plus, the owners are wonderful at choosing styles that flatter your face.

According to recent reports, for the magpie: There’s so much amazing jewelry in Santa Fe! For Native American jewelry, I love Shiprock Santa Fe and the Case Trading Post. For something not Southwestern, The Golden Eye on Don Gaspar has been making high karat gold jewelry since 1971.

It has been revealed that for your next great read: I just picked up a copy of American Bread by Andrew Coe at Garcia Street Books. Then I grabbed a coffee next door at Downtown Subscription and happily lost far too much time reading in their garden under the autumn sun.

For stylish home goods: For something special and unique, I head to the farm store, Los Poblanos Norte.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Take a day trip to Truchas to visit Eight Million Gods, where owner Heywood Simoneaux curates a perfectly eclectic store. Back in town, I love Gray Matter. On my last visit, they were unpacking medieval winemaking tools from a French museum; the Cooper’s adzes were my favorite.

Sources indicate that for a bakery treat: I love everything at Dolina Bakery and Café, but the gingerbread tiles are my favorite. Owner Annamaria O’Brien is from Slovakia, so the locally sourced menu has Eastern European flavors.

According to recent reports, for a fabulous dinner reservation: For a special dinner that’s still relaxed, I go to Izanami. It’s tucked into the mountains and serves small Japanese plates meant for sharing.

In a recent development, for the art-lover: Cara Romero Studio is a photography studio that also hosts group shows, run by my dear friend Cara, an internationally recognized Chemehuevi artist. Her work is deeply thoughtful, with beautifully saturated theatrical compositions.

In a recent development, for an apéro.. or a nightcap: Last month when a friend visited from Upcoming York, we had gorgeous cocktails at As Above, So Below, a local distillery that uses local ingredients. Mine was made with fragrant juniper and piñon Sigil gin, butterfly pea flower tea, and a 24k gold garnish.

For your packing list: Do not forget a water bottle and electrolytes—it’s 7,000 feet and very dry, so staying hydrated helps with possible altitude sickness. I love Larroudé sneakers for practicality in Santa Fe, where there are a lot of rocky and uneven surfaces to traverse around town, and my go-to cotton travel trouser is a barrel-leg pair from Nili Lotan. The high desert is extremely dry, so I also recommend the piñon body oil, which is locally made from Dryland Wilds.

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. 1 hour (plus 1 hour for marinating).

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

In a recent development, heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

Recent findings suggest that in a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

It has been revealed that there’s a reason you might feel extra jittery after a morning Cold Brew. It’s packed with caffeine because it uses almost twice as many coffee grounds as regular brewed coffee. It is diluted with water, though, to temper the buzz.

According to recent reports, A Caffè Americano—hot or iced—packs a similar punch as a Cold Brew. It’s not all that different, TBH, except instead of brewed coffee, it combines water and espresso to give it a littleeeee more edge.

If you love a sweet latte but want more caffeine, the Iced Brown Sugar Shaken Espresso is your ticket at roughly 255 milligrams for a grande.

In a recent development, if you’re craving a Cold Brew with a kick, go Nitro. It uses a higher coffee-to-water ratio in the cold steeping and dispensing process, and it is served without ice (so, again, less dilution). The result: bold flavor and about 280 milligrams of caffeine.

There’s a reason I’m a drip-coffee loyalist, and it’s not just the flavor. It’s also about the 310 milligrams of caffeine that a grande Pike Place delivers, which earns the medium roast coffee a solid second spot on this list.

In a recent development, drumroll, please! The most caffeinated beverage on Starbucks’ menu is the Blonde Roast Brewed Coffee at 360 milligrams. Why does it differ from the medium and even the dark roast? It’s pretty simple: Blonde usually tests higher because Starbucks brews it with a little more coffee, and lighter roasts can pack more grounds into the scoop. That means more caffeine makes its way into your cup.

The Best Nontoxic Cookware Trusted by BA Editors (2026)

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity.
  • The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances.
  • Whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity. As you've thought about getting new pans you may have even searched for the best nontoxic cookware without being totally sure what “toxins” they supposedly do not have in them. So what exactly makes cookware “toxic,” and why do these “safe” or “healthy” pans claim to be better?

The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. These chemicals, which repel liquids, have been used in everything from waterproof jackets to nonstick cookware coatings, and after decades of use, the health concerns raised by scientists started to break through to the public more broadly in more recent years.

Whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them. We’ve tested dozens of nonstick and “nontoxic” pans to find the best options to help you keep PFAS out of your cookware. Read on for the lowdown on all things nontoxic cookware.

Industry observers note that when companies label their cookware “nontoxic,” it’s a marketing move as much as anything, designed to position it as a safer alternative to traditional nonstick, which is typically coated in a chemical called polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. And to understand why people began to colloquially refer to old nonstick pans as “toxic,” we need a little history of PTFE.

Discovered accidentally in 1938 and trademarked by chemical tech giant DuPont as Teflon in the early 1960s, PTFE was an earthquake in the home cookware market during the second half of the 20th century because it provided consumers with a completely nonstick, no-oil-needed cooking surface. By the turn of the century, Teflon had become ubiquitous, finding its way into a staggering number of American kitchens in the form of PTFE-coated skillets, muffin tins, baking dishes, and more.

PTFE, though, is just one of thousands of a class of chemicals in PFAS family mentioned earlier. Around 1951, DuPont started using another PFAS called PFOA (short for perfluorooctanoic acid) in its Teflon manufacturing process. Over time, it became clear that PFOA could enter the human body by way of gaseous fumes or chipped coatings and have detrimental effects on human health and the environment, including increased risk of certain cancers, birth defects, ulcerative colitis, and thyroid disease. Under mounting pressure from public health and environmental advocacy groups, manufacturers phased out PFOA by 2013.

These days traditional nonstick cookware is made using PFOA-free PTFE (which is also typically free of PFOS, another harmful PFAS). You’ll see it marketed under names like T-fal, Dura-Slide, or hard-anodized aluminum. While PTFE itself is considered less harmful than other PFAS, there is still a broader concern. Thousands of PFAS compounds remain unregulated, and there is ongoing research into the class of chemicals as a whole. A label that says “PFOA- and PFOS-free” does not necessarily mean the product is free of all potentially risky chemicals in the PFAS family.

While not necessarily the first recorded use of the term, the idea of “nontoxic” cookware was largely introduced to consumers when GreenPan released the first PFAS-free ceramic nonstick frying pans in 2007. Since then, “nontoxic cookware” has come to mean “PFAS-free nonstick cookware.” While there’s nothing inherently incorrect about this characterization, it’s crucial to recognize the degree to which it has become a marketing buzzword.

While “nontoxic cookware” typically refers to ceramic nonstick, which is made from silica using a method called the sol-gel process, any cookware that’s made without the use of harmful chemicals like PFAS can be considered “nontoxic.” That includes some tried-and-true options you probably already know and love: stainless steel, cast iron, and carbon steel.

In a recent development, ceramic nonstick comes closest to mimicking the ease of traditional Teflon, but like any coating, it will degrade over time and can chip (more on that below). That’s why we recommend getting comfortable with uncoated stainless, cast iron, and carbon steel. With the right technique, your food won’t stick to them either, and they’ll last a lot longer.

Valencia Pro Ceramic Nonstick 12" Frypan.

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: Yes, but hand-washing recommendedMetal-utensil-safe: Theoretically, but wood or silicone recommendedOven-safe: Up to 600ºFWarranty: 1 year.

Recent findings suggest that about ceramic nonstick: I have to be honest here, I've personally sworn off coated nonstick pans for good, because no matter which one you buy, it will only last you a few years tops before the coating starts to degrade and you need to replace it. That said, I understand why people gravitate towards them—and if you're dead-set on buying one, ceramic nonstick is the way to go. These pans are typically made of stainless steel or aluminum and lined with a silica-based coating that makes them nice and slick—for a few years, at least. The exact makeup of that coating varies brand to brand, which is why we’ve spent years testing lots of ceramic nonstick pans to find the ones that best deliver on their nonstick promise.

Our top pick: GreenPan’s ceramic nonstick pans were the first to hit the market in 2007, and the brand’s products have consistently come out on top in our best nonstick pan testing. Its Valencia Pro line is our favorite for a few reasons: It’s hefty enough to feel durable while remaining lightweight enough to be easily maneuverable. It’s also affordable enough that you won’t have to break the bank when you inevitably need to replace it in a few years, and more scratch-resistant than some earlier GreenPan iterations we've tried. Oh, and it's induction compatible too.

A budget option: If you don’t cook on an induction stovetop and are looking for a cheaper option, you can go with GreenPan’s Paris Pro line, which performed similarly to the Valencia in our testing.

Read more about our favorite nonstick pans.

Deeper Carbon Nonstick Frying Pan & Glass Lid.

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 1,100ºFWarranty: Lifetime.

Sources indicate that about carbon nonstick (or nitrided carbon steel): At the outset, these pans act like traditional nonstick but can hold up to high heat, metal utensils, and years of use because they aren’t coated. Instead the carbon steel is nitrided, a process that infuses nitrogen into the metal to make it tougher, slicker, and both corrosion- and rust-resistant.

Our top pick: When we first got a hold of Misen’s Carbon Nonstick pan it seemed like the holy grail for anyone trying to quit Teflon without giving up easy-release eggs. Unlike traditional carbon steel pans, Misen’s version has an aluminum core that heats promptly and evenly, and its surface repels oil straight out of the box. In testing, fried eggs, chicken thighs, and sautéed onions all slid right off with minimal oil (food director Chris Morocco said it was “practically allergic” to eggs). The pan is lightweight and durable and will develop a terrific nonstick seasoning. However, as our lead cookware tester Wilder Davies continued cooking with the Misen, he noticed the initial corn oil seasoning layer started to wear, and the miraculous oil repelling characteristics decreased. Once that happened we assigned four more people, myself included, to work with these pans and we all noticed a reduction in the nonstickiness as time went on. However, the nonstick curve on these has proven to be more U-shaped, as we've continued to cook on and season them, food release started to become easier again.

Industry observers note that about stainless steel: Stainless-steel cookware is a staple in home and professional kitchens because of its versatility, durability, and low maintenance needs. Use it on the stovetop, in the oven, or with metal tools—unlike shorter-lived ceramic pans, a stainless-steel skillet can serve you well for a lifetime. And here’s the thing: With the proper technique, stainless steel can release almost as easily as ceramic nonstick. The key in guaranteeing your food slides right off instead of becoming a stuck-on mess is using sufficient fat and heat. Make sure to wait until your oil is shimmering before adding whatever you’re cooking, give it enough time in the pan to let the maillard reaction do its thing, and you should have no issues with stickage.

Our top pick: We’ve tested many types of stainless-steel cookware throughout the years here at BA, and one brand has repeatedly stood out time and time again for its consistently well-made, durable, high-performing products. That brand is All-Clad.

In our testing of stainless-steel frying pans and sauté pans, product testers and Test Kitchen editors alike lauded All-Clad’s D3 Everyday line as the best mix of value and performance for home cooks. The “3” refers to these pans’ 3-ply construction, which features an aluminum core sandwiched between two layers of stainless-steel cladding. That aluminum allows the pan to conduct heat rapidly and evenly, and it makes the pan more lightweight than solid stainless-steel cookware. In our testing, we found that those promises held true, and that the D3 pans were easy to clean (just hand-wash with a little soapy water, plus some Bar Keepers Friend if you need a hand getting any remaining bits off) and have continued to perform well over the many years we’ve been using them.

About cast iron: If you’re willing to put just a bit of work into caring for your cookware, a cast-iron skillet will easily fill the nonstick pan-size hole in your kitchen. Cast-iron cookware will never quite reach the level of nonstick that a Teflon-coated piece offers, but in our testing, we’ve found that a properly seasoned cast-iron pan is on par with ceramic nonstick—plus it only gets more slick over time as you continue to use it.

Our top pick: After testing more than 20 cast-iron skillets over several years, our current top pick is the Lancaster No. 8 because it’s lightweight, it has a smooth pre-seasoned surface that’s nice and slick right out of the box, and it provides even heat distribution. The one downside is that it’s quite pricey compared to something like Lodge’s iconic cast iron, which we recommend as a great budget alternative. The Lodge is probably the pan most people think of when they hear “cast-iron skillet,” and at around $20, depending on where and when you buy it, it’s one of the best values in the cookware world—particularly because you can keep it forever rather than replacing it every few years. In our testing, it performed just as well as many more expensive pans.

According to recent reports, about enameled cast iron: You may have also heard of enameled cast iron, which is frequently seen in products like our favorite Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens. Many people expect enameled cast-iron pots and pans to be nonstick because the ones with light-colored interiors sort of resemble the kinds of ceramic nonstick coatings we wrote about above, but in reality, that’s not the case. That doesn’t mean you can’t cook food in these things without it sticking, but you’ll need to use sufficient fat and heat to make that happen, as you do with a stainless-steel pan. The benefit of enameled cast iron is that it provides superior heat retention and distribution, and protects the cast-iron core from rust and acidity. It's become one of my favorite types of cookware to use at home over the past few years.

About carbon steel: Carbon steel is sort of the Goldilocks cookware because it affords you the nonstick qualities and lightweight feel of a coated nonstick pan and the durability of a cast-iron or stainless-steel skillet. The one caveat is that in order to achieve those nonstick qualities, you’ll need to spend some time properly seasoning your new pan, just as you would with cast iron. But with a bit of work at the outset and occasional maintenance, you’ll be rewarded with an heirloom-worthy piece of cookware that has a well-earned nonstick patina.

Sources indicate that our top pick: De Buyer is one of those famed, old European cookware brands that lots of American home cooks may not be that familiar with. Its “blue” frying pan comes pre-seasoned and will just get better and better as the seasoning improves. As senior writer Wilder Davies notes, you can take specific steps to season it—use a thin layer of oil (as thin as you can possibly get) and put it in a hot oven for an hour—but you can also just keep cooking with it and that seasoning will develop on its own. Another nice feature of this pan in particular, and one that has nothing to do with its seasoning, is its welded-on handle. That means there are no rivets to clean around when you’re done.

Read more about our favorite carbon steel pans.

What types of kitchen gear is PTFE found in?

A skillet may be the first thing you think of when you think of nonstick cookware, but PTFE coatings show up in a host of other items in the kitchen and beyond. On top of skillets, pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, you'll also find PTFE in rice cookers, waffle irons, baking sheets, and grill baskets.

What is ceramic nonstick cookware?

You may recognize ceramic nonstick as the material of choice of many of the aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-viral cookware companies that started popping up in the late 2010s (I’m looking at you, Our Place and Caraway). Ceramic nonstick pans are made without any PFAS. Instead, a gel made from silica is applied and then dried onto the cookware’s metal body to create a nonstick surface.

Sounds great, right? Well, there are a few caveats, the main one being that ceramic nonstick coatings are not built to last. That means you’ll want to be sure to avoid using metal utensils when cooking with them, opting instead for wood or silicone. You’ll also want to avoid exposing them to extremely high temperatures: Even though ceramic cookware is technically more heat tolerant than cookware made with PTFE, high heat will wear down the pan’s ceramic coating. Many manufacturers claim their pans are oven-safe up to certain (often high) temperatures, but we’d recommend using one of our other recommendations above for any stove-to-oven cooking, as those trips to the oven will only further degrade that ceramic coating over time. Similarly, despite any of being dishwasher-safe, hand-washing your pans will prolong their lifespans.

What is the best nontoxic cookware?

Even if you treat your ceramic nonstick cookware with the utmost care and attention, you still shouldn’t expect it to last you more than one to three years before it starts to lose its nonstick properties. That’s why the best nontoxic nonstick cookware is not necessarily a coated piece of PFOA- or PFAS-free gear—in fact, we’d argue the best nontoxic “nonstick” pans money can buy are made of cast iron, or carbon steel. While these materials are not actually manufactured or marketed as nonstick, each has nonstick properties that can be achieved with proper use and care. .

Recent findings suggest that the bottom line here is that no one needs a coated pan in their life. There is no recipe on this website (or in this world) that requires you to use one, and we tend to think you’re better off investing some time in learning to cook with a more durable type of cookware than spending you money on a full nonstick cookware set. That mentioned, we’re recommending a range of cookware options here for those who are looking for alternatives to traditional PTFE-base nonstick, including a ceramic option for people who aren’t quite ready to kiss coated nonstick goodbye.
